docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 14 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Rasāyana: Chemistry and Metallurgy. It surveys the history of chemical and metallurgical knowledge in the Indian subcontinent. It opens with the sources and methods of the subject and with the alchemical and iatrochemical literature of rasaśāstra, which grew up from about the end of the first millennium CE, heard where possible in its own words. It then turns to the mines from which the metals came and the archaeometallurgical methods by which their remains are studied, before following the metals themselves: the iron of the Delhi pillar and of the village smelters, the crucible steel known in Europe as “wootz”, the distillation of zinc at Zawar, and the precious and base metals, with the assay and refining of the Delhi and Mughal mints. Later chapters treat calcined metal medicines (bhasma) as history and as a problem of toxicology; gems; dyes and pigments; glass, ceramics and building materials; the salts, alkalis and acids—common salt, saltpetre, alum, sal ammoniac, borax—that were the everyday reagents of the crafts, together with sugar; and the Islamic alchemy (kīmiyā) of the Persianate courts, its meeting with rasaśāstra, and the history of distillation, from arrack to attar. A last chapter considers the legacy of the tradition.

The volume is an edited and corrected version of an earlier draft. In revision, verses that could not be verified as genuine, with a correct reference, were removed rather than repaired; the short passages from the Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdayatantra and the Rasaratnasamuccaya now quoted in Chapters 2 and 3 were checked against the electronic texts of printed editions named in the bibliography. Invented “studies” and unsourced modern measurements were deleted; dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship (with traditional dates labelled as such); and claims that ancient India was “first” in this or that field were checked against the archaeological and historical literature and corrected or removed. Where the classical texts make claims about rejuvenation, transmutation or cures, these are reported as what the texts say, not as established facts.

Two cautions apply throughout. First, this is a book of history. It describes what the rasa texts say about the processing of mercury, lead, arsenic, copper and other metals and minerals, but it deliberately gives no doses, proportions, durations or working recipes. Products made by these methods have repeatedly been found to contain toxic quantities of lead, mercury and arsenic, and they have caused serious poisoning; the evidence, including studies that defend these products, is set out in Chapter 9. Nothing in this volume is medical advice. Second, the dating of many Sanskrit technical texts is uncertain, and the attribution of alchemical works to famous names (Nāgārjuna above all) is a matter of tradition rather than history.

The work of P. C. Ray, David Gordon White, G. J. Meulenbeld and Dominik Wujastyk on the rasa literature, of R. Balasubramaniam on the Delhi pillar, of Sharada Srinivasan and S. Ranganathan on wootz, and of Paul Craddock and his colleagues on Zawar has been drawn on throughout and is listed in the select bibliography, together with a glossary, a chronology and a guide to further reading. Every quotation and every technical claim should be checked against the editions and studies cited before scholarly use.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Transliteration and Citation
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST): long vowels carry a macron (ā, ī, ū), retroflex consonants a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ), and ś is the palatal sibilant, so that rasaśāstra is pronounced roughly “ra-sa-shaas-tra”. Tamil words follow the system of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras (kammāḷar, centūram, Murukaṉ). Arabic and Persian words are transliterated with macrons for long vowels, a dot below for the emphatic consonants (ḥ, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ), ʿ for the letter ʿayn and ʾ for hamza (Āʾīn-i Akbarī, Abuʾl Faẓl, ʿaraq). Hindi and other modern Indian words are given in a simple form of the same system (phiṭkarī, nausādar). Words that have entered English (Mughal, Sufi, attar, ikat, Bidri), modern place names and the names of modern authors are spelt in their usual form, without diacritics.

The rasa texts are cited by chapter and verse. The Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdayatantra and the Rasaratnasamuccaya are quoted from the electronic texts of the Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages (GRETIL), each based on a printed edition named in the bibliography; verse numbers in other editions may differ slightly. The Āʾīn-i Akbarī is cited by the numbered āʾīns of Book 1 in Blochmann’s translation, and the Arthaśāstra by book and chapter in Kangle’s numbering, as translated by Olivelle.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Chemistry and Metallurgy in Indian History
docs.text:
raso vai saḥ. rasaṃ hy evāyaṃ labdhvānandī bhavati. “That, truly, is essence (rasa); having obtained the essence one becomes blissful.”

— Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7

docs.title: 1.1 Words and Scope
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word rasa has a wide range of meanings: sap or juice, the liquid essence of a thing, taste, the first bodily tissue produced from digested food, aesthetic emotion in poetics, and—in the alchemical literature that is one of the subjects of this book—mercury. Rasāyana is usually analysed as rasa + ayana, “the path (or abode) of rasa”. In classical Āyurveda it is the name of one of the eight branches of medicine (aṣṭāṅga āyurveda): rejuvenation therapy, intended to restore vigour and prolong life, and in the early compendia it is overwhelmingly a matter of herbal and dietary regimens (Wujastyk 2003; Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

From about the end of the first millennium CE a new body of Sanskrit literature appears whose central substance is mercury and whose subject is the transformation of metals and of the human body by means of processed mercury, sulphur, metals and minerals. Its authors called it rasaśāstra, rasavidyā or rasatantra, “the science (or teaching) of mercury”; historians call it Indian alchemy and, in its medical aspect, iatrochemistry (Ray 1956; White 1996). In modern Indian languages rasāyana (Hindi rasāyan) has come to mean simply “chemistry”.

This volume uses the word in its broadest, modern sense. It is a history of chemical and metallurgical knowledge in the Indian subcontinent, from the copper and faience of the Harappan cities to the crucible steel and distilled zinc of the medieval period, and from the alchemical laboratories of the rasa texts to the dyer’s vat and the glass-bead workshop. Much of this knowledge was never written down: it lived in the hands of smiths, potters, dyers and miners, and is known to us through archaeology, the observations of travellers and colonial officials, and modern laboratory analysis. Part of it was written down, in Sanskrit treatises on statecraft, medicine, gems and alchemy. The two kinds of evidence do not always meet, and one aim of this book is to keep them distinct.

Three Kinds of “Rasāyana”

  • Rasāyana in Āyurveda: rejuvenation therapy, one of the eight branches of classical medicine, mainly herbal.

  • Rasaśāstra: the medieval literature on mercury, metals and minerals, with two declared aims—the transmutation of metals (dhātuvāda or lohavāda) and the perfection or immortality of the body (dehavāda)—and a growing third, medicinal one.

  • Chemistry and metallurgy: the practical knowledge of ores, metals, alloys, glasses, pigments and dyes, most of it held by craft communities rather than by Sanskrit authors.

Health and Safety Note

Several chapters of this volume describe what the rasa texts say about processing mercury, lead, arsenic, copper and other toxic metals and minerals. They are described as part of the history of chemistry. The book deliberately gives no doses, proportions, durations or working procedures, and nothing in it is medical advice. Independent laboratory studies have repeatedly found lead, mercury and arsenic in Ayurvedic products sold in India and abroad: about one in five of the products tested by Saper and colleagues contained detectable levels, and products of the rasaśāstra type were the most likely to contain them (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). Serious poisoning from such products is documented (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004; Kales and Saper 2009). The texts hold that “purification” (śodhana) and calcination (māraṇa) make these substances safe. Toxicology has not confirmed that view; the studies on both sides are reviewed in Chapter 9. This note applies to every chapter of the book, and the shorter notes in later chapters refer back to it.

docs.title: 1.2 An Outline Chronology
docs.text:
The chronology of Indian chemical and metallurgical history rests on two very different kinds of dating. Archaeological sites are dated, with varying precision, by radiocarbon and other scientific methods; Sanskrit technical texts are dated mainly by cross-references and quotations, and many dates are uncertain by a century or more. Table 1.1 gives an outline; a fuller chronology appears at the end of the volume.

Table 1.1. Outline Chronology of Chemistry and Metallurgy in South Asia Period Developments c. 2600–1900 BCE Mature Harappan civilisation: copper and tin bronze, lost-wax casting, gold and silver work, faience, stoneware bangles, etched carnelian beads c. 1500–500 BCE Vedic texts name gold, ayas (metal, later iron), lead and tin; iron in the Ganga plain and the Deccan from the late 2nd millennium BCE (earlier dates claimed and debated) c. 600 BCE–300 CE Punch-marked silver coinage; Northern Black Polished Ware; crucible steel in south India; Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) on mines, metals and the mint c. 300–700 CE Gupta gold coinage; the iron pillar now at Delhi (c. 400 CE); gem chapters of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā c. 900–1300 CE Zinc distillation at Zawar (earliest retorts c. 9th–10th century); early rasa texts (Rasahṛdayatantra, Rasārṇava); Chola bronzes c. 1300–1700 CE Rasaratnasamuccaya and later compendia; large-scale zinc production; Golconda diamonds; export of Indian cottons, dyes and steel c. 1700–1900 CE European study of wootz and Indian dyeing; decline of traditional iron, steel and indigo industries under colonial rule and industrial competition

docs.title: 1.3 Metals in the Vedic Texts
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (core c. 1500–1200 BCE) knows gold (hiraṇya) and a metal called ayas. Since the Ṛgveda predates the general use of iron in north India, ayas there is usually understood as copper or bronze; the word later comes to mean iron (Chakrabarti 1992). Gold is everywhere in the hymns as ornament and as an image of brilliance; the cosmogonic hymn Ṛgveda 10.121 opens with the “golden embryo”:

Ṛgveda 10.121.1

hiraṇyagarbhaḥ sam avartatāgre bhūtasya jātaḥ patir eka āsīt In the beginning the Golden Embryo arose; once born, he was the one lord of all that exists.

The hymn is cosmology, not metallurgy, but it shows the symbolic weight that gold already carried. In the later Vedic texts (c. 1200–500 BCE) the vocabulary of metals grows. A list of substances in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (18.13) names, after stone, clay, hills, sand and plants, hiraṇya (gold), ayas, śyāma (“the dark one”, usually taken as iron), loha (“the red one”, usually taken as copper), sīsa (lead) and trapu (tin). Later Vedic texts, beginning with the Atharvaveda, distinguish a “dark” metal (śyāma ayas, later also kṛṣṇāyas, “black metal”) from a “red” one (lohita), most naturally iron and copper. These identifications are inferences from usage and from archaeology, not definitions given in the texts, and some remain debated.

docs.title: 1.4 The Arthaśāstra: Mines, Metals and the Mint
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra, the Sanskrit treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya), minister of Candragupta Maurya (c. 300 BCE), is in its present form a composite work compiled between about 50 BCE and 300 CE (Olivelle 2013). Its second book, on the duties of superintendents, contains the fullest early account of the state’s interest in minerals and metals. A superintendent of mines (ākarādhyakṣa) must know the science of ores and the techniques of smelting, and recognises ores by their colour, weight, smell and taste (Arthaśāstra 2.12). Beside him stand a superintendent of metals (lohādhyakṣa), who runs workshops for copper, lead, tin, iron, brass, bronze and other metals, and a superintendent of the mint (lakṣaṇādhyakṣa), who issues silver and copper coins of fixed composition and is checked by an examiner of coins (rūpadarśaka). The chapters on the state goldsmith describe the examination of gold and silver by touchstone, colour and fire (2.13–14), and list at length the ways in which artisans may cheat by alloying or substitution; gems, pearls and other precious goods are to be examined before they are received into the treasury (2.11).

The treatise also sets out punishments for debasing coin and for fraud by goldsmiths. Its interest is fiscal and administrative: mines and metal workshops are sources of revenue to be controlled, and its technical content is a series of lists rather than a description of processes. It is nonetheless good evidence that by the early centuries CE the state recognised mining, smelting, alloying, assaying and coinage as distinct specialisms (Olivelle 2013; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

docs.title: 1.5 Weights, Measures and Assay
docs.text:
Quantitative work with materials depends on reliable weights. The Harappans used a remarkably uniform system of cubical weights, usually of chert, found across the whole area of the civilisation. The smaller weights double in a binary series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 units), and the larger ones follow a decimal pattern; the most commonly found weight is about 13.7 g (Kenoyer 1998). Such weights would have served for trade in precious materials such as beads, metals and spices.

The Arthaśāstra has a superintendent of standards of weights and measures, who is to have balances and weights made of iron or of stone from particular regions and to inspect those used in the market; it gives tables of units, from the māṣa and suvarṇa upwards, used for gold, silver and other goods (Olivelle 2013). The goldsmith’s touchstone and the assayer’s balance, together with fixed weight standards, allowed the state and merchants to check the fineness and weight of coin and bullion. Later Indian systems of weights, with units such as the ratti (the seed of Abrus precatorius), māśā and tolā, continued in use in jewellery and medicine into modern times.

docs.title: 1.6 Chemical Knowledge in the Medical Compendia
docs.text: Long before the rasa literature, the classical medical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta (Caraka’s redaction c. 100 BCE–200 CE; the Suśruta-saṃhitā in its present form by c. 500 CE) and the later synthesis of Vāgbhaṭa (c. 600 CE) recorded a considerable amount of practical chemistry, embedded in pharmacy and surgery (Wujastyk 2003; Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Both compendia are available in standard Sanskrit editions and in English translation (Trikamji Acharya 1941; Sharma 1981–1994; Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938; Bhishagratna 1907–1916).

docs.title: 1.6.1 Alkalis
docs.text: The Suśrutasaṃhitā devotes a chapter of its first book (Sūtrasthāna 11) to caustic alkali (kṣāra), which it ranks above surgical instruments for some purposes because it can cut, cauterise and scrape. The alkali is made from the ashes of particular plants, leached with water and concentrated by boiling, and a milder form for internal use is distinguished from a stronger, caustic form for external application (Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938; Bhishagratna 1907–1916). It is one of the clearest descriptions of a deliberate chemical preparation in ancient Indian literature; its chemistry is discussed in Section 13.2.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Salts
docs.text: The compendia classify salts (lavaṇa) into several kinds, commonly five: rock salt (saindhava, “from Sindh”), sauvarcala, viḍa, sea salt (sāmudra) and salt obtained from saline earth (audbhida). Some of these were prepared by heating common salt with other materials, and modern authors have tried to identify them with particular mixtures of sodium chloride with sulphides, carbonates or other salts; the identifications are uncertain. Other mineral substances used in the compendia include alum, red ochre, collyrium (añjana), orpiment and realgar (for external use), and iron and other metals.

docs.title: 1.6.3 Fermentation
docs.text: The compendia describe many fermented medicinal liquors (āsava and ariṣṭa), made by allowing decoctions or juices with sugar or honey to ferment, often with the flowers of dhātakī (Woodfordia fruticosa), which are generally thought to have supplied the yeasts that start the fermentation. The Arthaśāstra similarly lists the kinds of liquor (medaka, prasannā, āsava, ariṣṭa, maireya and others) whose production was supervised by the state (Olivelle 2013). Fermentation, the oldest of the chemical arts, was thus thoroughly familiar to Indian physicians and administrators.

docs.title: 1.6.4 Metals in Early Medicine
docs.text: Caraka and Suśruta prescribe iron, and to a lesser extent gold, silver, copper, tin and lead, usually in the form of thin leaves heated and quenched in plant decoctions, ground to powder, or used to prepare medicated waters, and they use some minerals externally. Mercury plays almost no part. The great expansion of metallic and mineral medicine, and the internal use of mercury, belong to the rasa literature of the following centuries (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 1.7 Philosophical Frameworks
docs.text: Indian thinkers did not develop a theory of chemical composition in the modern sense, but several philosophical schools offered frameworks within which material change could be discussed.

docs.title: 1.7.1 The Five Elements
docs.text: Most Indian schools accepted that the material world is made of five “great elements” (pañcamahābhūta): earth, water, fire, air and ether (ākāśa). Āyurveda used this scheme to explain the qualities of foods and drugs, and the rasa texts often describe metals and minerals in its terms. The scheme is classificatory; it does not predict what will happen when two substances are heated together.

docs.title: 1.7.2 Vaiśeṣika Atomism
docs.text:
The Vaiśeṣika school, whose foundational Vaiśeṣikasūtra (attributed to Kaṇāda) is usually dated between the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE, held that earth, water, fire and air are composed of eternal, partless atoms (paramāṇu); ether is not atomic. Two atoms form a dyad (dvyaṇuka), which is still imperceptible; three dyads form a triad (tryaṇuka), the smallest perceptible unit. The qualities of compound substances derive from those of their atoms.

Pīlupāka and Piṭharapāka

A famous debate concerned what happens when a clay pot is baked and turns red. The Vaiśeṣikas (from Praśastapāda, c. 6th century CE, onwards) held the pīlupāka (“atom-baking”) view: heat breaks the pot down to its atoms, changes their colour, and the pot is re-formed, all in an imperceptibly short time. The Naiyāyikas held the piṭharapāka (“pot-baking”) view: heat penetrates the whole pot, which changes colour without being destroyed. The debate is a genuine attempt to explain a physical change in atomic terms; it is not, however, a theory of chemical reaction, and neither side proposed experiments to settle it.

docs.title: 1.7.3 Alchemical Correspondences
docs.text: The rasa texts have their own framework, drawn from Tantric Śaivism. Mercury is the seed (semen) of Śiva and sulphur the uterine blood of the Goddess; their union in the laboratory reproduces divine union. The texts assume that a mercury capable of transmuting base metal into gold will, taken into the body, make the body imperishable (White 1996). The Rasaratnasamuccaya builds the assumption into one of the names of mercury: it is called sūta because “it brings forth (sūte) perfection in body and in metal” (dehalohamayīṃ siddhiṃ sūte, 1.78; Chapter 3) (GRETIL 2020). This analogical reasoning, not atomism, is what governed alchemical practice.

docs.title: 1.8 Who Knew What: Craft Knowledge and Textual Knowledge
docs.text:
Most of the achievements discussed in this volume—the Delhi pillar, wootz steel, Zawar zinc, Chola bronzes, Indian dyeing—were the work of hereditary craft communities: smiths (lohār, karmakāra), the five-craft Viśvakarma communities of the south (Tamil kammāḷar, Kannada pāñcāḷa), bronze-casters (sthapati), dyers and printers (rangrez, chhīpā), potters, bead-makers, miners, and forest communities such as the Agaria who smelted iron (Mukherjee 1978; Elwin 1942). Their knowledge was passed on orally and by apprenticeship within families and caste groups.

In the hierarchy of the Brahmanical law books, manual crafts ranked low, and some of the groups who smelted iron or tanned leather were treated as untouchable. Sanskrit authors wrote about metals mainly as administrators (Arthaśāstra), physicians (Āyurveda), connoisseurs (the gem treatises) and alchemists (rasaśāstra). Their texts preserve names, classifications and some processes, but rarely the practical details of a working furnace. The historian therefore has to read texts, archaeology and ethnography together, while keeping in mind that the people who made the steel and the people who wrote the books were seldom the same.

docs.title: 1.9 Classifying Substances in the Rasa Texts
docs.text:
The rasa texts developed elaborate classifications of metals and minerals. They differ from text to text; the most influential scheme is that of the Rasaratnasamuccaya (late 13th or 14th century), which places mercury (rasa, pārada) in a class of its own and groups other substances as in Table 1.2: eight mahārasas, eight uparasas, eight sādhāraṇa rasas, the gems and the metals.

Table 1.2. The Mineral Classes of the Rasaratnasamuccaya (with Usual Modern Identifications) Class Members (usual identification; “?” = uncertain) Mahārasa abhraka (mica), vaikrānta (?), mākṣika (copper/iron pyrites), vimala (pyrite variety?), śilājatu (shilajit), sasyaka (blue vitriol), capala (?), rasaka (calamine, a zinc ore) Uparasa gandhaka (sulphur), gairika (red ochre), kāsīsa (green vitriol), kāṅkṣī (alum), haritāla (orpiment), manaḥśilā (realgar), añjana (stibnite or galena), kaṅkuṣṭha (?) Sādhāraṇa rasa kampillaka (powder of Mallotus fruit), gaurīpāṣāṇa (white arsenic?), navasādara (sal ammoniac), kapardikā (cowrie shell), agnijāra (?), girisindūra (?), hiṅgula (cinnabar), mṛddāraśṛṅga (litharge) Ratna diamond, ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, yellow sapphire (or topaz), blue sapphire, hessonite (gomeda), cat’s eye (vaidūrya) Loha gold, silver, copper, iron (in several grades), tin, lead; alloys such as brass and bronze; zinc in some texts

Several of these identifications are uncertain, and the same Sanskrit name may denote different substances in different texts and regions. Many members of the lists—orpiment, realgar, white arsenic, cinnabar, litharge, lead and the copper salts—are highly toxic. The texts also describe in detail the laboratory (rasaśālā) in which such substances were to be processed, with its shrine, furnaces, heating pits and apparatus; these are discussed in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 1.10 Nāgārjuna and the Attribution of Alchemical Works
docs.text:
No name is more often attached to Indian alchemy than Nāgārjuna’s, and none is more confused. At least three figures must be distinguished (White 1996; Wujastyk 1984; Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

  1. Nāgārjuna the Buddhist philosopher (c. 2nd–3rd century CE), founder of the Madhyamaka school and author of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. Nothing in his securely attributed philosophical works concerns alchemy (on the philosopher, see Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā).

  2. Nāgārjuna of legend. By the 7th century the philosopher had attracted alchemical legends: Xuanzang, on his journey of c. 629–645, records a story that Nāgārjuna prepared a drug of long life for a Sātavāhana king and could turn stone into gold (Beal 1884). Tibetan tradition later identified the philosopher with the alchemist and the tantric adept.

  3. Nāgārjuna the alchemist or alchemists. Al-Bīrūnī, writing c. 1030, mentions a Nāgārjuna from a fort near Somnāth who excelled in alchemy, wrote a book on it and lived about a century before al-Bīrūnī’s time (Sachau 1888). A Sanskrit alchemical text, the Rasendramaṅgala, is attributed to a Nāgārjuna; its date is uncertain, and estimates range from the 8th to the 12th century. A siddha named Nāgārjuna also appears in the lists of the Nāth and Siddha traditions, and the 12th-century commentator Ḍalhaṇa names a Nāgārjuna as the redactor of the Suśrutasaṃhitā.

Modern scholarship treats these as different people, or as a legendary name attached to later works, and does not identify the Madhyamaka philosopher with any alchemical author. The often-cited “Rasaratnākara of Nāgārjuna”, described by P. C. Ray as one of the oldest rasa texts, is an instance of how such attributions arise: Wujastyk showed that it is a “ghost”, and that the work cited under that name is in fact the Rasendramaṅgala (Wujastyk 1984). The well-known Rasaratnākara is a later work by Nityanātha (13th–14th century). Statements that Nāgārjuna “systematised” Indian alchemy, or that the eighteen saṃskāras go back to him, therefore have no secure basis.

docs.title: 1.11 The Harappan Legacy
docs.text: The Indus or Harappan civilisation (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) provides the earliest large body of evidence for chemical crafts in South Asia (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002).

docs.title: 1.11.1 Metals
docs.text: Harappan smiths worked copper, tin bronze, arsenical copper, lead, silver, gold and electrum. Most copper objects are of nearly pure or arsenical copper; tin bronze is less common, and tin must have been imported. Objects were cast in open and closed moulds and by the lost-wax method—the famous “dancing girl” from Mohenjo-daro is a lost-wax casting in copper alloy—and sheet metal was raised, riveted and soldered (Kenoyer and Miller 1999; Agrawal 2000). Copper ores were probably obtained from the Aravalli hills (the Ganeshwar–Jodhpura region) and from Baluchistan and Oman.

docs.title: 1.11.2 Vitreous Materials and Beads
docs.text: The Harappans also commanded a high-temperature chemistry of non-metallic materials: faience, fired and glazed steatite, partly vitrified “stoneware” bangles fired in sealed containers, and stone beads whose colour and surface were altered by heat and by alkaline pastes (Kenoyer 1998). These crafts are described in Section 12.1, and the carnelian bead industry in Section 10.7.

docs.title: 1.12 The Textual Corpus
docs.text:
The oldest of the written sources used in this volume is the Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE), on mines, metals, the mint and gems (Olivelle 2013). The classical Āyurvedic compendia of Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa (c. 100 BCE to c. 600 CE) use some metals and minerals, mainly externally or in small quantities, and describe rejuvenation (rasāyana) therapy (Wujastyk 2003). A separate literature on gems runs from the gem chapters of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century) to Buddhabhaṭṭa’s Ratnaparīkṣā and the Agastimata (Bhat 1981–1982; Finot 1896).

The rasa literature proper (Chapter 2) begins with the Rasahṛdayatantra of Govinda (c. 10th–11th century) and the Rasārṇava (c. 11th–12th century), continues with the Rasendracūḍāmaṇi of Somadeva (12th–13th century), the Ānandakanda (13th century) and the Rasaprakāśasudhākara of Yaśodhara (13th century), and reaches its most influential form in the Rasaratnasamuccaya attributed to Vāgbhaṭa (late 13th or 14th century) and Nityanātha’s Rasaratnākara (13th–14th century); all these dates are approximate (White 1996; Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Later compendia such as the Āyurvedaprakāśa of Mādhava (17th century) and the Rasataraṅgiṇī of Sadānanda Śarmā (20th century) remain the basis of modern rasaśāstra teaching. Travellers and observers, from Xuanzang to al-Bīrūnī, Tavernier and Francis Buchanan, supply what the texts leave out.

docs.title: 1.12.1 Indo-Islamic and Early Modern Sources
docs.text:
The Sanskrit texts are only part of the written record. From the 11th century, Arabic and Persian authors wrote about Indian materials and techniques, and from the 13th century the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and its successors produced their own administrative and technical literature.

Al-Bīrūnī (973–after 1050), who spent years in north-west India under the Ghaznavids, described Indian rasāyana in his India (c. 1030) and wrote on gems and on drugs (Chapter 14) (Sachau 1888). Ṭhakkura Pherū, a Jain official of the Khaljī treasury and mint, wrote in the early 14th century short treatises in Apabhraṃśa (a late literary Prakrit) on gems, coins and metals (Section 8.12). The Āʾīn-i Akbarī of Abuʾl Faẓl (completed c. 1598), the great gazetteer of Akbar’s empire, describes the imperial mint, the manufacture of arms, the cooling of water with saltpetre, the distillation of spirits and the perfumery of the court (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873); its account of the mint is discussed in Section 8.13. European travellers and officials—Tavernier on the diamond mines, Buchanan and Voysey on steel, the authors of district gazetteers and economic surveys—recorded processes in the 17th–19th centuries, often because they wished to profit from or imitate them.

These sources are a valuable corrective to a narrowly Sanskritic view. Much of the metallurgy, minting, perfumery, dyeing and glass-making of medieval and early modern India took place in a Persianate court and urban culture, and was practised by Muslim as well as Hindu and Jain artisans. The Islamic alchemical tradition in India and its contacts with rasaśāstra are discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 1.13 India in the Wider History of Technology
docs.text:
Several Indian products and processes had a significance far beyond the subcontinent. They are treated in detail later; here it is enough to state them with the qualifications that current scholarship requires.

Crucible steel High-carbon steel made by melting iron with carbonaceous material in sealed crucibles was produced in south India from at least the last centuries BCE, and in Sri Lanka in the first millennium CE. It was exported as ingots to Iran and the Arab world, where some was forged into the patterned “Damascus” blades. Crucible steel was also made in Central Asia and Iran, so South Asia was one of several centres of the technology, not the only one (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Rehren and Papachristou 2003). Zinc distillation Zawar in Rajasthan has the earliest securely dated evidence for the production of metallic zinc by distillation on an industrial scale, from about the 9th–10th century CE and on a very large scale from about the 14th century (Craddock et al. 1983; Craddock 2017). The Delhi iron pillar A forge-welded wrought-iron pillar of c. 400 CE, more than six tonnes in weight, whose slow corrosion has been explained by Balasubramaniam’s work on its phosphorus-rich protective film (Balasubramaniam 2000). Indigo and mordant dyeing India was for many centuries a leading producer and exporter of indigo, and Indian mordant-dyed cottons were prized across the Indian Ocean and later in Europe. The English word “indigo” comes, through Spanish or Portuguese and Latin indicum, from Greek indikon, “Indian (substance)” (Balfour-Paul 1998; Riello 2013). Diamonds Until the discovery of Brazilian deposits in the 1720s, India was the world’s main source of diamonds (Tavernier 1889).

Older books often go further and call India “the first” to do many things. Such claims are usually unnecessary and often wrong: technologies were developed in several places, evidence is incomplete, and new discoveries regularly move the dates. This volume describes what the evidence shows and leaves aside contests of priority.

docs.title: 1.14 How the History Has Been Written
docs.text:
The history of Indian chemistry and metallurgy has been written from several standpoints, each of which has left its mark on the literature.

Colonial Many 19th-century European writers assumed that India had produced philosophy and religion but not science, and that its crafts, however skilful, were matters of unreflective custom. At the same time colonial officials collected much valuable information about Indian crafts, often with an eye to their commercial exploitation or replacement. Nationalist In response, Indian scholars of the late 19th and early 20th centuries set out to show that ancient India had possessed genuine sciences. P. C. Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry (Ray 1902–1909) and Brajendranath Seal’s The Positive Sciences of the Ancient Hindus (1915) (Seal 1915) are the classic works. They were careful and learned, but they sometimes dated texts too early and read modern ideas into ancient ones—tendencies that popular writing has since greatly exaggerated. Marxist and social Later historians, such as Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya, asked why empirical science had flourished in some periods and declined in others, and related the fate of science to social structure, especially caste and the devaluation of manual labour (Chattopadhyaya 1986). Institutional surveys After independence the Indian National Science Academy sponsored A Concise History of Science in India (1971), and the multi-volume History of Science, Philosophy and Culture in Indian Civilization devoted a volume to chemistry and chemical techniques, edited by B. V. Subbarayappa (1999); both gather textual and technical material and remain useful guides (Bose et al. 1971; Subbarayappa 1999). Archaeometric Since the 1970s, the most important new evidence has come from archaeology and laboratory analysis—the work of Agrawal, Balasubramaniam, Srinivasan, Craddock, Juleff, Kenoyer and many others—which has made it possible to test claims against material evidence (Agrawal 2000; Craddock 1995). Religious-historical Scholars of religion, especially David Gordon White, have placed rasaśāstra in its Tantric context, showing that it cannot be understood simply as proto-chemistry (White 1996).

This volume draws on all of these, but especially on the last two, and tries to avoid both the colonial dismissal and the nationalist exaggeration.

docs.title: 1.15 A Comparative Frame
docs.text:
Indian chemical history is best understood alongside the histories of other regions, with which it was often in contact.

China Chinese metallurgy developed cast iron early (by the mid-first millennium BCE), using furnaces hot enough to melt iron, whereas South Asia relied on bloomery iron and crucible steel. Chinese alchemy, with its elixirs of cinnabar and mercury, flourished from the Han dynasty, and gunpowder was discovered in China, probably in the 9th century, in the course of alchemical experimentation. Porcelain, a high-fired white ceramic, was a Chinese achievement without an Indian counterpart. The Islamic world From the 8th century, Arabic-writing chemists inherited Greek, Syriac, Persian and possibly Indian knowledge. The writings attributed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān and those of the physician al-Rāzī (Rhazes, d. c. 925) classified substances into minerals, plants and animal products, described laboratory apparatus such as the alembic and the aludel, and developed the theory that metals are formed from sulphur and mercury. Al-Bīrūnī’s work shows that learned Muslims were interested in Indian sciences, including rasāyana (Sachau 1888; Principe 2013). Europe Latin Europe received alchemy from Arabic in the 12th century. In the 16th century Paracelsus promoted chemical medicines, including preparations of mercury and antimony—a development parallel in some ways to the medical turn of Indian rasaśāstra. Modern chemistry emerged in Europe from the 17th century, through the work of Boyle, Lavoisier, Dalton and others, out of this alchemical and pharmaceutical background (Principe 2013).

Seen in this frame, India’s distinctive contributions lie in particular technologies—crucible steel, zinc distillation, high-tin bronze, mineral-soda-alumina glass, mordant dyeing of cotton, crystalline sugar—and in a rich alchemical literature, rather than in a single path towards modern chemistry.

docs.title: 1.16.1 Dating the Rasa Texts
docs.text: Many rasa texts are attributed to legendary or semi-legendary authors, were expanded by later hands, and survive in manuscripts much younger than the works themselves. Relative dates can be established from quotations (a text that quotes another is later), and absolute dates from a few datable authors and manuscripts. The result is a framework accurate to perhaps a century; P. C. Ray’s early dates, still repeated in popular books, have generally been revised downwards (Meulenbeld 1999–2002; White 1996).

docs.title: 1.16.2 Reading Processes in Texts
docs.text: Technical texts in Sanskrit verse are compressed and often deliberately obscure. Their names for substances may not correspond to modern mineral species, and the same procedure may be described differently in different works. Modern rasaśāstra textbooks often present a single standardised reading; the historian has to remember that this is a modern interpretation.

docs.title: 1.16.3 Laboratory Analysis
docs.text:
Modern analytical methods—X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, X-ray fluorescence, mass spectrometry, radiocarbon and other dating techniques—have transformed the study of ancient materials. They have shown, for example, how the Delhi pillar resists corrosion and when Zawar’s zinc retorts were used. When the same methods are applied to modern “traditional” medicines, they show what those products contain—including, in many cases, toxic levels of heavy metals—but they do not by themselves show that a product is safe or effective. Those are questions for toxicology and for properly conducted clinical trials. Table 1.3 lists the main techniques; what archaeometallurgists use them to find out is explained in Section 4.5, at the start of the chapters on metals, and Figure 4.1 shows where the principal sites lie.

Table 1.3. Some Analytical Techniques and Their Use in this Field Technique Information provided Example of use Metallography Microstructure of metals Wootz ingots; forge-welds of iron pillars SEM/EDS Microstructure and elemental composition Slag inclusions; crucible fabrics XRD Crystalline phases Corrosion products on the Delhi pillar XRF, ICP-MS Elemental composition, trace elements Glass compositions; heavy metals in medicines Radiocarbon Age of organic material Charcoal and timber from Zawar and early iron sites

docs.title: 1.17 Scope and Structure of this Volume
docs.text:
The volume is organised in fifteen chapters. After this introduction, Chapter 2 surveys the rasa literature, its texts, apparatus, classifications and social world, quoting a few of its programmatic verses, and Chapter 3 describes what the texts say about mercury and its eighteen saṃskāras and what modern toxicology says about mercury. Chapter 4 turns to the mines from which the metals came and explains the methods of archaeometallurgy on which the following chapters rely. Chapters 5–8 treat the metals: iron and the Delhi pillar; crucible steel; zinc and Zawar; and gold, silver, copper, lead, tin and their alloys, with the Delhi and Mughal mints. Chapter 9 discusses calcined metal preparations (bhasma) as a historical tradition and as a contemporary safety problem.

The non-metallic crafts follow: gems and minerals (Chapter 10); dyes, pigments and inks (Chapter 11); glass, ceramics and building materials (Chapter 12); and the salts, alkalis and acids—kṣāra, common salt, saltpetre, alum, the vitriols, sal ammoniac and borax—that were the everyday reagents of pre-modern chemistry, together with sugar (Chapter 13). Chapter 14 turns to Islamic alchemy (kīmiyā) in India, its meeting with rasaśāstra, and the history and chemistry of distillation, from spirits to attar. Chapter 15 considers the legacy of this tradition, its place in the history of world chemistry, and the questions that remain open.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the three senses of rasāyana; the state’s interest in mines, metals and the mint in the Arthaśāstra; the alkalis, salts and fermented liquors of the medical compendia; and the distinction between the Madhyamaka philosopher Nāgārjuna and the alchemists who bore his name. Debated: the dates of almost every rasa text, which are relative and uncertain by a century or more; the identity of many minerals named in the texts; and how far the craft knowledge that made Indian steel, zinc and dyes ever reached the authors of Sanskrit treatises.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Rasaśāstra: The Alchemical Literature and Its World
2.1 What Rasaśāstra Was
docs.text:
Rasaśāstra, “the science of mercury”, is the name the Sanskrit alchemical literature gives itself. Its texts are concerned with the processing of mercury and of a large number of metals and minerals, with two declared goals. The first is dhātuvāda or lohavāda, the transformation of base metals into silver and gold. The second is dehavāda, the transformation of the human body, by means of processed mercury, into a body free of disease, old age and death—the body of a perfected being (siddha). From the beginning there was also a medical use of mercurial and mineral preparations, and over time this became dominant: the later rasa texts are largely pharmacopoeias, and rasaśāstra is today taught in India as a branch of Āyurvedic pharmaceutics (White 1996; Ray 1956; Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Its place in medical practice is treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda, and its Tantric setting in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama; this chapter concentrates on the literature as a chapter in the history of chemistry.

The phrase “Indian alchemy” is appropriate, provided it is not taken to imply that the rasa texts are simply Indian versions of European or Arabic alchemy. Like those traditions, rasaśāstra combined practical laboratory operations—grinding, heating, sublimation, distillation, amalgamation—with a theory of transformation that modern chemistry does not accept. Unlike European alchemy, it was embedded in Tantric Śaivism, with its initiations, mantras and goddess worship, and in the medical culture of Āyurveda.

Health and Safety Note

The substances discussed in this chapter—mercury, lead, arsenic sulphides, copper salts and others—are toxic. The chapter is history and gives no doses or working procedures; see the full note in Section 1.1.

docs.title: 2.2 Antecedents and Origins
docs.text:
The classical medical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta (c. 100 BCE–500 CE) use a number of mineral substances—salts, alkalis, ochres, collyria, metals such as iron and gold—and describe the heating and quenching of metal leaves for medicinal use. Mercury, however, plays only a marginal role in them, and there is no doctrine of mercury as the key to transmutation or immortality (Wujastyk 2003; Meulenbeld 1999–2002). The Arthaśāstra mentions liquid ores and the refining of metals, but again not a mercurial alchemy.

The rasa literature proper emerges towards the end of the first millennium CE. Its earliest surviving works belong roughly to the 10th–12th centuries, and several streams flowed into it (White 1996). Tantric Śaivism supplied its ritual framework, its dialogue form (Bhairava or Śiva instructing the Goddess), its use of mantras and initiation, and the identification of mercury with Śiva’s semen and of sulphur (or mica) with the Goddess’s generative fluid. The Siddha traditions, groups of ascetic adepts who sought bodily immortality and supernatural powers (siddhi) through yoga, ritual and drugs, supplied its goal and many of its heroes: the lists of “perfected masters of mercury” (rasasiddha) in the rasa texts overlap with the lists of Nāth and other siddhas. Buddhist Tantra cultivated the pursuit of elixirs and powers as well, although no surviving rasa text of the early period can be shown to be Buddhist; the Kakṣapuṭa, a compendium of magical rites ascribed to a Siddha Nāgārjuna and sometimes cited in this connection, is of uncertain date and sectarian affiliation. Finally Āyurveda adopted mercurial and mineral preparations as medicines and eventually absorbed rasaśāstra into its curriculum.

Whether the Indian alchemical tradition was influenced by, or influenced, the Chinese and Islamic alchemies with which it shares many features is uncertain. Mercury and cinnabar were central in Chinese alchemy many centuries before the earliest rasa texts, and Arabic alchemy was flourishing by the 9th century. Contacts through trade, Buddhist pilgrimage and the Persianate courts make some exchange likely, but specific borrowings have not been demonstrated (White 1996; Principe 2013).

docs.title: 2.3 The Principal Texts
docs.text: All the dates in this section are approximate; most rest on relative chronology established by quotation, and scholars differ by a century or more (Meulenbeld 1999–2002; White 1996).

docs.title: 2.3.1 Rasahṛdayatantra
docs.text:
The Rasahṛdayatantra (“Tantra of the Heart of Mercury”) is ascribed to Govinda, styled bhagavat or bhikṣu. A later tradition identifies him with Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the Advaita philosopher Śaṅkara; there is no evidence for this, and the work is usually dated to about the 10th or 11th century. It is one of the earliest surviving systematic treatments of mercury, organised around the processing of mercury through a sequence of operations culminating in its “binding” (bandha) and its use for transmutation and for the body. Its opening verses state the claims of the whole tradition in a single stanza, which the Rasaratnasamuccaya later repeats almost word for word (1.34):

Rasahṛdayatantra 1.3

mūrchitvā harati rujaṃ bandhanam anubhūya muktido bhavati amarīkaroti sumṛtaḥ ko ’nyaḥ karuṇākaraḥ sūtāt Swooned, it takes away disease; having undergone binding, it becomes the giver of liberation; well killed, it makes one immortal. What other source of compassion is there than mercury?

The three participles name three of the operations described below—“swooning” (mūrchana), “binding” (bandha) and “killing” (māraṇa)—and attach to each a promised result. A few verses later the text explains why the body matters: liberation, it says, “comes from knowledge, knowledge from practice, and practice is possible only in a stable body” (muktau sā ca jñānāt tac cābhyāsāt sa ca sthire dehe, 1.10), and no herbal or metallic elixir can give that stability except mercury (1.11–13). The passages are quoted from the GRETIL e-text of the Chaukhambha edition (GRETIL 2020a).

docs.title: 2.3.2 Rasārṇava
docs.text:
The Rasārṇava (“Ocean of Mercury”), probably of the 11th–12th century, is a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess and is the most important early statement of Tantric alchemy. It describes the qualifications of the alchemist and his helpers, the laboratory and its shrine, the apparatus and furnaces, the classes of minerals, the eighteen operations (saṃskāra) on mercury, the “digestion” of metals and minerals by mercury, transmutation, and the use of mercury to perfect the body (White 1996; Ray 1956). The text was edited by P. C. Ray and Hariśchandra Kaviratna in the Bibliotheca Indica (Ray and Kaviratna 1908–1910). It opens with the Goddess asking Bhairava about “liberation in life” (jīvanmukti) and the means to it, and Bhairava’s answer sets out the doctrine of the body on which the rest depends:

Rasārṇava 1.18

karmayogena deveśi prāpyate piṇḍadhāraṇam rasaś ca pavanaś ceti karmayogo dvidhā mataḥ By the yoga of action, O Queen of the gods, the preservation of the body is attained; and the yoga of action is held to be twofold: mercury and breath.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Rasaratnasamuccaya
docs.text: The Rasaratnasamuccaya (“Compendium of the Jewels of Mercury”) is attributed to a Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta—the name and parentage also given for the author of the Āyurvedic Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (c. 600), which is why the two have often been confused. The compendium is centuries later than that work, and its author must be a different person, or the ascription a borrowed one. The work is generally placed in the late 13th or the 14th century. It describes itself as a compilation: after naming the authorities on whom it draws, the author says that “having examined the tantras of these and of others, the son of Siṃhagupta makes this compendium, the Rasaratnasamuccaya, of mercurial preparations that are perfected and useful for the purposes of treatment” (1.8–9) (GRETIL 2020b). It is arranged in thirty chapters: roughly the first third deals with materials (mercury, the mineral classes, gems, metals), apparatus, furnaces and the laboratory; the rest is a pharmacopoeia arranged by disease. It became the most influential rasa text in later Āyurvedic teaching (Meulenbeld 1999–2002; Ray 1956).

docs.title: 2.3.4 Other Texts
docs.text:
Table 2.1 lists some other works that are often cited, with their approximate dates.

Table 2.1. Some Other Works of the Rasa Literature (dates approximate) Text Date Notes Rasendramaṅgala uncertain (8th–12th c.?) Attributed to Nāgārjuna; partly preserved Rasendracūḍāmaṇi 12th–13th c. By Somadeva; much quoted by later texts Ānandakanda 13th c. A large Tantric compendium of alchemy and rejuvenation, probably from the south Rasaprakāśasudhākara 13th c. By Yaśodhara Rasaratnākara 13th–14th c. By Nityanātha; not to be confused with the “ghost” Rasaratnākara of Nāgārjuna (Chapter 1) Rasendracintāmaṇi 14th–16th c. Title of separate works by Rāmacandra Guha and by Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, often confused Bhāvaprakāśa 16th c. General Āyurvedic compendium of Bhāvamiśra, including metals and minerals Āyurvedaprakāśa 17th c. By Mādhava; an important late rasa compendium Rasataraṅgiṇī 20th c. By Sadānanda Śarmā; basis of much modern teaching

docs.title: 2.4 Apparatus (Yantra)
docs.text:
The rasa texts describe dozens of pieces of apparatus, often with names that are hard to interpret. Table 2.2 groups some of the commonest by purpose.

Table 2.2. Principal Groups of Apparatus Named in the Rasa Texts Group Examples Purpose described Grinding khalva (mortar) Grinding with liquids (bhāvanā, mardana) Heating in liquids ḍolāyantra, svedanīyantra Boiling or steaming a substance tied in cloth Sublimation and distillation ūrdhvapātana, adhaḥpātana, tiryakpātana yantras; vidyādharayantra Raising mercury or other volatiles to a cooler surface, or leading them downwards or sideways Controlled heating vālukāyantra (sand-bath), bhūdharayantra (vessel buried in heated earth) Gentle and sustained heat Containers mūṣā (crucibles of many kinds), śarāvasampuṭa (two sealed earthen dishes) Holding a charge during heating Furnaces and heating pits koṣṭhī (furnace), puṭa (pit of burning fuel) Smelting; calcination

Figure 2.1 shows three of them schematically.

Figure 2.1. Three pieces of rasa apparatus, drawn schematically from the texts’ descriptions as modern authors usually interpret them. Shapes, sizes and materials varied from text to text; no working details are given.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Ḍolāyantra
docs.text: In the ḍolāyantra (“swing apparatus”) a substance tied in a cloth bundle is hung from a rod laid across the mouth of a pot, so that it is suspended in a boiling liquid without touching the bottom. It is used in many “purification” procedures. Comparisons with modern extraction apparatus are sometimes made, but the ḍolāyantra is simply a means of boiling a solid in a liquid while keeping it off the hot base of the vessel.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Pātanayantras
docs.text: The texts describe raising mercury upwards (ūrdhvapātana), driving it downwards (adhaḥpātana) or sideways (tiryakpātana) from a heated vessel into a cooler one, where it condenses. These are sublimation and distillation operations. Mercury vapour is extremely toxic, and the texts’ descriptions of sealing joints with clay and other pastes show an awareness that the volatile metal would otherwise be lost.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Crucibles and Sealed Vessels
docs.text: Many kinds of crucible (mūṣā) are distinguished by shape and by the clays and additives from which they are made. For calcination a substance is enclosed between two shallow earthen dishes sealed with clay-smeared cloth (śarāvasampuṭa) and heated in a puṭa.

docs.title: 2.5 Furnaces and Heating Pits
docs.text: The texts distinguish furnaces (koṣṭhī), used with bellows for melting and for extracting metals from minerals, from puṭas, pits or heaps of fuel in which a sealed vessel is heated and then left to cool. The puṭas are named after animals and birds—the “elephant” (gaja), “boar” (varāha), “cock” (kukkuṭa), “pigeon” (kapota) and “quail” (lāvaka) puṭa—and graded by the size of the pit and the amount of fuel, generally dried cow-dung cakes. The graded puṭas are an empirical way of controlling the intensity and duration of heating. Exact temperatures for them, which appear in some modern books, are modern estimates for particular reconstructions, not information given by the texts.

docs.title: 2.6 The Rasa Worldview
docs.text:
The rasa texts present alchemy as a religious path. Mercury is Śiva’s seed, and sulphur the Goddess’s menstrual or uterine fluid; their combination (black or red mercuric sulphide) is a material image of divine union. The alchemist must receive initiation from a teacher, worship Bhairava and the Goddess, and perform the laboratory operations at auspicious times with the prescribed mantras. A liṅga of “bound” mercury is the focus of worship in the laboratory (White 1996).

The texts claim that mercury, properly processed, can transmute base metals into gold and can make the body immortal, and they promise the adept supernatural powers. These claims are part of the religious and literary world of the texts. Nothing in them has been demonstrated, and transmutation of base metals into gold by chemical means is impossible.

Living Liberation through the Body

The goal of dehavāda is often described in the texts as liberation in this life (jīvanmukti) in a body made imperishable by mercury. The Rasārṇava defines jīvanmukti as “the knowledge of identity with Śiva of one whose body is free from old age and death” (ajarāmaradehasya śivatādātmyavedanam, 1.8), rare, it adds, even for the gods (Ray and Kaviratna 1908–1910). White argues that this links rasaśāstra closely to haṭha yoga and to the Nāth Siddhas, for whom the body was likewise the instrument of perfection; others see the connections as looser (White 1996).

docs.title: 2.7 The Eighteen Saṃskāras: An Overview
docs.text:
The central technical scheme of the rasa texts is a sequence of eighteen operations (aṣṭādaśa saṃskāra) to which mercury is subjected. The list varies somewhat between texts; Table 2.3 gives the usual names. The first eight are described as making mercury fit for medicinal use; the later ones aim at making mercury “bind” other substances and finally transmute metals and transform the body. The Rasahṛdayatantra presents the whole sequence as the preliminary to its goal: whoever seeks a divine body must first, it says, “come to know with effort the eighteen saṃskāras” (aṣṭādaśasaṃskārā vijñātavyāḥ prayatnena, 1.34) (GRETIL 2020a). Chapter 3 discusses them further.

Table 2.3. The Eighteen Saṃskāras of Mercury (usual list) Group Operations 1–8 (“for medicine”) svedana (steaming), mardana (grinding), mūrchana (“swooning”), utthāpana (“raising”, restoring fluidity), pātana (sublimation or distillation), rodhana or bodhana (“confining” or “awakening”), niyamana (“restraining”), dīpana (“kindling” appetite) 9–16 (“digestion” and fixation) gaganagrāsa (“swallowing” mica), cāraṇa (“feeding”), garbhadruti (internal liquefaction), bāhyadruti (external liquefaction), jāraṇa (“digestion”), rañjana (colouring), sāraṇa, krāmaṇa (penetration) 17–18 (application) vedha (“piercing”: transmutation of metals), śarīrayoga or bhakṣaṇa (use in the body)

docs.title: 2.8 Defects of Mercury
docs.text:
The texts regard natural mercury as carrying defects (doṣa) that make it dangerous and must be removed by the saṃskāras. In the scheme commonly given, mercury has “natural” defects such as poison (viṣa), fire (vahni) and dirt (mala), defects due to admixture with lead (nāga) and tin (vaṅga), and several “sheaths” (kañcuka) acquired from its surroundings. Each defect is said to cause particular diseases if impure mercury is taken.

The doctrine shows that the alchemists knew raw mercury to be harmful, and it is reasonable to suppose that some of their operations (washing, grinding with abrasive powders, distillation) removed solid impurities and some base metals. But the doctrine of doṣas is a theory of the texts, not a description of the chemical toxicity of mercury. Mercury itself, in any form, remains toxic; no operation removes the “poison” from mercury, because the poison is the mercury.

docs.title: 2.9 Reading a Rasa Text
docs.text:
Rasa texts are not easy to read. Like most Sanskrit technical literature they are written mainly in verse, in which quantities, materials and operations are compressed into a few words and the order of operations may be left implicit. Every substance has many names—mercury alone has dozens, and plants and minerals are named by epithets that change from text to text—and the lexicons of materia medica (nighaṇṭu), such as the Madanapālanighaṇṭu (14th century) and the Rājanighaṇṭu, help the reader while showing how unstable the vocabulary was. The texts insist that their teaching must be received from a teacher and kept from the unworthy, and they sometimes use deliberately obscure or coded language, so that some procedures may never have been fully written down. And the texts are layered: they were compiled from earlier works, quote one another and were expanded by later hands, so that a procedure ascribed to an ancient authority may be a late addition. The verse shared by the Rasahṛdayatantra and the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Section 2.3.1) is a small example of such borrowing.

For these reasons, modern “reconstructions” of rasa procedures—including those in present-day textbooks—involve a good deal of interpretation. The historian’s task is to describe what the texts say, how their readers understood them, and, where possible, what was actually done; it is not to produce working recipes.

docs.title: 2.10 The Technical Vocabulary
docs.text:
The rasa texts share a vocabulary of operations, many of them borrowed from metallurgy and pharmacy, which can be roughly matched to modern chemical operations (Table 2.4).

Table 2.4. Some Technical Terms of the Rasa Texts Term Literal meaning What the texts describe śodhana purification Preliminary processing, often heating and quenching in liquids or boiling with plant materials māraṇa killing Calcination until the metal loses its metallic character bhāvanā impregnation Wet grinding with a plant juice or decoction mardana grinding Prolonged trituration in a mortar jāraṇa digestion Causing mercury to absorb another substance bandha binding Fixing mercury so that it is no longer volatile or fluid sattvapātana extracting the essence Heating a mineral strongly to obtain a metal from it pātana causing to fall Sublimation or distillation amṛtīkaraṇa making ambrosial A further treatment of a calcined product, said to remove residual harmfulness

Some of these operations correspond closely to real chemical processes—sattvapātana, for instance, is the reduction of a metal from its ore, and one of its applications appears to be the extraction of zinc from calamine (Chapter 7). Others, such as jāraṇa or rañjana, rest on alchemical ideas with no modern equivalent.

docs.title: 2.11 The Alchemist, the Laboratory and the Patron
docs.text:
The rasa texts describe the ideal alchemical enterprise in some detail (White 1996; Ray 1956). The alchemist should be learned in the scriptures, devoted to his teacher and to Śiva, truthful, free from greed, and skilled in the preparation of medicines. He requires a teacher who has himself been initiated into the lineage and who will reveal the methods only to a qualified pupil; the texts repeatedly insist that their teachings are secret and must not be given to the unworthy. He needs assistants: people to work the bellows, tend the fires and grind for long hours, who are to be strong, diligent and loyal.

The laboratory is to be built in a pleasant, well-watered place, in a kingdom with a righteous ruler, with access to the plants and minerals required. The texts prescribe its layout—the shrine of the mercury liṅga at its centre, the furnaces in the south-east (the direction of Agni, the fire god), the grinding and storage areas in their places—and the rituals that consecrate it. They also describe the apparatus, the stocks of materials, and the protective rites against the obstacles that hostile beings might raise.

This is an idealised picture, combining practical requirements with the conventions of Tantric ritual manuals. But it makes clear that alchemy, as the texts imagined it, was an expensive and collective undertaking. Fuel, metals (including gold), mercury and imported minerals cost money, and so did assistants’ labour. The figure of the royal patron who funds the alchemist in the hope of gold or long life recurs in the texts and in stories about alchemists; al-Bīrūnī notes Indian rulers’ interest in the art (Sachau 1888). Stories of kings ruined by alchemists, and of alchemists who were frauds, circulated as well.

docs.title: 2.12 Alchemy, Yoga and the Siddhas
docs.text:
The rasa texts share their goal of bodily perfection with the haṭha yoga traditions associated with the Nāth Siddhas, which developed in the same centuries. Both speak of a perfected, imperishable body; both use the vocabulary of fluids—semen, the “nectar” of the moon in the head, the fire of the belly—and of their transformation; and some figures, such as Nāgārjuna, Gorakṣa and Carpaṭi, appear in both alchemical and yogic lineages. White’s The Alchemical Body argues that alchemy, haṭha yoga and Tantric sexual ritual formed parts of a single “Siddha” project in which the adept transformed his own body by internal processes parallel to the external transformation of mercury in the laboratory (White 1996).

White’s thesis has been influential, but it should be read with some care. The surviving haṭha yoga texts say relatively little about laboratory alchemy, and many of the rasa texts, especially the later ones, are medical rather than yogic in orientation. What is clear is that, in medieval India, the ideal of a perfected body could be pursued by several routes—yogic, ritual, medicinal and alchemical—and that the boundaries between them were permeable. Some texts present alchemy as an alternative to yoga for those unable to master it; others present the two as complementary.

docs.title: 2.13 The Masters of Mercury
docs.text:
The rasa texts open with lists of “perfected masters of mercury” (rasasiddha), mythical and semi-historical figures said to have attained perfection through mercury. The Rasaratnasamuccaya begins (1.2–5) with twenty-seven “bestowers of perfection in mercury” (rasasiddhipradāyaka), among them Vyāḍi, Nāgārjuna and Govinda, and then adds further names (GRETIL 2020b). Such lists set the famous names alongside obscure or purely legendary ones, and they overlap with the lists of Nāth and other siddhas, including Matsyendra and Gorakṣa (White 1996). They are statements of lineage and authority, not historical records. The famous names—Nāgārjuna above all—were attached to texts in order to give them prestige (Chapter 1).

Travellers’ accounts show that the pursuit of longevity through mercury was a visible practice. Marco Polo, describing south India in the late 13th century, reports that certain ascetics drank a mixture of quicksilver and sulphur regularly in the belief that it prolonged their lives (Yule and Cordier 1903).

docs.title: 2.14 The Tamil Siddha Tradition
docs.text:
Tamil literature contains a large body of verse attributed to the cittar (Sanskrit siddha), traditionally eighteen in number, which deals with yoga, mysticism, medicine and alchemy (vātam). Its oldest and most respected text is the Tirumantiram of Tirumūlar, the tenth book of the Tamil Śaiva canon (Tirumuṟai), whose date is much disputed—proposals range from the middle of the first millennium CE to the 10th century or later—and which teaches that the body must be preserved and perfected as the instrument of liberation, a Tamil counterpart to the doctrine of the Sanskrit rasa texts. The medical and alchemical works proper are ascribed to Akattiyar (Agastya), Pōkar (Bhogar), Koṅkaṇar, Karuvūrār and others, and circulate under titles that give their length in verses, such as the large compilation known as Pōkar Ēḻāyiram (“Pōkar’s Seven Thousand”). The traditional dates of these figures are mythical; the works themselves are mostly late medieval or early modern in their present form, and many were first printed in the 19th and 20th centuries, when publishers and practitioners assembled them into the canon of Siddha medicine (Zvelebil 1996; Weiss 2009). Siddha medicine, as an institutionalised system, was shaped in the 20th century as a Tamil counterpart to Āyurveda, and its advocates have presented it as older than, and independent of, the Sanskrit tradition; historians generally see the two as intertwined (Weiss 2009).

Siddha pharmacy makes extensive use of metals and minerals, including mercury, arsenic and lead compounds, in preparations such as calcined powders (parpam) and red calcined or sublimed powders (centūram) (Section 9.9). A well-known temple tradition holds that the image of Murukaṉ at Palani was made by Pōkar from a compound of nine “poisons” (navapāṣāṇam); this is a pious tradition, and no published scientific analysis of the image supports it. The south Indian vocabulary of the forge is older than any of these texts: the word for steel in Kannada and Telugu, ukku, and its Tamil cognate urukku, “that which is melted”, lie behind the English “wootz” (Chapter 6), and the Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions and crucible-steel debris of Kodumanal place literate Tamil-speaking communities beside the furnaces around the turn of the era. A history of Tamil metal-working that draws systematically on the Caṅkam poems and the inscriptions has yet to be written, and this volume does not attempt it.

docs.title: 2.15 Buddhist and Tibetan Connections
docs.text:
The Buddhist tantras of the late first millennium share with Śaiva Tantra an interest in elixirs (rasāyana) and powers, and Buddhist tradition attaches alchemical legends to Nāgārjuna. The Rasavaiśeṣikasūtra attributed to a Bhadanta Nāgārjuna, sometimes cited as a Buddhist alchemical work, is in fact a treatise on the theory of tastes and drug action in Āyurvedic pharmacology, not on alchemy (Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

Tibetan medicine developed its own mercury processing. The most elaborate procedure, known as tsotel (btso thal), produces a detoxified mercury sulphide ash used as an ingredient in “precious pills”. Tibetan tradition traces it to the 13th-century master Orgyenpa Rinchen Pel, who is said to have learned it in India. It is the most elaborate living descendant of Indian mercurial alchemy, and is still performed by Tibetan physicians in Tibet, India and Nepal in large collective sessions lasting several weeks. Gerke’s studies describe how it is carried out and how its practitioners understand its safety. In Tibetan Buddhist terms a poison can be “tamed” and turned into a medicine, and practitioners distinguish raw mercury from processed tsotel; this understanding now coexists, uneasily, with international concern about mercury in medicines and with the Minamata Convention (Section 3.10) (Gerke 2013, 2021).

docs.title: 2.16.1 China
docs.text: Chinese “external alchemy” (waidan) prepared elixirs of immortality from cinnabar, mercury, lead, arsenic and other minerals from at least the Han dynasty onwards; it was later partly displaced by “internal alchemy” (neidan), a meditative discipline using alchemical language. The Chinese records include many deaths from elixir poisoning, among them several Tang emperors. The parallels with Indian dehavāda are striking, and contacts were possible, but direct transmission in either direction has not been shown.

docs.title: 2.16.2 The Islamic World and Europe
docs.text: Arabic alchemy, from the 9th century, inherited Greek theories of the transmutation of metals and developed the theory that metals are formed from mercury and sulphur. It is primarily concerned with transmutation, though it also had medicinal applications. The word “alchemy” comes, through Arabic al-kīmiyāʾ, from a Greek word of uncertain origin; it has no Indian etymology. European alchemy, inheriting from the Arabic tradition, developed medicinal “chymistry” in the 16th century (Paracelsus) (Principe 2013). Al-Bīrūnī’s sceptical account of Indian rasāyana (c. 1030) shows that educated Muslims of his time knew of the Indian art; it is discussed, with the evidence for contact between Islamic alchemy and the rasa literature, in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 2.17 The Social World of Alchemy
docs.text:
The rasa texts envisage an alchemist (rasavādin or rasavaidya), initiated by a teacher, working in a well-endowed laboratory with assistants, often under royal patronage. Some works name royal patrons, and court physicians later prepared mercurial and metallic medicines. But the texts give little direct information about who their readers were. Alongside the Sanskrit-educated physicians and ascetic adepts, metal-workers, goldsmiths and refiners supplied practical knowledge of metals; the boundary between alchemy, metallurgy and pharmacy was porous.

The social history of Indian alchemy remains under-researched. What is clear is that by the early modern period the alchemical goals of transmutation and immortality had receded, and rasaśāstra had become mainly a branch of pharmacy, the form in which it survives in Āyurvedic colleges today.

docs.title: 2.18 Chronological Phases
docs.text:
The history of the literature can be divided, very roughly, into the phases summarised in Table 2.5.

Table 2.5. Phases of the Rasa Literature (approximate) Phase Period Characteristics Antecedents to c. 900 CE Minerals and metals in classical Āyurveda; alchemical legends (Nāgārjuna); Tantric and Siddha traditions Early rasa texts c. 900–1200 Rasahṛdayatantra, Rasārṇava: Tantric alchemy with transmutation and bodily immortality as goals Compendia c. 1200–1450 Rasendracūḍāmaṇi, Ānandakanda, Rasaratnasamuccaya, Rasaratnākara: growing medical content Integration with Āyurveda c. 1450–1800 Bhāvaprakāśa, Āyurvedaprakāśa; rasaśāstra largely pharmaceutical Modern 20th c. onwards Textbooks, college curricula, industrial manufacture; scientific and toxicological scrutiny

docs.title: 2.19 Manuscripts and Editions
docs.text:
Manuscripts of rasa texts are held in many Indian collections (among them the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, the Oriental Research Institute in Mysore, the Sarasvati Mahal Library in Thanjavur, the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Chennai and the Asiatic Society in Kolkata) and in libraries abroad. Many texts have been printed, often with Hindi commentaries, but few have critical editions, and only a handful have reliable English translations. P. C. Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry (1902–1909) gave the first extended survey, with extracts (Ray 1902–1909; Ray 1956); Meulenbeld’s History of Indian Medical Literature gives the most detailed bibliographical account (Meulenbeld 1999–2002); and White’s The Alchemical Body is the standard study of the Tantric context (White 1996).

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: rasaśāstra arose late in the first millennium CE in a Tantric Śaiva and Siddha milieu, with transmutation and bodily perfection as its declared goals, as its own opening verses say; its laboratory vocabulary of grinding, steaming, sublimation, sealed heating and graded puṭas; and its later turn to pharmacy. Debated: the absolute dates of the early texts; how closely alchemy was tied to haṭha yoga, as White argues; whether the Indian, Chinese and Arabic alchemies were historically connected; and the relation between the Tamil and Sanskrit traditions.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Pārada: Mercury in Alchemy, Medicine and Toxicology
3.1 Mercury in the Rasa Tradition
docs.text:
Mercury is the centre of rasaśāstra. The rasa texts identify it with Śiva, and more particularly with Śiva’s semen; they praise it in hymns, worship it in the form of a liṅga, and promise that mercury properly processed and “bound” will transmute metals and confer an imperishable body (White 1996). Its many names were explained in the same spirit. The Rasaratnasamuccaya derives four of them from what mercury does:

Rasaratnasamuccaya 1.77–79a

rasanāt sarvadhātūnāṃ rasa ity abhidhīyate jarāruṅmṛtyunāśāya rasyate vā raso mataḥ rasoparasarājatvād rasendra iti kīrtitaḥ dehalohamayīṃ siddhiṃ sūte sūtas tataḥ smṛtaḥ rogapaṅkābdhimagnānāṃ pāradānāc ca pāradaḥ It is called rasa because it “tastes” (that is, consumes) all the metals; or it is held to be rasa because it is tasted to destroy old age, disease and death. Because it is king of the rasas and uparasas it is celebrated as rasendra. Because it brings forth (sūte) perfection in body and in metal it is known as sūta; and because it gives the far shore (pāra-da) to those sunk in the ocean of the mire of disease, it is pārada.

The etymologies are not philology but doctrine: in four words they state the tradition’s claims over metals, over the body, and over disease. The passage is quoted from the GRETIL e-text of the Ānandāśrama edition, whose verse numbers may differ slightly from those of other printings (GRETIL 2020).

The properties that made mercury so fascinating are real. It is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary temperatures; it is very dense (about 13.5 times as dense as water), so that iron floats on it; it dissolves gold, silver, tin and other metals to form amalgams; it combines readily with sulphur, forming a black sulphide on grinding and a brilliant red one (vermilion) on sublimation; and it vaporises on heating, apparently vanishing, and reappears as droplets on a cool surface. To a pre-modern observer, a substance that could “eat” gold, change colour from silver to black to red, and escape and return through fire must have seemed uniquely alive.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Sources of Mercury
docs.text:
The principal ore of mercury is cinnabar (mercuric sulphide), Sanskrit hiṅgula or darada. The second name connects it with the Daradas, a people of the north-western mountains, and the rasa texts tell a myth of mercury welling up from a deep well in the far north-west (White 1996). India has few workable deposits of cinnabar, and most of the mercury used in Indian alchemy and medicine must have been imported—from Central Asia, from China, and in the early modern period from Spain (Almadén) via European traders. The rasa texts describe obtaining mercury from cinnabar by heating it and collecting the mercury in a cooled vessel, a process known in the Mediterranean world since antiquity.

Health and Safety Note

Mercury is a poison in all its forms: its vapour damages the brain, nerves and kidneys, its soluble salts are corrosive, and even mercuric sulphide is absorbed to some extent and accumulates with long use (Liu et al. 2008). No procedures or doses are given; see the full note in Section 1.1.

docs.title: 3.2 The Eighteen Saṃskāras
docs.text: The rasa texts subject mercury to a long sequence of operations, usually counted as eighteen; the usual list was given in Table 2.3 (Chapter 2). The list and its order vary somewhat between works (White 1996; Ray 1956). The first eight are described as preparing mercury for medicinal use; the remainder belong to transmutational and bodily alchemy.

docs.title: 3.2.1 What the Operations Were
docs.text:
The texts describe the operations in compressed verse, with long lists of plant juices, mineral powders and other materials. Read historically, they fall into a few types.

Washing and grinding (1–2). Mercury is heated in plant decoctions and ground with plant juices and mineral or brick powders. Such treatment would remove dirt and some surface oxides, and abrasive powders would carry off solid impurities. “Swooning” and “raising” (3–4). Mercury is ground until it loses its fluidity and lustre and becomes a dull paste—a dispersion of fine droplets in the grinding medium—and is then recovered as liquid metal. Sublimation and distillation (5). Mercury is driven off by heat and condensed in another vessel, upwards, downwards or sideways. Distillation separates mercury from less volatile metals such as lead and tin and is the one operation in the list that genuinely purifies the metal. Further “awakening” and “kindling” (6–8). Operations intended to restore the “vigour” and “appetite” of mercury after the preceding treatments, so that it will “eat” other substances. “Feeding” and “digestion” (9–16). Mercury is made to absorb mica, metals (gold above all), sulphur and other substances, to dissolve them and to be “coloured” by them. In chemical terms this involves the formation of amalgams and sulphides; in the texts’ terms, the mercury grows in strength with each substance it consumes. Application (17–18). The perfected mercury “pierces” base metals, transmuting them into gold, and is consumed to perfect the body.

The later operations, and especially vedha, rest on the alchemical theory that transmutation is possible. It is not: gold cannot be made from base metals by chemical means. Apparent transmutations in alchemical practice can be explained by gilding, by colouring alloys, or by the recovery of gold already present in the materials.

docs.title: 3.3 Binding Mercury and the Mercury Liṅga
docs.text: “Binding” (bandha) mercury—making it stable in fire and no longer fluid—is the alchemist’s central goal, and the texts distinguish many kinds of binding by the substances and methods used. A solid, “bound” mercury could be shaped into a liṅga and worshipped, or into beads and pills. Chemically, mercury can be made solid at room temperature only by combining it: with sulphur (as mercuric sulphide) or with other metals as an amalgam. Objects sold in India today as “mercury liṅgas” (pārad śivliṅg) are generally amalgams; handling or heating them can release mercury vapour.

docs.title: 3.4 Mercury and Sulphur: Kajjalī and Rasasindūra
docs.text:
Many mercurial medicines of the rasa texts are based on two mercury–sulphur products.

  • Kajjalī (“lamp-black”) is a black powder made by prolonged grinding of mercury with sulphur. Modern analyses identify it as black mercuric sulphide (metacinnabar), usually with some unreacted mercury and sulphur.

  • Rasasindūra (“mercury vermilion”) and related products are made by heating mercury–sulphur mixtures in a clay-coated glass bottle embedded in a sand-bath (the kūpīpakva, “bottle-cooked”, method) until a red sublimate collects in the neck. This is red mercuric sulphide (cinnabar or vermilion).

  • Makaradhvaja and similar preparations are sublimed mercuric sulphide products, in some recipes made with gold, which the texts praise as rejuvenatives and aphrodisiacs.
