Vermilion had long been made in this way in many parts of the world as a pigment; its production by sublimation was known in China and in medieval Europe. What is distinctive in the rasa texts is its internal medicinal use.

The texts claim that these products, prepared from properly processed mercury and sulphur, are not only harmless but powerfully therapeutic. Modern work has shown that mercuric sulphide is much less soluble, and much less readily absorbed from the gut, than mercury salts or methylmercury. It has not shown that it is harmless. Experimental studies find that cinnabar is absorbed to some degree, accumulates in the kidney and brain with prolonged use, and can cause toxicity; very small particle size and organic coatings may alter its absorption in ways that are not well understood (Liu et al. 2008). Products sold as mercury–sulphur preparations can also contain free mercury and other heavy metals.

docs.title: 3.5 Mercurial Preparations in the Pharmacopoeia
docs.text: From the 13th century onwards the rasa compendia include hundreds of compound medicines containing mercury, usually in the form of kajjalī or rasasindūra, often combined with other minerals (mica, copper, iron, arsenic sulphides, aconite) and herbs. The texts name them after their claimed actions or ingredients—“fever-destroying”, “lord of the elixirs” and so on—and recommend them for fevers, digestive complaints, skin diseases, respiratory diseases, impotence and as general rejuvenatives. Many such preparations are still manufactured. Their claimed benefits rest on the authority of the texts and on practitioners’ experience; they have not been established by adequate clinical trials, while their content of mercury and other heavy metals is well documented (Saper et al. 2008; Ernst 2002).

docs.title: 3.6 What the Texts Knew of Mercury’s Dangers
docs.text: The rasa authors knew that mercury was dangerous. They warn that impure or improperly processed mercury causes a list of diseases and can kill, and they built the doctrine of mercury’s “defects” (doṣa) and their removal on this knowledge (Chapter 2). Their response, however, was to multiply the processing steps rather than to abandon internal use. From the standpoint of modern toxicology, the defects that matter are not the “poison”, “fire” and “dirt” of the texts but the mercury itself, and no traditional operation removes the toxicity of a mercury compound taken into the body. The tradition was not unusual in this: European medicine, too, gave patients mercury for centuries (Section 3.8), and what has changed is the toxicological knowledge now available to every tradition. The Tibetan form of mercury processing, tsotel, which raises the same questions, is described in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 3.7 A Modern Chemical Reading
docs.text:
From the standpoint of modern chemistry, the rasa operations on mercury may be summarised as follows:

  1. mechanical cleaning by washing, grinding and filtering through cloth;

  2. separation of mercury from less volatile metals by distillation;

  3. formation of mercury compounds, especially the black and red sulphides, and of amalgams with gold, silver, tin and other metals;

  4. a large number of treatments with plant materials whose chemical effect, if any, is unknown.

The first three are real chemical operations and show genuine practical skill in handling a difficult and dangerous substance. They were embedded, however, in a theory—the progressive perfecting of mercury until it could transmute metals and the body—that has no chemical basis.

docs.title: 3.8 Mercury in World History
docs.text:
Mercury and cinnabar were known and used across the ancient world long before the rasa texts. Cinnabar was used as a red pigment in Neolithic Anatolia and in China, where it was also placed in tombs. The Greek philosopher Theophrastus (c. 300 BCE) describes the preparation of quicksilver by grinding cinnabar with vinegar in a copper mortar, and the Roman writers Vitruvius, Dioscorides and Pliny describe both the extraction of mercury from cinnabar and its use for gilding and for recovering gold. The great mines of Almadén in Spain were worked in Roman times and supplied much of the world’s mercury until the 20th century (Craddock 1995).

Two uses of mercury were especially important in pre-modern technology:

  • Fire-gilding. An amalgam of gold and mercury is spread on a copper or silver object and heated; the mercury evaporates, leaving a thin layer of gold. Fire-gilding was used in South Asia as elsewhere, for example on images and on metalwork, and was extremely dangerous to the gilders, who breathed the mercury vapour.

  • Amalgamation. Mercury dissolves fine gold and silver, and can be used to collect them from crushed ore or river sand; the mercury is then driven off by heat. From the 16th century the Spanish used amalgamation on a huge scale to extract silver in the Americas, with terrible consequences for the miners.

In China the pursuit of elixirs of immortality made from cinnabar and mercury caused many deaths, including those of several emperors of the Tang dynasty. In Europe mercury was a standard medicine from the 16th to the early 20th century, especially for syphilis, and mercurous chloride (calomel) remained in use as a purgative and in teething powders into the 20th century, when it was found to cause “pink disease” (acrodynia) in infants. The harm to patients was very serious. The rasa tradition’s medicinal use of mercury is therefore part of a widespread pre-modern pattern.

docs.title: 3.9 Vermilion
docs.text: Red mercuric sulphide, made by subliming mercury with sulphur or by grinding natural cinnabar, has been prized as a pigment for millennia. In India vermilion was used in painting, in manuscript illumination, and—with red lead, red ochre and, in modern times, synthetic dyes—in the sindūr applied to the hair parting by married Hindu women and to images of deities. The name sindūra covers several red powders, and its composition in any particular case can only be determined by analysis. Lead- and mercury-containing sindūr products are a source of exposure to these metals (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 3.10 Mercury Today
docs.text: Mercury is now recognised as a global pollutant. Released into the environment by coal burning, small-scale gold mining, industry and waste, it is converted by micro-organisms into methylmercury, which accumulates in fish and is highly toxic to the developing brain—as the disaster at Minamata in Japan, from the 1950s, showed. The Minamata Convention on Mercury, adopted in 2013 and in force since 2017, commits its parties, including India, to reduce the use and release of mercury, to phase out mercury-containing products such as many thermometers and batteries, and to control mercury trade. Traditional medicines are not its main target, but the convention reflects a global consensus that human exposure to mercury should be minimised. The continued use of mercury as a medicine sits uneasily with that consensus.

docs.title: 3.11 Comparative Mercury Alchemy
docs.text:
Table 3.1 sets the Indian treatment of mercury beside those of Chinese and Arabic alchemy.

Table 3.1. Mercury in Three Alchemical Traditions (simplified) Feature Indian rasaśāstra Chinese alchemy Arabic alchemy Main aims Transmutation; bodily immortality; medicine Elixirs of immortality (waidan); later meditative neidan Transmutation; also medicine Key substances Mercury, sulphur, mica, gold Cinnabar, mercury, lead Mercury, sulphur, sal ammoniac Theory of metals Mercury as Śiva’s seed; sulphur as the Goddess’s fluid Yin–yang and the five phases Metals formed from mercury and sulphur Processing Eighteen saṃskāras Repeated cyclical transformations (“nine-cycled elixir”) Distillation, sublimation, calcination Fate Absorbed into Āyurvedic pharmacy Displaced by neidan Transmitted to Latin Europe

The resemblances are close, and all three traditions handled mercury with skill. The Indian tradition is distinctive in its Tantric religious framework and in the way its medicinal branch survived into modern institutional medicine. Whether the traditions were historically connected remains an open question (White 1996; Principe 2013).

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the chemistry behind the main operations—washing and grinding, distillation, and the formation of amalgams and of black and red mercuric sulphide—and the fact that most mercury used in India was imported. Secure, too, is that the texts knew raw mercury to be dangerous. Debated: how far the mercury–sulphur products of the pharmacopoeia are absorbed and what harm they do in the doses used, a question on which the studies cited in Chapter 9 disagree; and whether the Indian, Chinese and Arabic mercury alchemies were historically connected.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Ākara: Mines, Ores and the Archaeometallurgy of South Asia
4.1 Mines in the Historical Record
docs.text:
Every metal described in this volume began as rock in the ground, and every account of Indian metallurgy rests, in the end, on mining. Yet mining is the least documented stage of that history. The Sanskrit word for a mine, ākara (also khani), occurs often enough, and the Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) gives the state a superintendent of mines who is to recognise ores by their colour, weight, smell and taste and to control their working (Section 1.4) (Olivelle 2013). But no Sanskrit, Persian or vernacular text describes how a shaft was sunk, how a mine was drained, or how ore was sorted and washed. The miners themselves left no writings, and their names are almost never recorded.

The evidence is therefore archaeological and, for the last two centuries, documentary. Old workings, spoil heaps and slag dumps survive in many parts of the subcontinent; colonial geologists recorded them in the 19th century, often because they were looking for ore that their predecessors had found first (Ball 1881); and from the 1970s archaeologists and metallurgists began to survey, sample and date them. The richest results have come from the lead–zinc–silver mines of the Aravalli hills in Rajasthan, studied by a British Museum project whose work on zinc is described in Chapter 7 (Willies et al. 1984; Craddock 2017). This chapter surveys the great mining districts—the Aravalli lead–zinc belt, the copper belts of Khetri and Singhbhum and the gold fields of Kolar and Hutti—and then explains, for the general reader, the methods by which scientists study the remains of mining and smelting. These methods, grouped under the name archaeometallurgy, lie behind most of the dates and processes reported in the chapters on the metals that follow (Chapters 5–8) (Killick and Fenn 2012).

The record has a paradox at its centre. Modern mining is often the only reason that ancient workings become accessible: a new shaft or open pit cuts through old galleries, exposes timbers and tools, and brings archaeologists to the site. But the same mining destroys what it exposes, and the best-preserved remains of ancient Indian mining are those of districts where the ore is now exhausted or uneconomic. Much of the evidence at Kolar, for example, was lost when the 19th-century companies followed the old workings down and replaced them with their own.

docs.title: 4.2 Recognising and Dating Old Workings
docs.text:
An old mine can usually be recognised by its form. Pre-modern miners followed the richest ore and left the rest, so that their workings are irregular, narrow and sinuous, tracking the vein or ore body through the rock; modern mines, driven by explosives and machines, are straight and regular. Where the rock was hard, pre-modern miners broke it by fire-setting: a fire was built against the face, and the heated rock, expanding unevenly, cracked and could be prised away with iron tools. Fire-set surfaces have a characteristic smooth, concave, scalloped profile, quite unlike the marks of drilling and blasting, and the soot and charcoal left behind are datable (Craddock 1995). Softer ores and gravels were dug with picks and hoes, and gold-bearing river sands were simply panned.

Dating such workings is difficult. Mines are holes, not deposits: they contain no stratified sequence of floors and finds, and a working may have been abandoned, reopened and extended many times. The usual approach is to date organic material left inside by the miners—charcoal from fire-setting, wooden props, ladders, bowls and torches—by radiocarbon. Craddock’s team obtained such dates from the Rajasthan mines, showing that mining at Rajpura–Dariba and Zawar had begun by the first millennium BCE (Willies et al. 1984; Craddock 2017). The method has well-known pitfalls. Timber may have been old when it was cut or reused from an earlier structure, so that its date is older than the working (the “old wood” problem); charcoal from a fire-set face dates the fire, but not necessarily the first opening of the gallery; and samples that survive are those that happened to be protected, often in the deepest or wettest parts of a mine. A single date therefore proves little, and a mine’s chronology rests on series of dates combined with the dates of the associated smelting sites and their pottery.

Two further kinds of evidence help. Dumps of crushed rock and discarded ore near the mouth of a mine record the dressing of the ore, and stone hammers, grinding stones and washing floors are often found with them. Slag heaps, which are usually close to the mine or to sources of fuel and water, can be dated by the charcoal they contain and analysed to show what was smelted and how (Section 4.5). Together, mine, dump and slag heap make up the landscape of an ancient mining district, and the most informative studies have treated them as a single system.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Old Workings and Modern Prospecting
docs.text:
The first systematic record of old workings was made by the geologists of the colonial state. The Geological Survey of India, founded in 1851 and at first concerned mainly with coal, extended its work in the following decades to metallic ores, and its officers noted old pits, shafts and slag heaps wherever they found them. Valentine Ball’s volume on economic geology in the official Manual of the Geology of India (1881) gathered these observations for the whole subcontinent, district by district, and is still a useful guide to remains that have since disappeared (Ball 1881). The interest of these geologists was practical: old workings were the surest sign of ore, and the pre-modern miners, who had prospected by eye over many centuries, had usually found the outcropping ore bodies first.

The modern mining industry therefore grew, again and again, out of the old. At Kolar the 19th-century companies sank their shafts on the lines of the old workings; at Hutti a British company reopened the ancient mine in the early 20th century, and the field was revived again after independence; in the copper belts of Khetri and Singhbhum and in the Aravalli lead–zinc belt, the slag heaps and old pits directed exploration (Section 4.3). This continuity has a double consequence for the historian. It shows how good the empirical knowledge of the old prospectors was; and it explains why the evidence of their work so often survives only in the descriptions of the people who destroyed it.

docs.title: 4.3 The Major Mining Districts
docs.text:
Table 4.1 lists the principal districts whose pre-modern workings have been studied or recorded, and Figure 4.1 shows where they lie, together with the other mining, smelting and craft sites discussed in this volume. Iron ore, which is widespread and was smelted by small groups in many regions, is treated in Chapter 5, and the diamond fields in Chapter 10.

Figure 4.1. Principal sites discussed in this volume, plotted by latitude and longitude. Only a simplified coastline is drawn; land frontiers, rivers and relief are omitted. Site positions are approximate to within about 20 km. docs.title: 4.3.1 The Aravalli Lead–Zinc–Silver Belt
docs.text: The mines of Zawar and Rajpura–Dariba, and their smelting sites, are described in Chapter 7; here their place in the longer history of mining needs only a few words. They are the best-dated ancient mines in South Asia. Willies, Craddock, Gurjar and Hegde’s survey, published in 1984, showed that the workings had been driven by fire-setting deep into the ore bodies along the strike of the veins, with timber supports and with stopes so large that they must represent centuries of work (Willies et al. 1984). The production of silver from argentiferous galena was the first object, and zinc distillation came much later (Chapter 7). After a long decline, the district was explored again in the 20th century, and the Rajasthan deposits are now among the largest sources of zinc and lead in the world. The state company Hindustan Zinc, formed in 1966, worked them until it was privatised in 2002. It was the opening of modern workings at Zawar and Rajpura–Dariba that made the ancient galleries accessible to the British Museum team.

docs.title: 4.3.2 The Copper Belts: Khetri and Singhbhum
docs.text:
India has two major historic copper districts. The Khetri belt runs for some 80 km through the Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts of northern Rajasthan, at the northern end of the Aravallis. Old workings and slag heaps are found at many places along it, and the scale of the slag shows that copper was produced there over a long period. How long is uncertain. The copper objects of the Ganeshwar–Jodhpura culture, found a short distance away and dated to the third and second millennia BCE, suggest that the ores were exploited very early (Chapter 8), but few of the workings or slag heaps themselves have been securely dated, and most of the surviving debris may belong to the first and second millennia CE (Agrawal 2000; Kenoyer and Miller 1999). Copper was still being smelted in the belt in the 19th century, when it was described by British officers and geologists (Ball 1881); the indigenous industry declined as imported copper became cheap, and modern mining was revived after independence by the state company Hindustan Copper, founded in 1967.

The Singhbhum copper belt of Jharkhand follows a shear zone for more than 100 km through the hills of the Chota Nagpur plateau. Here too 19th-century geologists recorded old workings and slag along the belt, and saw in them the best guide to where ore was to be found (Ball 1881). Modern working began in the first half of the 20th century under a British company, the Indian Copper Corporation, with a smelter at Ghatsila, and passed to Hindustan Copper in the 1970s. The age of the old workings has not been established by modern dating.

Where the Harappan cities obtained their copper is a long-standing question that illustrates both the promise and the limits of archaeometallurgy. Three sources are usually considered: the Khetri belt and the Aravallis, close to the Ganeshwar–Jodhpura sites; the copper deposits of Baluchistan and Afghanistan; and Oman, across the Arabian Sea, which Mesopotamian texts name as Magan, a land of copper, and where Harappan pottery and other objects have been found (Kenoyer and Miller 1999). Trace elements and lead isotope ratios can in principle distinguish these sources, and several studies have attempted it. The results so far point to more than one source, varying between sites and periods, rather than to a single supplier; but the scattered sampling of both objects and ores, and the habit of recycling copper, mean that no answer is yet secure. The arsenic present in many Harappan copper objects may in part reflect the character of the ores rather than deliberate alloying, another question that analysis has raised but not settled.

India’s own copper was never sufficient for its needs. From antiquity copper was imported by sea—the Periplus lists it among the imports of western Indian ports (Casson 1989)—and in the 17th century the Dutch East India Company shipped large quantities of Japanese copper to the markets of Gujarat, the Coromandel coast and Bengal (Prakash 1985). The brass and bronze vessels of early modern India were made in part from imported metal, and the history of Indian copper is a history of trade as much as of mining.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Gold: Kolar and Hutti
docs.text:
The two great gold fields of peninsular India lie in Karnataka. Both are in ancient volcanic and sedimentary rocks (greenstone belts), in which gold occurs in quartz reefs, and both were worked long before the modern period (Biswas and Biswas 1996; Craddock 1995).

At Kolar, east of Bengaluru, the reefs had been followed by old workings that the 19th-century prospectors found and used as a guide. Reports of the old pits and of local gold-washing were recorded by a survey officer in the early 19th century, and from the 1870s a succession of concessions and companies took up the field; the London mining firm of John Taylor and Sons assumed the management in 1880. The Kolar Gold Fields became one of the deepest mining operations in the world. The main mines followed the Champion reef to depths of more than three kilometres, where rock temperatures and sudden rock-bursts made work extremely dangerous. In 1902 the mines received electric power from a hydro-electric station on the Kaveri at Śivanasamudra, one of the first in Asia. The mines were taken over by the state after independence, passed to the central public-sector company Bharat Gold Mines in 1972, and were closed in 2001 when the cost of working at such depths could no longer be met. How far down the ancient miners went at Kolar, and when they worked, is poorly known, because the old workings were largely destroyed by the modern ones.

Historical Note: Physics at the Bottom of a Gold Mine

The depth of the Kolar mines gave them an unexpected second life in science. More than two kilometres of rock shield the deep levels from almost all the cosmic radiation that reaches the surface, and physicists of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, working with colleagues from Osaka and Durham, installed detectors there. In 1965 they reported muons produced deep underground by neutrinos that cosmic rays had generated in the atmosphere—one of the first two detections of such neutrinos, made at about the same time as a similar experiment in a South African gold mine (Achar et al. 1965). Later experiments at Kolar, from the 1980s, searched for the decay of the proton. The underground experiments ended in the early 1990s, some years before the mines closed.

At Hutti, in Raichur district, the old workings are better preserved. They are among the deepest pre-modern mine workings recorded in India, but their age has not been established by published modern dating. Hutti, unlike Kolar, is still worked, by a company owned by the state of Karnataka.

The ancient miners of these fields broke the quartz by fire-setting, crushed it with stone hammers and on grinding stones, and recovered the gold by washing the crushed rock, in which the gold, many times heavier than quartz, settles out. Large numbers of grinding stones and hammer-stones are reported from near old workings in the Deccan gold fields. The same principle of gravity separation was used for alluvial gold.

docs.title: 4.3.4 River Gold and Gold-Washers
docs.text: Much Indian gold came not from reefs but from rivers. Gold weathered out of its parent rock is carried by streams and concentrated in gravels and sands, from which it can be recovered by washing in a wooden dish or trough. Rivers in eastern and central India, in the north-western mountains and in the south were washed for gold, and the name of the Subarnarekha (“streak of gold”) records the practice (Section 8.1). Colonial surveys describe families and communities in Chota Nagpur, Odisha and the central Indian hills who washed the river sands for gold in the dry season, earning a meagre living from small quantities of gold dust (Ball 1881). Their work is almost invisible archaeologically, but it may have supplied much of the gold that circulated within India before the great imports of the early historic period.

docs.title: 4.4 From Ore to Metal: The Chemistry of Ore Treatment
docs.text: Ore as it leaves the mine is a mixture of the valuable mineral with worthless rock (gangue). Before smelting, the mineral must be concentrated, and some ores must be chemically transformed. Each step leaves its own residue, and the residues are the archaeologist’s evidence (Figure 4.2).

docs.title: 4.4.1 Dressing
docs.text: The first step, ore dressing, is mechanical. The ore is broken by hammering and sorted by hand, the rich pieces being kept and the poor discarded; it is then crushed and ground, and the heavy mineral is separated from the light gangue by washing. Galena, sphalerite and the copper sulphides are all much denser than quartz and the other common rock-forming minerals, and gold is denser still, so that washing in a stream of water concentrates them. These operations leave heaps of discarded rock and fine sand, and stone hammers, anvils and grinding stones, near the mine.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Roasting
docs.text:
Most of the metal ores of the Aravallis and of the copper belts are sulphides. Sulphide ores cannot be reduced directly by charcoal in the way that oxides can, and they were first roasted: heated in air, on open heaps or in kilns, so that the sulphur burned off as sulphur dioxide and the metal was left as an oxide. For sphalerite, the zinc ore of Zawar, the reaction is

\[2\,\text{ZnS} + 3\,\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2\,\text{ZnO} + 2\,\text{SO}_2 .\]

Roasting was slow, it had to be controlled to avoid melting the ore, and the choking fumes made it one of the most unpleasant stages of the work. Roasting sites leave discoloured, sulphur-rich ground and partly roasted ore.

docs.title: 4.4.3 Smelting and Slag
docs.text:
In smelting, the roasted or oxide ore is heated with charcoal in a furnace. Carbon monoxide from the burning charcoal reduces the metal oxide to metal, as described for iron and copper in Chapters 5 and 8 below. The gangue, chiefly silica, must also be removed, and it is removed by making it into a molten slag that separates from the metal. Silica on its own melts only at a very high temperature, but combined with iron oxide it forms iron silicate, mainly the mineral fayalite, which melts at about 1200 °C, within the reach of a charcoal furnace:

\[2\,\text{FeO} + \text{SiO}_2 \longrightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{SiO}_4 .\]

In iron smelting the iron oxide for the slag comes from the ore itself, which is why bloomery smelting wastes much of the iron. In copper and lead smelting, iron oxide or other fluxes were added, or were already present in the ore, so that the slag would run. Because the smelter needs the slag to be fluid, slag composition is a record of how well he controlled his furnace.

docs.title: 4.4.4 Copper Sulphides and Matte
docs.text:
Copper sulphide ores, of which chalcopyrite (a copper–iron sulphide) is the commonest, are the most complex. If they are only partly roasted and then smelted, the product is not copper but matte, a molten mixture of copper and iron sulphides that is heavier than slag and collects beneath it. The matte must then be roasted and smelted again, sometimes several times, before metallic copper is obtained; in simplified form the final stage can be written

\[\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2\,\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2 .\]

Fragments of matte trapped in slag are among the clues that tell an archaeometallurgist that sulphide ores were being worked.

docs.title: 4.4.5 Gold from Quartz
docs.text: Gold occurs as the native metal and needs no smelting, but in reef ores it is often in particles too small to see. Pre-modern miners recovered it by fine grinding and washing, and in some places by amalgamation with mercury, which takes up the gold; the mercury was then driven off by heat. The same technique was used to recover gold from the sweepings of the Mughal mint (Section 8.13). The colonial companies at Kolar used mechanised crushing and amalgamation and later the cyanide process, which dissolves gold from finely ground ore and is the basis of most modern gold extraction. Both mercury and cyanide are deadly poisons, and the tailings of gold mining in India and elsewhere remain a source of contamination.

docs.title: 4.5 Archaeometallurgy: How the Evidence Is Read
docs.text:
Archaeometallurgy is the study of past mining and metal production by the combined methods of archaeology, materials science and chemistry (Killick and Fenn 2012; Pollard and Heron 2008). Its starting point is that every stage of production leaves physical traces, and that these traces—far more abundant than finished objects, which were reused, melted down or lost—record the processes that made them. Figure 4.2 sets out the chain of operations and what each stage leaves behind. The main analytical techniques are listed in Table 1.3; this section explains what they are used to find out.

Figure 4.2. The chain of operations in metal production and the remains that each stage typically leaves. Not every stage applies to every metal: native gold needs no smelting, and oxide ores no roasting.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Reading Slag
docs.text: Slag is the most abundant and the most informative waste of metal production, and it is almost indestructible. Its form shows how it left the furnace: slag that was tapped while molten flows out in ropy, layered cakes with smooth upper surfaces, while slag that solidified inside the furnace is irregular and full of charcoal impressions. Its chemical composition, determined by X-ray fluorescence or electron-microprobe analysis, shows what ore and fluxes were used, and its mineral phases, seen under the microscope, show how hot the furnace was and how quickly the slag cooled. Droplets of metal or matte trapped in it reveal what was being made, and how much was lost. Slag also allows a rough estimate of output: if the volume of a slag heap is measured and the ratio of slag to metal is known from analysis, the total production of a site can be estimated, though such figures carry wide margins of error (Bachmann 1982; Craddock 1995). A practical point matters here: slags from the smelting of iron, copper and lead can look alike in the field, and only analysis can tell them apart.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Technical Ceramics
docs.text: Crucibles, retorts, tuyères and furnace linings were made of clay and were in direct contact with the hot charge. Their inner surfaces react with it and preserve a record of what it was: a glassy layer on a crucible wall may contain droplets of metal, traces of zinc, or the oxides of the elements being melted. The analysis of such ceramics has been central to three of the stories told in this volume—the crucible steel of south India and Sri Lanka, whose crucibles were made of specially selected refractory clays (Chapter 6) (Rehren and Papachristou 2003); the zinc retorts of Zawar (Chapter 7); and the cupels and litharge that show silver being refined at Rajpura–Dariba (Craddock 2017). The ceramics themselves are a technical achievement, and their composition shows how potters met the demands of the smelter (Section 12.7).

docs.title: 4.5.3 Metal Objects
docs.text:
Finished objects are studied in two ways. Metallography—the examination of a polished and etched section under the microscope—shows the internal structure of the metal: whether it was cast or hammered, annealed or quenched, made of one piece or forge-welded from many. It was by metallography that the wrought and quenched high-tin bronzes of Kerala were distinguished from cast bell metal (Srinivasan and Glover 1995), and that the structure of crucible steel was explained (Chapter 6). Chemical analysis gives the composition of the alloy and its trace elements. Here care is needed: corrosion changes the composition of a metal surface, so that surface analysis by portable X-ray fluorescence, though non-destructive and convenient, can mislead, and reliable figures usually require a small sample drilled from the clean metal beneath. Trace elements such as arsenic, antimony, nickel, silver and bismuth come mainly from the ore, and can group objects made from the same source.

Wrought iron carries a record of its own making. Because bloomery iron was never fully molten, it retains small inclusions of the slag from which it was separated, drawn out into threads by forging. The inclusions preserve much of the chemical character of the smelting slag, and through it of the ore, the furnace lining and the fuel ash; their analysis can distinguish iron made directly in a bloomery from iron refined from cast iron, and can sometimes group iron objects by the region or workshop that smelted them. In South Asia the slag inclusions and the high phosphorus content of bloomery iron, derived from the ores, have been central to the explanation of the Delhi pillar’s resistance to corrosion (Chapter 5) (Balasubramaniam 2000). Steel tells a further story through its microstructure: the proportion and form of pearlite and cementite show its carbon content and how it was cooled, and the banded structures of crucible steel record the segregation of impurities during the slow solidification of the ingot (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 4.5.4 Lead Isotopes and Provenance
docs.text:
The most widely used method of tracing metal to its source is lead isotope analysis. Lead has four stable isotopes. One, lead-204, has existed unchanged since the Earth formed; the others, lead-206, lead-207 and lead-208, are produced continuously by the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium. The proportions of the four in an ore deposit therefore depend on the geological age of the deposit and on the uranium and thorium in its source rocks, and different ore fields often have distinctive ratios. Crucially, the ratios do not change appreciably when ore is smelted, refined or alloyed, so that lead in a coin, a weight or a bronze image preserves the “signature” of its ore (Pollard and Heron 2008; Rehren and Pernicka 2008).

The method has limits that its users stress. Ore fields of similar geological age can have overlapping signatures, so that a match shows only that an object is consistent with a source, not that it came from it. Metal was often mixed and recycled, blending signatures. And in copper alloys, the lead may have come from the copper ore or from lead deliberately added, so that it traces the lead and not necessarily the copper. In South Asia the method has been applied to Harappan copper, to coins and to South Indian bronze images (Section 8.6) (Srinivasan 1999), but the reference database of Indian ore fields is still incomplete, and many conclusions remain provisional.

The sources of gold are harder to trace, because gold contains little lead. One approach uses the tiny grains of platinum-group metals (alloys of osmium, iridium and ruthenium) that are often found as inclusions in gold from river gravels but not in gold mined from quartz reefs, so that their presence in an object points to alluvial gold. Another uses the silver and copper contents of native gold, which differ from deposit to deposit, though they are altered by any refining or alloying. It has been suggested that some Harappan gold came from the reef deposits of the Deccan, but this has not been established, and the river gold of the north-western mountains is an equally plausible source.

docs.title: 4.5.5 Analysing Coins
docs.text:
Coins are the most closely dated and most numerous metal objects of the historical period, and their analysis is one of the main tools of economic history. Debasement—the reduction of the precious-metal content of a coinage, usually under fiscal pressure—can be read directly from a series of analyses, and the fineness of coins issued in a ruler’s name is a measure of the state of his treasury. Analyses have shown, for example, the decline in the gold content of the later Gupta coinage (Section 8.11).

The oldest method of analysing a coin without damaging it is the measurement of its specific gravity, by weighing it in air and in water—the principle discussed by al-Bīrūnī and reproduced in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Section 8.13). Because gold is almost twice as dense as silver and more than twice as dense as copper, the specific gravity of a gold coin gives a good estimate of its fineness, provided that it is an alloy of gold with only one other metal and has no hidden cavities. Modern methods are more precise but have their own pitfalls. Coins of debased gold or silver are often enriched at the surface, either deliberately, by treatments that removed base metal from the surface to make the coin look finer than it was, or by corrosion, which removes copper preferentially; a surface analysis then overstates the fineness. Some methods analyse the whole volume of a coin non-destructively, and others require a tiny sample from a cut edge. The comparison of such analyses with the written standards of the mint—the Arthaśāstra’s prescriptions, Ṭhakkura Pherū’s register of coins and the Mughal assayer’s grades (Sections 8.12 and 8.13)—is one of the places where the textual and the material history of Indian metallurgy can be tested against each other.

docs.title: 4.5.6 Dating Metallurgy
docs.text: Metallurgical sites are dated chiefly by radiocarbon dating of the charcoal used as fuel, which is often trapped in slag and furnace debris and was usually made from young wood, avoiding much of the “old wood” problem of mine timbers. Fired clay from furnaces and crucibles can sometimes be dated by thermoluminescence, which measures the time since the clay was last heated. Iron and steel present a special opportunity: because the carbon in iron smelted or carburised with charcoal comes from the charcoal, the iron itself can in favourable cases be dated by accelerator radiocarbon methods, which need only small samples (Killick and Fenn 2012). Dates from associated pottery, coins and inscriptions complete the picture. The dating of early iron in South Asia (Chapter 5) and of zinc distillation at Zawar (Chapter 7) both rest on radiocarbon series of this kind, and both show why single dates should not be over-interpreted.

docs.title: 4.5.7 Experiment and Ethnography
docs.text: Analysis shows what was made and in what conditions, but not always how. Two further methods help. In experimental archaeology, researchers rebuild furnaces on the excavated pattern and run them, to test whether a reconstruction works and what it produces; Juleff’s experimental smelts in wind-driven furnaces in Sri Lanka showed that the excavated furnaces could have produced high-carbon iron with the monsoon wind alone (Section 5.4) (Juleff 1996). In ethnoarchaeology, researchers record crafts still practised by traditional methods—iron smelting among the Agaria of central India (Elwin 1942), high-tin bronze working in Kerala (Srinivasan and Glover 1995), lost-wax casting at Swamimalai and among the Dhokra casters—as models for interpreting ancient remains. Both approaches need caution: an experiment shows what was possible, not what was done, and a living craft has its own history and is not a fossil of ancient practice.

docs.title: 4.5.8 What Archaeometallurgy Cannot Do
docs.text: Laboratory analysis is sometimes presented as if it could settle any historical question. It cannot. It can show the composition, structure, source and date of materials; it cannot by itself show who made them, under whose authority, for what purpose, or what they meant. The most secure conclusions in this volume are those in which archaeology, analysis and written sources agree (Section 15.5). Sampling also raises ethical questions: drilling a sample from a temple image or a museum object is destructive, however small, and needs the consent of its owners and custodians. Much Indian archaeometallurgy has been carried out jointly by Indian and foreign institutions; its continued growth depends on Indian laboratories, on access to sites before they are destroyed by modern mining, and on the publication of results in full.

docs.title: 4.6 Miners and the Costs of Mining
docs.text:
Pre-modern mining in India, as elsewhere, was hard, dangerous and badly rewarded. The narrow, hot, smoke-filled galleries of fire-set mines, the lifting of ore and water by hand, and the roasting and smelting of lead and sulphide ores all took a heavy toll on health. The Arthaśāstra’s state controlled mines as a source of revenue, and for its farms and workshops it envisaged slaves, hired labourers and convicts working off fines alongside free artisans (Olivelle 2013); in later periods the mines of Mewar and of the Deccan were worked for rulers who drew revenue from them, by communities about whom almost nothing is recorded. Specialist mining and smelting groups, like the iron-smelting Agaria (Section 5.9), had low social standing, and their skills did not raise it.

The colonial and modern mines brought new forms of labour. The Kolar Gold Fields drew tens of thousands of workers, most of them Tamil-speaking migrants from the neighbouring districts of the Madras Presidency, many of them from Dalit communities; they lived in company “lines” and worked at great depths for low wages. Silicosis, caused by breathing the fine quartz dust of the gold reefs, was a lasting occupational disease of the field, as it was in the deep gold mines of South Africa, and rock-bursts killed many. The workforce of the fields became a centre of trade unionism and of Dalit political and religious movements in the 20th century. The closure of the mines in 2001 left a large population without its livelihood, amid heaps of cyanide tailings.

Mining also has environmental and social costs that outlast the mines. The slag and spoil of the Aravalli lead and zinc mines, and the soils around old smelting sites, are rich in lead, zinc and cadmium. Much of India’s present mining takes place in the forest and hill regions where Adivasi communities live, and conflicts over land, displacement and consent, of which the Niyamgiri bauxite case in Odisha is the best known, are discussed in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti. The historian of mining has to hold together the ingenuity of the miners, the wealth that their work created for others, and the costs that they and their landscapes bore.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Fuel
docs.text:
Mining was only the first claim that metal production made on the land. All the crafts described in this volume depended on fire, and pre-modern fire meant wood, charcoal, dung and crop residues. Smelting iron in a bloomery furnace consumed several times the weight of the iron in charcoal, and charcoal itself was made from a still larger weight of wood; glass furnaces, brick clamps, lime kilns, salt boiling and sugar boiling all required large quantities of fuel. Around major production centres—the iron-smelting regions of central India, the mining districts of the Aravallis—woodland was cut back, and 19th-century observers described the scarcity of fuel as a limit on production. Colonial forest laws, which restricted the access of smelters and charcoal-makers to forests, were partly a response to such pressures and partly a means of reserving timber for the state. These facts are a useful corrective to the idea that traditional technologies were inherently sustainable: they were small in scale by modern standards and used renewable fuels, but they could and did exhaust local resources and harm their workers.

Health and Safety Note

Sulphur dioxide from roasting, lead fume from smelting, quartz dust, and the mercury and cyanide used in gold extraction are all serious hazards. Old workings, spoil heaps and tailings can be unstable or contaminated and should not be entered or disturbed. See also the note in Section 1.1.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the Rajasthan lead–zinc–silver mines were worked from the first millennium BCE, as a series of radiocarbon dates shows; pre-modern miners broke hard rock by fire-setting and smelters relied on iron-silicate slags; and the methods of archaeometallurgy described here can establish the composition, structure and date of materials. Debated or unknown: the age of most workings in the Khetri and Singhbhum copper belts and the Kolar and Hutti gold fields; where the Harappans obtained their copper; and how far lead isotopes can assign Indian metal to particular ore fields while the reference data remain incomplete.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Loha: Iron and the Delhi Pillar
5.1 Iron in South Asian History
docs.text:
Iron (Sanskrit ayas, later loha, kṛṣṇāyas) transformed the economies of South Asia, as it did elsewhere, in the first millennium BCE: iron axes, ploughshares, sickles and weapons accompanied the expansion of farming and of cities in the Ganga plain and the Deccan. From then until the 19th century, iron was smelted throughout the subcontinent in small charcoal-fuelled furnaces by specialist communities, and Indian smiths produced both ordinary wrought iron and, in some regions, high-quality steel (Chakrabarti 1992; Agrawal 2000).

Three features of the Indian iron tradition stand out. Iron working began early, and probably independently of developments in western Asia. Smiths were able to forge-weld large masses of bloomery iron into objects weighing several tonnes, of which the Delhi pillar is the most famous. And in south India and Sri Lanka, iron was converted into high-carbon crucible steel, the subject of Chapter 6.

docs.title: 5.2 The Beginnings of Iron
docs.text:
Until the 1990s it was usual to date the beginning of iron in India to about 1000 BCE and to associate it with the Painted Grey Ware culture of the Ganga plain. Radiocarbon dates from several sites have since pushed the beginnings back. Rakesh Tewari’s excavations at Malhar, Raja Nal-ka-tila and Dadupur in Uttar Pradesh yielded iron objects and smelting debris in levels dated to the early second millennium BCE, perhaps from about 1800 BCE (Tewari 2003). In the southern Deccan, sites such as Hallur and Komaranahalli in Karnataka have iron in levels of the late second millennium BCE. These early dates have been debated—over the calibration and context of the samples, and over whether small quantities of iron indicate regular smelting—but most specialists now accept that iron working in South Asia began in the second millennium BCE and developed largely independently of that of western Asia (Chakrabarti 1992; Agrawal 2000). Table 5.1 lists some of the key sites.

Table 5.1. Some Early Iron Sites in South Asia (dates approximate and debated) Site Region Date (approx.) Evidence Malhar, Raja Nal-ka-tila, Dadupur Uttar Pradesh early–mid 2nd mill. BCE Iron objects, slag, furnace remains Hallur, Komaranahalli Karnataka late 2nd mill. BCE Iron objects Atranjikhera Uttar Pradesh late 2nd–early 1st mill. BCE Iron objects and slag Painted Grey Ware sites Ganga–Yamuna plain c. 1200–600 BCE Iron tools and weapons Megalithic burials Deccan and south India 1st mill. BCE Abundant iron weapons and tools Kodumanal Tamil Nadu late centuries BCE Iron smelting; crucible steel

In January 2025 the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology published radiocarbon (AMS) dates on charcoal and luminescence dates on pottery from sites in Tamil Nadu, notably Sivagalai, which it interpreted as showing the use of iron in the fourth millennium BCE (Rajan and Sivanantham 2025). If confirmed, these dates would be by far the earliest for iron anywhere. They have attracted considerable public debate, and their acceptance will depend on publication of the full data in a peer-reviewed form, independent dating and close scrutiny of the association between the dated samples and the iron objects. Until then they should be treated as a claim under review.

docs.title: 5.3 Iron and the Early Historic World
5.3.1 Iron and the Second Urbanisation
docs.text: In the middle of the first millennium BCE cities and states grew up again in the Ganga plain—the “second urbanisation” after the Harappan cities. An influential argument, associated especially with the historian R. S. Sharma, held that iron tools made this possible, by allowing the clearing of the dense forests of the middle Ganga plain and the cultivation of its heavy soils. Archaeologists such as D. K. Chakrabarti have criticised this view: iron appears in the region well before the cities, the forests were probably less dense than supposed, and fire and copper tools could clear land. Most scholars now see iron as one of several factors—alongside rice cultivation, population growth, trade and political change—rather than as the single cause of urbanisation (Chakrabarti 1992).

docs.title: 5.3.2 Iron in the Megalithic South
docs.text: In the Deccan and south India the first millennium BCE is the period of the “megalithic” burials—stone circles, cists and urn burials—which contain great quantities of iron objects: swords, daggers, spearheads, arrowheads, axes, sickles, hoes, tripods, lamp-hangers and horse-bits. The quantity and variety of these grave goods show that iron working was well established and widely practised, and they include some of the earliest high-carbon iron and steel in South Asia (Agrawal 2000; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004). Settlements of the period, such as Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu, have yielded evidence for smelting and smithing as well as for crucible steel.

docs.title: 5.3.3 Iron in the State
docs.text: In the Arthaśāstra, the superintendent of metals runs workshops for iron among other metals, and the armoury supplies iron weapons and tools; iron is listed among the “forest products” and mineral resources that the state controls (Olivelle 2013). Buddhist and Jain texts mention smiths (kammāra in Pali) as a recognised occupation; the Buddha’s last meal, according to the Pali canon, was given by Cunda, a smith’s son. By the early centuries CE iron was the ordinary metal of agriculture, carpentry and war throughout the subcontinent.

docs.title: 5.4 Smelting in the Bloomery Furnace
docs.text:
Before modern blast furnaces, iron in India was made by the bloomery process. Iron ore and charcoal were charged into a small clay shaft furnace, and air was blown in with hand- or foot-operated bellows (bhastrā) through clay pipes (tuyères). The carbon monoxide produced by the burning charcoal reduced the iron oxide to metallic iron at temperatures well below its melting point, and the iron collected as a spongy, slag-laden lump, the bloom, which was then repeatedly reheated and hammered to expel the slag and consolidate the metal (Figure 5.1).

Figure 5.1. Schematic section of a bloomery furnace. Furnace shapes and sizes varied widely between regions and periods.

The main reactions are the reduction of iron oxide by carbon monoxide, for example

\[\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\,\text{CO} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{Fe} + 3\,\text{CO}_2 ,\]

and the formation of a fluid slag (largely iron silicate) from the gangue of the ore, which carries away impurities but also consumes some of the iron. Bloomery iron is usually low in carbon, contains slag inclusions, and in South Asia often has a relatively high phosphorus content derived from the ores.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Wind-Powered Furnaces in Sri Lanka
docs.text: Gill Juleff’s work at Samanalawewa in southern Sri Lanka revealed a different solution: rows of furnaces built along the crests of hills facing the strong monsoon winds, which supplied the air blast without bellows. Dated to the later first millennium CE, these furnaces produced high-carbon iron and show how closely South Asian smelters adapted their technology to local conditions (Juleff 1996, 1998).

docs.title: 5.5 The Delhi Iron Pillar
docs.text:
The iron pillar standing in the Quwwat al-Islām mosque in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi, is the best known iron object from ancient India (Figure 5.2). It is about 7.2 m long, of which roughly a metre is below ground, tapers from about 42 cm in diameter at the base to about 30 cm below the capital, and weighs more than six tonnes (Balasubramaniam 2002; Anantharaman 1996).

Figure 5.2. The iron pillar in the Quwwat al-Islām mosque, Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi. The pillar is a forge-welded wrought-iron column of c. 400 CE. Photo: Aiwok, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.5.1 Date and Inscription
docs.text: A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta-period Brāhmī on the pillar records that it was set up as a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu on a hill called Viṣṇupada by a king named Candra. On the basis of the script and the content, most historians identify Candra with the Gupta emperor Candragupta II (r. c. 375–415 CE), and date the pillar to around 400 CE. The inscription is a eulogy in verse. It praises the king’s victories—over enemies who had united against him in Vaṅga (Bengal), and over the Vāhlīkas after crossing the seven mouths of the Indus—and speaks of his sole sovereignty over the earth; some scholars read it as composed after the king’s death. The identification with Candragupta II rests on the palaeography and the historical fit rather than on an explicit dynastic name. The pillar was not made for its present site. Its original location is uncertain—Balasubramaniam argued for Udayagiri near Vidisha in central India—and it was moved to Delhi in the medieval period, probably in the 11th to 13th centuries (Balasubramaniam 2002).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Manufacture
docs.text: The pillar was made by forge-welding: lumps of bloomery iron were heated and hammered together, piece by piece, to build up the column. Weld lines and slag inclusions visible in the metal confirm this. How exactly the smiths handled a growing mass of several tonnes is still debated; it would have required many furnaces, a large team, and great skill in keeping the welding surfaces clean and hot (Balasubramaniam 2002).

docs.title: 5.5.3 Why It Has Corroded So Little
docs.text:
The pillar is famous because, after some sixteen centuries in the open, it shows little rust. Many explanations were once proposed, from a coating of ghee to a “lost” metallurgy. Research over the 20th century, culminating in the work of R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur, has explained the phenomenon in ordinary scientific terms (Balasubramaniam 2000, 2002).

  1. Composition. The iron is very low in carbon and sulphur but has a relatively high phosphorus content (around 0.1 per cent or more in different analyses), derived from the ore and the smelting process. In modern steels phosphorus is avoided, but in wrought iron exposed to the atmosphere it promotes the formation of a protective surface layer.

  2. A protective film. Analysis of the surface layer shows, next to the metal, a compact amorphous layer of iron oxyhydroxide (\(\delta\)-FeOOH, misawite) and, within the rust, crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate. Phosphorus catalyses the formation of this dense, adherent layer, which slows further corrosion greatly. Slag particles in the metal may also contribute.

  3. Environment. Delhi’s climate, with long dry periods and a pattern of alternate wetting and drying, favours the formation of the protective layer, and the relative humidity is high enough for corrosion only for part of the year.

The explanation was reached gradually. Robert Hadfield’s analysis in 1912 established the pillar’s low carbon and sulphur and relatively high phosphorus (Hadfield 1912). Through the middle of the 20th century, investigators variously emphasised the purity of the iron, the dry climate of Delhi, the slag particles in the metal, or the protective effect of the pillar’s surface film, and popular writers added explanations of their own. T. R. Anantharaman’s The Rustless Wonder summarised the debate in the 1990s (Anantharaman 1996). Balasubramaniam’s detailed characterisation of the surface layers, published from 2000 onwards, combined these elements into a coherent mechanism and is now the standard account (Balasubramaniam 2000, 2002). The episode is a good example of how a historical object can become a research problem in modern materials science.

The pillar is therefore not “rustless”. It corrodes, but very slowly, and the part that was buried in the ground, where it was damp, corroded more. Its durability is the result of a particular iron composition interacting with a particular environment, an outcome that its makers achieved without, of course, understanding the mechanism. Balasubramaniam’s studies are also of practical interest to corrosion scientists working on weathering steels.

docs.title: 5.6 Other Large Iron Objects
docs.text:
The Delhi pillar is not unique. Other large forge-welded iron objects include (Balasubramaniam 2002):

The Dhar pillar At Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, a forge-welded iron pillar now in three pieces, usually attributed to the Paramāra period (c. 11th century). Its original length was greater than that of the Delhi pillar. The Kodachadri pillar A smaller iron pillar at a temple on Kodachadri hill in Karnataka. Temple beams Large forge-welded iron beams were used in temples at Puri and Konark in Odisha (12th–13th centuries). Forge-welded cannon Early modern rulers commissioned large wrought-iron guns, built up from forge-welded bars and rings; examples survive at Thanjavur, Bishnupur and elsewhere.

docs.title: 5.7 Iron in the Medieval and Early Modern Economy
docs.text:
Between the Delhi pillar and the colonial period, iron was produced across the subcontinent by thousands of small furnaces. The demand came from agriculture (ploughshares, sickles, hoes), building (clamps, nails and, in some temples, beams), transport (tyres and fittings), and above all war. The armies of the Sultanates, the Vijayanagara empire, the Mughals and their successors consumed iron and steel for swords, spears, arrowheads, armour, horse equipment and, from the 16th century, guns and shot.

Mughal administrative sources describe imperial workshops (kārkhānas) for arms and other goods, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī gives an account of the imperial arsenal and of the making of matchlock barrels. Earlier barrels, it says, had been made by flattening iron and welding the edges together, and often burst; the method it credits to Akbar’s workshops was to twist a flattened strip of iron obliquely into a roll, so that the folds overlapped, and to weld them gradually in the fire (Āʾīn 1.37) (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873). Large guns were made either by forge-welding, like the wrought-iron cannon mentioned above, or by casting in bronze; the great bronze guns of the Deccan sultanates are among the largest pre-modern cannon in the world (Khan 2004).

The scale of production was considerable. When British surveyors and geologists examined indigenous iron-making in the 19th century, they found furnaces in operation in central India, the Deccan, the eastern hills, the Himalaya and the south, with regional differences in furnace design, ores and fuels. Their reports, together with Elwin’s ethnography, are the main record of a technology that was disappearing as they wrote (Elwin 1942; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

docs.title: 5.8 Iron in the Texts
docs.text:
The later Vedic texts distinguish a “dark” metal, iron, from copper (Chapter 1), and the Arthaśāstra’s interest in iron has been noted above. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) records Indian iron and steel among the goods shipped from western India to the Red Sea (Chapter 6) (Casson 1989).

The rasa texts, interested in iron mainly as a medicine, classify it into three main kinds, muṇḍa, tīkṣṇa and kānta, each with sub-varieties. Tīkṣṇa (“sharp”) is generally understood as steel. Kānta is associated with the lodestone (ayaskānta, “beloved of iron”) and is praised as the best kind; muṇḍa is the ordinary or inferior iron. Attempts to equate the three exactly with modern wrought iron, steel and cast iron are not secure, since the texts’ descriptions mix physical and medicinal qualities (Ray 1956; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

docs.title: 5.9 Iron-Smelting Communities
docs.text:
Iron smelting continued in many parts of India into the 20th century, carried on by specialist groups such as the Agaria of central India, the Asur of Jharkhand, the Lohar of many regions and smith castes in the south. Verrier Elwin’s The Agaria (1942) is the classic ethnography (Elwin 1942). It describes small clay shaft furnaces worked with paired bellows, the separation of the bloom and its forging, and the rich mythology that surrounded the work: the furnace as a living being, the iron spirit Lohasur to whom offerings were made, and the myths that explained why the Agaria worked iron. Elwin also documented their poverty and the pressures on their craft from forest restrictions and imported iron.

Historical Note: The Decline of Indigenous Iron

During the 19th century traditional iron smelting in India declined sharply. Cheap imported British iron and steel undercut the local product; forest laws restricted the cutting of wood for charcoal; and the new railway and colonial markets favoured standardised factory iron. Modern iron and steel making in India began with colonial-era ventures and, decisively, with the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur (production from 1912). The knowledge of the village smelters survives today mainly in ethnographic records and in a few demonstration revivals (Elwin 1942; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

docs.title: 5.10 Iron in the North-East: The Khasi Hills
docs.text:
The iron industry of the Khasi Hills in Meghalaya is one of the best documented outside the peninsula. Its ore is described as the fine grains of magnetite released by the weathering of the local rock: the iron-bearing sand was washed out of the decomposed rock in running water, concentrated, and smelted with charcoal in small bloomery furnaces worked with bellows. The British officer Henry Yule described the industry in 1842, when Khasi iron was still traded down to the Sylhet plain (Yule 1842); the trade seems to have dwindled later in the century, as imported iron became cheap in the plains.

Modern fieldwork has given the industry a depth that the 19th-century accounts could not. Paweł Prokop and Ireneusz Suliga dated charcoal embedded in slag heaps on the plateau by radiocarbon and found a sequence of smelting covering roughly the last two thousand years; the oldest dated slag layer, at about 2040 \(\pm\) 80 radiocarbon years before present (calibrated to between about 350 BCE and 130 CE), is the earliest smelting site so far dated in the region (Prokop and Suliga 2013). The minerals of the slag—wüstite, fayalite, glass and droplets of metallic iron—are those of a bloomery process. The authors argue that the industry was probably of local origin, given the isolation of the plateau, while allowing that knowledge may have come from outside. Two thousand years of charcoal-fuelled smelting on the plateau imply a long demand on its woodland, of the kind discussed in Section 4.6.1.

The Khasi case matters for the wider history in two ways. It shows that iron-making in the hills of the north-east was neither late nor derivative of the Ganga plain, and that a technology based on placer magnetite rather than on lumpy ore could sustain a regional trade for centuries. And it shows how much remains to be done: comparable surveys of the iron-smelting traditions of the Naga, Mizo and other hill peoples, and of the Himalayan valleys, have hardly begun.

docs.title: 5.11 Making Steel from Iron
docs.text:
Indian smiths knew several ways of making steel (tīkṣṇa loha), that is, iron with enough carbon to be hardened by quenching:

  1. In the bloomery: by adjusting the ratio of charcoal to ore and the air blast, some smelters produced a higher-carbon bloom or steely parts of a bloom.

  2. By carburisation: heating wrought iron in contact with charcoal, so that carbon diffused into the surface.

  3. In the crucible: melting iron with carbonaceous matter in a sealed crucible to produce a homogeneous high-carbon steel—the crucible or “wootz” steel described in the next chapter.

  4. By decarburising cast iron: high-carbon iron produced in some furnaces could be decarburised, and some south Indian and Sri Lankan crucible processes appear to have combined these approaches (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Juleff 1998).

docs.title: 5.12 Iron in Medicine
docs.text:
Iron has been used in Āyurveda since the classical compendia, which prescribe iron filings and iron leaves heated and quenched in plant decoctions, notably for pāṇḍu, a condition of pallor that includes what is now recognised as anaemia. The rasa texts add elaborate methods for preparing calcined iron (loha bhasma or lauha bhasma), discussed in Chapter 9.

Iron deficiency is a real and common cause of anaemia, and iron given in a suitable form is an effective treatment; it is therefore plausible that iron preparations helped some patients. That does not establish that any particular traditional preparation is effective or safe. Iron in excess is itself toxic—iron overdose is a well-known cause of poisoning in children—and traditional iron preparations sold today may contain other metals. Claims that loha bhasma works better or more safely than standard iron supplements have not been established by adequate trials.

Health and Safety Note

Iron is dangerous in excess, and traditionally prepared iron medicines may also contain other metals. Anaemia has several causes and needs a doctor’s diagnosis. No procedures or doses are given; see the full note in Section 1.1.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: iron was made in South Asia from the second millennium BCE in small bloomery furnaces, and by wind-blown furnaces in Sri Lanka; the Delhi pillar (c. 400 CE) is forge-welded wrought iron whose slow corrosion is explained by its composition, its protective film and the climate; Khasi smelting goes back some two thousand years. Debated: how early regular smelting began, and above all the fourth-millennium dates announced in Tamil Nadu in 2025; the identification of the pillar’s Candra with Candragupta II, which rests on script and historical fit; and the weight of the several causes of the 19th-century decline.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Ukku: Crucible Steel and the “Wootz” Tradition
6.1 Crucible Steel
docs.text:
Crucible steel is steel made by melting iron together with carbon-bearing material in a closed clay crucible, so that the iron absorbs carbon and becomes a homogeneous liquid alloy, which solidifies on cooling as a small ingot. The result is a high-carbon steel (typically 1–2 per cent carbon), much richer in carbon than ordinary bloomery iron and free of the slag that bloomery iron contains. In south India crucible steel was made from at least the last centuries BCE, and in Sri Lanka from the first millennium CE, until the 19th century (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Juleff 1998).

The English name “wootz” first appears in the 1790s, when the physician Helenus Scott sent samples of Indian steel from Bombay to the Royal Society in London. It is usually explained as a misreading or mishearing of ukku, the word for steel in Kannada and Telugu (Tamil urukku, “melted”). In Persian and Arabic sources Indian steel is called hindī or hinduwānī, and steel in general fūlād (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Bronson 1986).

Crucible steel was not made only in South Asia. Archaeological work in Central Asia—at Merv in Turkmenistan and Akhsiket in Uzbekistan—has revealed large-scale crucible steel production in the early Islamic centuries, using rather different crucibles and charges, and Iranian sources describe further variants (Rehren and Papachristou 2003). South Asia was one of several centres of the technology. The crucible finds from Kodumanal, in contexts of the late centuries BCE and early centuries CE, are older than the Central Asian evidence, which dates from about the 9th century CE; but the South Asian contexts are not closely dated, the earliest stages of the technology are poorly known everywhere, and the question of where it began remains open.

docs.title: 6.2 Historical Evidence
docs.text:
The early written evidence for Indian steel is suggestive rather than precise:

  • Quintus Curtius Rufus (1st century CE), describing Alexander’s campaign in the Punjab, lists “white iron” (ferrum candidum) among the gifts presented by Indian peoples. Whether this was steel, polished iron or something else is uncertain.

  • The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) lists “Indian iron and steel” among the goods shipped from Ariakē in western India to Adulis on the Red Sea coast (Casson 1989).

  • Arabic authors of the 9th–11th centuries, among them the philosopher al-Kindī in his treatise on swords and al-Bīrūnī, discuss Indian steel and Indian swords and rank them highly (Bronson 1986).

Al-Kindī’s 9th-century treatise on swords is particularly informative. It classifies swords by the kind of iron or steel from which they were made and by their place of manufacture, distinguishing swords made in India from those made elsewhere of imported steel, and it describes how the qualities of blades were judged from their patterns, their ring and their behaviour in use. Later Persian and Arabic writers on swords and on steel continued to treat Indian steel as a standard of quality (Bronson 1986).

Archaeological evidence is more secure. Crucible fragments with steel residues have been identified at Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu in contexts of the late centuries BCE and early centuries CE, and at a number of later sites in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. In Sri Lanka crucible steel was made in the Samanalawewa area in the first millennium CE (Srinivasan 1994; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Juleff 1998). Table 6.1 summarises the evidence for the trade in Indian steel.

Table 6.1. Indian Crucible Steel in Trade (indicative) Destination Period Evidence Red Sea, East Africa 1st c. CE onwards Periplus: Indian iron and steel Iran and the Arab world late 1st mill. CE onwards Arabic and Persian writings on Indian steel and swords Europe 17th–19th c. Samples and travellers’ reports; scientific study

docs.title: 6.3 The Process
docs.text:
Our knowledge of how crucible steel was made in India comes from the accounts of European observers in the late 18th and early 19th centuries—Francis Buchanan in Mysore (observed 1800–1801, published 1807), H. W. Voysey at Konasamudram in the Deccan (1832), J. M. Heath and others—and from archaeological study of crucibles and debris (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Bronson 1986). The accounts describe several regional variants, but the main steps were similar (Figure 6.1).

Figure 6.1. Generalised steps of crucible steel production in south India, based on 19th-century accounts and archaeological evidence. Regional practices differed.

docs.title: 6.3.1 The Crucible
docs.text: The crucibles were made of refractory clay mixed with organic temper such as rice husk, which burned out in firing and left the walls porous and resistant to thermal shock, while the silica of the husk raised the clay’s refractoriness. They were small, typically a few centimetres across and somewhat taller, and produced ingots weighing a few hundred grams. The crucible was sealed with a clay lid before firing.

docs.title: 6.3.2 The Charge
docs.text: In the Deccani process described by Voysey, pieces of wrought iron were packed into the crucible with wood chips and green leaves, which supplied the carbon. Other variants appear to have used other carbon sources, and in some cases a mixture of high- and low-carbon irons. Archaeological study of the crucibles has helped to distinguish these traditions (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

docs.title: 6.3.3 Firing and Cooling
docs.text: Dozens of crucibles were stacked in a furnace and fired for several hours with bellows. As the iron absorbed carbon its melting point fell, so that the charge could become fully liquid at temperatures attainable in a charcoal furnace. The way the ingots were cooled affected their structure: slow cooling encouraged the growth of coarse structures of iron carbide (cementite) that, after forging, produced the visible surface pattern.

docs.title: 6.4 The Metallurgy of the Watered Pattern
docs.text:
Blades forged from crucible steel ingots in Iran, Syria, India and elsewhere could show a “watered” pattern of light and dark wavy bands when etched—the “Damascus” pattern that made them famous in Europe. The pattern is quite different from the “pattern-welded” or “Damascus” steel made by forge-welding layers of different irons together.

Modern research has explained the watered pattern (Verhoeven et al. 1998; Wadsworth and Sherby 1980; Smith 1960):

  • The steel contains about 1–2 per cent carbon, so that in the solid it consists of a matrix (pearlite, or martensite if quenched) with many particles of iron carbide (cementite).

  • During solidification, small amounts of carbide-forming impurities such as vanadium and molybdenum segregate between the growing dendrites. When the ingot is repeatedly heated and forged at relatively low temperatures, cementite particles cluster in these impurity-rich regions, forming bands.

  • Forging at too high a temperature dissolves the cementite and destroys the pattern; forging at too low a temperature cracks the steel. Successful smiths worked within a narrow temperature range, judged by colour.

  • Etching attacks the matrix and the carbide differently, revealing the bands as the watered pattern. Persian and Indian smiths named different patterns; one, with ladder-like cross-bars, was called kirk narduban (“forty steps”) or “Muhammad’s ladder”.

J. D. Verhoeven and the bladesmith A. H. Pendray showed in the 1990s that the pattern could be reproduced only when suitable impurity levels were present, which explains why many 19th-century European attempts failed and why the quality of Indian steel depended on the ores from which the iron was made (Verhoeven et al. 1998).

Scholarly Note: Nanotubes in a Damascus Sabre

In 2006 Reibold and colleagues reported carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires in a sample from a 17th-century Damascus sabre examined by high-resolution electron microscopy (Reibold et al. 2006). The finding is interesting for materials science, but it concerns one blade, the mechanism of formation is uncertain, and there is no evidence that these nanostructures were responsible for the qualities of Damascus blades. Popular claims that Indian smiths “practised nanotechnology” misrepresent the study.

docs.title: 6.5 Damascus Blades
docs.text: Indian crucible steel ingots were traded to Iran and the Arab world, where smiths forged them into blades; Iran and Central Asia also produced their own crucible steel. The name “Damascus” probably reflects the city’s role as a market and production centre for fine blades, or the “watered” appearance of the steel, rather than the origin of the metal. The best Damascus blades combined a hard, sharp edge with toughness; stories of blades that cut floating silk scarves or sliced through rifle barrels belong to legend. Crusaders may well have encountered such blades, but the European fascination with “Damascus steel” belongs mainly to the 18th and 19th centuries (Smith 1960).

docs.title: 6.6 Swords, Armour and Tools in India
docs.text:
Crucible steel was used in India itself as well as exported. Surviving Indian arms of the 16th–19th centuries include many blades of watered crucible steel: the curved talwār, the straight, broad khaṇḍā of the Rajputs and Marathas, daggers such as the kaṭār and khanjar, and armour, arrowheads and spear points. Mughal and Deccani armouries prized such steel, and blades were frequently inscribed, inlaid with gold (koftgari) or fitted with hilts of jade and precious stones. Many of the finest surviving pieces are in the collections of former princely states and in museums in India and abroad. Not all Indian blades were crucible steel, however; many were made of ordinary bloomery iron and steel, sometimes pattern-welded. The arms themselves are treated in Volume 20, Yuddha and Dhanurveda, and the trade in steel in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra.

Crucible steel was also used for tools that needed a hard edge, such as chisels, files and the dies used to strike coins. The early European interest in wootz was in part an interest in its use for surgical instruments and fine cutlery.

docs.title: 6.7 Two Eyewitness Accounts
docs.text:
The accounts of European observers are our most detailed sources for how crucible steel was made in practice (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Bronson 1986).

Francis Buchanan, travelling through Mysore and the neighbouring regions in 1800–1801 on behalf of the East India Company, described the making of steel in small village workshops. He recorded the preparation of crucibles from local clay and husk, the packing of each with pieces of iron and wood, the sealing of the crucibles, their firing in numbers in a furnace blown by bellows, and the extraction of the small cakes of steel, which were sold to merchants. He also recorded the prices and the organisation of the trade, with the eye of an official surveying the resources of newly conquered territory.

H. W. Voysey, a geologist, described production at Konasamudram in the Deccan in an account published in 1832. He emphasised the use of green leaves in the charge, the careful sealing of the crucibles, and the furnace arrangements. Voysey’s and Buchanan’s descriptions differ in detail, a reminder that crucible steel was made in several local variants rather than by a single standard method.

Both accounts were written when the industry was already under pressure, and both were written by men who regarded the processes as interesting curiosities of a subject people. They are nonetheless invaluable, and archaeological work has confirmed many of their details.

docs.title: 6.8 Crucible Steel in Sri Lanka and Central Asia
docs.text:
Gill Juleff’s survey of the Samanalawewa area in Sri Lanka located not only wind-powered iron smelting furnaces but also evidence for crucible steel production in the first millennium CE, using crucibles different in form and composition from those of south India (Juleff 1998). Sri Lanka thus appears as a centre of crucible steel making in its own right, not merely as an outlier of the south Indian industry.

In Central Asia, excavations at Merv (Turkmenistan) and Akhsiket (Uzbekistan) have revealed large-scale crucible steel production between about the 9th and 12th centuries CE. Rehren and Papachristou’s comparison of these crucibles with South Asian ones shows that the two regions used different clays, shapes and charges, and probably different chemical routes—in Central Asia, at least in part, by melting cast iron with wrought iron—while arriving at similar products (Rehren and Papachristou 2003). Whether the Central Asian industry derived from South Asian knowledge, or developed independently, is not yet known.

docs.title: 6.9 Production Centres
docs.text:
Historical and archaeological sources point to several regions of production (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Srinivasan 1994):

Telangana and the Deccan Konasamudram near Nizamabad, described by Voysey (1832), where a hoard of crucible-steel ingots has recently been studied (Jaikishan et al. 2021), and other Deccani sites associated with the Golconda and Hyderabad markets. Karnataka The Mysore region, where Buchanan observed production in 1800–1801; archaeological sites with crucible debris such as Gatihosahalli.
