Tamil Nadu Kodumanal (early); Mel-siruvalur and other sites in the Salem and Tiruvannamalai regions. Sri Lanka Crucible steel making in the Samanalawewa area and elsewhere (Juleff 1998).

docs.title: 6.10 European Study and Attempts at Replication
docs.text:
Indian steel attracted intense interest in Europe once samples became available in the 1790s (Smith 1960; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004):

  • Michael Faraday and the cutler James Stodart (1819–1822) analysed wootz and experimented with alloys of steel with various metals, believing wrongly that aluminium was the key.

  • Jean-Robert Bréant in Paris (early 1820s) recognised that high carbon content and slow cooling were essential.

  • Pavel Anosov, at the Zlatoust works in the Urals, produced patterned crucible steel (Russian bulat) in the 1830s and published his results in 1841.

  • Robert Hadfield (1912) analysed ancient Sinhalese iron and steel and the Delhi pillar (Hadfield 1912).

  • Jeffrey Wadsworth and Oleg Sherby, American materials scientists, related Damascus steel to modern ultra-high-carbon superplastic steels (Wadsworth and Sherby 1980).

  • J. D. Verhoeven and A. H. Pendray identified the role of trace impurities and reproduced the pattern (Verhoeven et al. 1998).

European steel-makers also learned from crucible steel more generally: Benjamin Huntsman’s crucible process at Sheffield (1740s) was developed independently, but the analyses of wootz contributed to the 19th-century understanding of the role of carbon in steel.

docs.title: 6.11 The Crucible as a Ceramic Achievement
docs.text: The crucible had to withstand temperatures well above those of ordinary pottery firing for hours, resist the corrosive slags formed inside it, survive thermal shock, and hold its seal while allowing gases to escape. South Indian and Sri Lankan potters met these requirements with local clays, organic temper and, in some traditions, other additives. Comparative study of crucibles from South Asia and Central Asia shows that different regions arrived at different but equally effective ceramic recipes (Rehren and Papachristou 2003; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004). Crucibles are discussed further in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 6.12 Producers and Markets
docs.text: Crucible steel was made by specialist smiths, often in villages close to sources of good ore and fuel, and sold as ingots to merchants who carried it to sword-making centres in India, Iran and the Arab world. The south Indian smiths belonged to the artisan communities that worked iron and other metals, such as the Viśvakarma groups (Tamil kammāḷar, Kannada pāñcāḷa, Telugu kamsali and kammari). Production was in small batches, labour-intensive and dependent on charcoal (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Mukherjee 1978).

docs.title: 6.13 Decline
docs.text: Indian crucible steel making declined during the 19th century and had largely ceased by its end. Contributing factors included the decline of demand for swords and armour as firearms spread; the collapse of the courts and armies that had patronised armourers; competition from cheaper imported steel, especially after the introduction of the Bessemer and open-hearth processes; restrictions on forest use that made charcoal scarce; and the general depression of Indian crafts under colonial economic policy. The precise weight of each factor is debated, and the decline of the Central Asian and Iranian crucible steel traditions shows that changes in warfare and markets mattered as well as colonial rule (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Bronson 1986).

docs.title: 6.14 Modern Research
docs.text:
Since the 1980s, crucible steel has been studied intensively. Sharada Srinivasan and Srinivasa Ranganathan, at the National Institute of Advanced Studies and the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, have documented production sites, analysed crucibles and ingots, and synthesised the historical and metallurgical evidence (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004). Archaeologists such as Gill Juleff in Sri Lanka and Thilo Rehren in Central Asia have reconstructed regional traditions (Juleff 1998; Rehren and Papachristou 2003), and experimental smiths have reproduced patterned blades. Open questions include the date at which crucible steel first appeared in South Asia, the relationships between the South Asian and Central Asian traditions, and the provenance of the steel in surviving historical blades.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: crucible steel of 1–2 per cent carbon was made in south India from at least the last centuries BCE, in Sri Lanka in the first millennium CE, and in Central Asia and Iran by other routes; the 18th- and 19th-century eyewitness accounts agree in outline with the excavated crucibles; and the watered pattern is explained by banded cementite and trace impurities. Debated: when and where the technology began; whether the Central Asian industry derived from South Asian knowledge; and which surviving blades were forged from Indian steel.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Yaśada: Zinc and the Zawar Retorts
7.1 The Problem of Zinc
docs.text:
Zinc (Sanskrit yaśada or jasada; the rasa texts’ rasaka is its ore, calamine) is chemically awkward. Copper, lead, tin and iron can be obtained by heating their ores with charcoal, and the metal collects in the furnace as a liquid or a solid bloom. Zinc oxide, however, is reduced by carbon only at temperatures of roughly 1000 °C or more, while zinc boils at 907 °C. At the temperature of reduction, therefore, zinc is produced as a vapour; in an ordinary furnace it is carried away with the furnace gases and re-oxidised to zinc oxide as soon as it meets air.

To obtain the metal, the vapour has to be led out of the hot reduction zone and condensed in the absence of air. This is a distillation, and it requires closed vessels, a reducing atmosphere, and a way of cooling the vapour quickly enough to condense it as metal rather than as oxide.

Before zinc could be distilled, it was already used in brass (an alloy of copper and zinc). Brass can be made without metallic zinc by the cementation process, heating copper with zinc ore and charcoal in a closed crucible so that zinc vapour is absorbed directly into the copper. Cementation brass was made in the Mediterranean world from about the 1st century BCE, and brass objects appear in north-west India from around the same period. Cementation, however, limits the zinc content to about 30 per cent and gives limited control over the composition (Craddock 1998; Craddock 1995).

docs.title: 7.2 Zawar: The Site
docs.text:
Zawar lies in the Aravalli hills about 40 km south of Udaipur in Rajasthan. Its ore bodies, like those of nearby Rajpura–Dariba, contain sphalerite (zinc sulphide) and galena (lead sulphide, often with silver). The ancient workings follow the ore deep underground. Radiocarbon dates from timber and charcoal in old workings at Zawar and Rajpura–Dariba show that mining began in the first millennium BCE, at first, it seems, for lead and silver (Craddock 2017, 1995).

The site was investigated from the late 1970s by a joint project of the British Museum, Hindustan Zinc Limited and Indian archaeologists, led on the British side by Paul Craddock. The project excavated smelting areas, recorded the mine workings, and studied the enormous mounds of discarded zinc-distillation retorts that surround the old smelting sites (Craddock et al. 1983; Craddock 2017).

docs.title: 7.3 Mining in the Aravallis
docs.text: The lead–zinc–silver deposits of southern Rajasthan—at Zawar, at Rajpura–Dariba and Agucha, and elsewhere—were worked for well over two thousand years. The miners followed the richest parts of the ore bodies underground by shafts, inclined adits and large stopes, broke the rock by fire-setting, propped the galleries with timber and sorted the ore by hand at the surface; how such workings are recognised and dated was explained in Chapter 4 (Craddock 2017, 1995). The deepest workings reached well below the water table, so that the mines had to be drained, probably by hand-lifting. Mining of this kind was dangerous and laborious. Little is known about the people who did it, but they were presumably members of specialist mining and smelting communities working for rulers or merchants who controlled the mines; in the medieval period the mines of Mewar were an important source of revenue for its rulers.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Lead and Silver
docs.text: Before zinc, the main products of the Aravalli mines were lead and silver. Galena was smelted to lead, and the silver it contained was recovered by cupellation, leaving large quantities of litharge (lead oxide) as a by-product. Craddock and his colleagues found extensive remains of lead–silver smelting at Rajpura–Dariba and Zawar, dated from the late first millennium BCE onwards; the scale of the remains indicates production well beyond local needs, at a time when silver was the metal of the punch-marked coinage (Craddock 2017). The smelting of lead and the cupellation of silver released large amounts of lead fume; the health of the workers was presumably severely affected, as it was in lead and silver mining elsewhere in the pre-modern world.

docs.title: 7.4 The Distillation Process
docs.text:
The Zawar process, as reconstructed from the excavated furnaces and retorts, worked as follows (Figure 7.1) (Craddock et al. 1983; Craddock 1998).

  1. Ore preparation. The sulphide ore was concentrated and roasted to convert zinc sulphide into zinc oxide.

  2. Charging the retorts. The roasted ore was mixed with organic material and packed into elongated clay retorts, each with a narrow neck. A stick placed in the charge seems to have been used to keep a channel open for the vapour.

  3. Setting the retorts. The retorts were placed upside down—mouth downwards—in perforated clay plates that formed the floor of a furnace chamber, so that the body of each retort lay in the hot chamber above and its neck projected into a cooler chamber below. Each furnace held a large number of retorts.

  4. Heating. The upper chamber was fired. In the retorts, carbon reduced the zinc oxide, and zinc vapour formed.

  5. Condensation. The vapour passed downwards through the necks into the cooler lower chamber, where it condensed in collecting vessels as liquid zinc, protected from air.

Figure 7.1. Schematic of downward distillation of zinc as practised at Zawar (after the reconstruction by Craddock and colleagues). Not to scale; the numbers and arrangement of retorts varied.

The essential idea is distillation per descensum: the vapour is led downwards, away from the hot zone, into a cool, air-free space where it condenses. The rasa texts knew downward distillation (adhaḥpātana) as a general laboratory technique, and the Zawar furnaces applied the same principle on an industrial scale.

docs.title: 7.5 Dating and Scale
docs.text:
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and organic material associated with the retorts indicates that zinc distillation at Zawar was under way by about the 9th–10th century CE. Production expanded greatly from about the 14th century, when the bulk of the surviving retort debris was formed, and continued, with fluctuations, into the early 19th century (Craddock et al. 1983; Craddock 2017). Older claims that distillation at Zawar began in the 6th century, or earlier, are not supported by the published dates.

The scale was very large. The heaps of discarded retorts and furnace debris are among the largest remains of pre-industrial metallurgy anywhere, and they represent production over several centuries. Estimates of the total output vary and depend on assumptions about yields; what is clear is that Zawar was an industrial enterprise, not an experimental workshop. Table 7.1 outlines the sequence of activity.

Table 7.1. Outline of Activity at Zawar (after Craddock and colleagues) Period Activity 1st mill. BCE Mining of the lead–zinc–silver ores begins (Zawar, Rajpura–Dariba) c. 9th–10th c. CE Earliest dated zinc-distillation retorts c. 14th–16th c. CE Large-scale production; bulk of retort debris to early 19th c. Continued production at lower levels; eventual cessation

docs.title: 7.6 Zinc in the Sanskrit Texts
docs.text: The rasa texts describe the treatment of rasaka (calamine) and the extraction of its “essence” (sattva) by heating it with organic materials in a closed crucible, with the product collected as a tin-like metal. Historians from P. C. Ray onwards have read these passages as describing the distillation of zinc (Ray 1956; Biswas and Biswas 1996). Zinc as a named metal (yaśada, jasada) appears in Sanskrit lexicons and medical texts from the later medieval period, and the later rasa compendia list it among the metals. The textual descriptions are small-scale laboratory procedures; there is no Sanskrit account of the Zawar furnaces, which belonged to the world of miners and smelters rather than of alchemists.

docs.title: 7.7 Brass
docs.text:
The main use of metallic zinc was to make brass (rīti, pittala) by direct alloying with copper, which allowed higher and better-controlled zinc contents than cementation. Brass became the dominant metal for domestic vessels, lamps, ritual objects and many images in medieval and early modern India, and it was used for coins, astronomical instruments and inlay work.

The difference between the two methods of making brass can be seen in analyses. Cementation brass rarely contains more than about 28–30 per cent zinc, because the copper cannot absorb more zinc vapour under the conditions of the process; brasses with substantially higher zinc contents, or with very consistent compositions, indicate the use of metallic zinc. Analyses of dated Indian brass objects, especially inscribed Jain images, show a rise in zinc contents in the medieval period that is consistent with the availability of zinc from Zawar (Craddock 1998).

Zinc was also used for the alloy of Bidri ware, the blackened, silver-inlaid metalwork named after Bidar in the Deccan, whose body is mainly zinc with a little copper (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.8 Zinc Elsewhere
docs.text:
Table 7.2 places Zawar beside the later zinc industries of China and Europe.

Table 7.2. Zinc Distillation in Global Perspective Region Date Notes India (Zawar) from c. 9th–10th c.; large scale from c. 14th c. Downward distillation in clay retorts China from c. 15th–16th c. Retort process described in the Tiangong Kaiwu (1637); large-scale production; much zinc exported to Europe Europe 18th c. William Champion’s English patent (1738) and works at Bristol (downward distillation); later Silesian and Belgian horizontal retorts Modern 20th c. Electrolytic and blast-furnace processes

Before Champion, Europe imported zinc (known as tutenag or spelter) from Asia, mainly from China. Champion’s process used downward distillation like that of Zawar, and it has been suggested that he learned of the Indian method from reports brought back from Asia. There is no direct evidence for this; the similarity may equally reflect the fact that downward distillation is an obvious solution once the problem is understood (Craddock 1998). What can be said firmly is that the Zawar retorts are the earliest known evidence for the distillation of zinc on an industrial scale.

docs.title: 7.9 Thermodynamic Notes
docs.text:
The difficulty of zinc can be summarised in a few numbers (Table 7.3).

Table 7.3. Some Physical Data Relevant to Zinc Smelting Quantity Significance Boiling point of zinc: 907 °C Zinc is a vapour at the temperature needed to reduce its oxide Reduction of ZnO by carbon: appreciable only above c. 1000 °C Requires a hot, strongly reducing environment Melting point of zinc: 420 °C Zinc condenses as a liquid if cooled below its boiling point without air Re-oxidation of zinc vapour by CO\(_2\) or air Condensation must be rapid and protected from air

The Zawar smelters solved these problems empirically: the closed retort kept the charge in a reducing atmosphere; the inverted orientation led the vapour quickly out of the hot zone; and the cooler chamber below allowed it to condense. This is an impressive piece of practical chemical engineering, achieved without any theory of chemical thermodynamics.

docs.title: 7.10 Zinc in Medicine
docs.text:
The later rasa texts prescribe calcined zinc (yaśada bhasma) and preparations of calamine, for example for eye diseases and for the urinary disorders grouped as prameha, a category that includes but is not identical with diabetes. Zinc is an essential trace element, and zinc oxide is used externally in modern medicine; but neither fact shows that a traditional zinc preparation is effective for any particular disease. Claims that the use of yaśada bhasma in prameha “anticipated” modern knowledge of zinc and insulin read modern science back into the texts.

Health and Safety Note

Zinc ores such as those of Zawar occur with lead, and traditionally prepared zinc medicines may contain lead; zinc itself is harmful in excess. No doses or methods are given; see the full note in Section 1.1.

docs.title: 7.11 Zawar as Heritage
docs.text:
The remains at Zawar—mine workings, smelting areas and retort mounds—are of international importance for the history of technology. Modern mining by Hindustan Zinc Limited continues in the area, which has both made the ancient workings accessible and threatened them. The British Museum project, whose results Craddock has published in full (Craddock 2017), provides the basis for any future protection and interpretation of the site.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: zinc must be distilled because it boils below the temperature at which its oxide is reduced; at Zawar it was distilled downwards in clay retorts from about the 9th–10th century CE and on a very large scale from about the 14th, the earliest known industrial production of the metal; and metallic zinc made high-zinc brass and Bidri possible. Debated: the total output of Zawar; whether the rasa texts’ extraction of the “essence” of calamine describes the same process; and whether Indian knowledge reached the zinc-makers of China or of 18th-century England.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Gold, Silver, Copper, Lead, Tin and Their Alloys
8.1 Gold (Suvarṇa, Hiraṇya)
docs.text: Gold—hiraṇya in the Ṛgveda, later usually suvarṇa (“of good colour”), with many poetic synonyms—was the most prestigious of metals in South Asia as elsewhere, associated with the sun, with fire and with ritual purity, and used for ornament, coinage, gifts to temples and, in medicine, as a rejuvenative.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Sources
docs.text: Gold was obtained both from reefs and from river sands. The ancient workings in the Kolar and Hutti fields of Karnataka followed gold-bearing quartz veins to considerable depths (Section 4.3); the age of the deepest ancient workings is uncertain, but mining there goes back at least to the first millennium CE (Biswas and Biswas 1996; Craddock 1995). Alluvial gold was panned in many rivers—the Subarnarekha (“streak of gold”) of eastern India takes its name from it—and in the north-western mountains. Herodotus’s story of gold-digging “ants” in India, larger than foxes, is probably a garbled account of gold dust collected in the north-western highlands. A great deal of gold also entered India through trade: Roman gold coins in the early centuries CE, and gold and silver from many sources in later periods. Hoards of Roman gold and silver coins, mostly of the 1st century CE, have been found in large numbers in south India, especially in the Coimbatore region and elsewhere in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, along the routes that brought pepper, beryl, textiles and other goods to the coast. Roman writers complained of the drain of precious metal to India; Indian rulers and merchants, for their part, often valued the coins as bullion, and some were cut or defaced to prevent their circulation as currency.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Assaying
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra describes the testing of gold by touchstone (nikaṣa): the streak left by an object on a black stone is compared with the streaks of reference pieces of known fineness. It also describes testing by colour and by fire, and lists the many ways in which goldsmiths could adulterate gold (Olivelle 2013). The touchstone was used throughout the ancient world and is still used by Indian goldsmiths.

docs.title: 8.1.3 Refining
docs.text:
Two refining processes were widespread in the pre-modern world and were known in India:

  • Cupellation: base metals are removed from gold or silver by melting it with lead in a porous vessel under an air blast; the lead and base metals oxidise and are absorbed by the vessel, leaving the precious metal.

  • Cementation with salt: thin sheets of gold–silver alloy are heated with salt and brick dust; the silver is converted to silver chloride and absorbed, leaving purer gold.

These are well-understood processes, and both are described in detail in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Section 8.13). Statements that Sanskrit texts knew aqua regia or other mineral acids are not supported by the evidence.

docs.title: 8.2 Silver (Rajata, Rūpya)
docs.text: Silver was obtained mainly from argentiferous lead ores (galena). The ore was smelted to lead, and the silver separated by cupellation. The Rajpura–Dariba and Zawar mines in Rajasthan were exploited for silver and lead from the first millennium BCE, and Craddock’s work there has documented both the mining and the cupellation (Craddock 2017). Silver was the main metal of the early punch-marked coinage and, from the 16th century, of the rupee. Large quantities came from abroad: Roman silver in the early centuries CE, and in the early modern period American silver brought by European trade to pay for Indian textiles and spices.

docs.title: 8.3 Copper (Tāmra)
docs.text:
Copper was the first metal to be smelted in South Asia. Copper objects appear at Mehrgarh in the Neolithic, and copper metallurgy was well established in the Chalcolithic cultures of the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE and in the Harappan civilisation (Kenoyer and Miller 1999; Agrawal 2000). The Ganeshwar–Jodhpura culture of north-eastern Rajasthan, near the Khetri copper belt, produced large numbers of copper objects and probably supplied the Harappan cities; the “Copper Hoards” of the Ganga–Yamuna region (2nd millennium BCE) include harpoons, flat axes and anthropomorphic figures of copper. Table 8.1 lists some of the ancient copper-producing regions.

Table 8.1. Some Ancient Copper-Producing Regions of India Region Modern state Evidence Khetri belt, Ganeshwar Rajasthan Ancient workings and slag; Ganeshwar–Jodhpura copper objects Ahar (Banas culture) Rajasthan Chalcolithic copper working Singhbhum Jharkhand Ancient workings and slag Agnigundala Andhra Pradesh Ancient workings

Copper was smelted from oxide and carbonate ores (malachite, azurite, cuprite) and from sulphide ores (chalcopyrite), which require roasting before smelting. In simplified form, the smelting of a carbonate ore can be written

\[\text{CuCO}_3 \cdot \text{Cu(OH)}_2 \xrightarrow{\ \text{heat}\ } 2\,\text{CuO} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}, \qquad \text{CuO} + \text{CO} \longrightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{CO}_2 .\]

docs.title: 8.4 Tin (Vaṅga, Trapu) and Lead (Nāga, Sīsa)
docs.text:
South Asia has little tin. Small deposits are known (for example in Hazaribagh and in the Bastar region), but much of the tin used for bronze must have been imported—probably from Central Asia or Afghanistan in early periods, and later from Southeast Asia, where the Malay peninsula was a major source (Kenoyer and Miller 1999; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

Lead, by contrast, was abundant, especially in the lead–zinc ores of Rajasthan. It was used for weights, for alloys (leaded bronze, pewter), for cupellation, and in the form of its oxides (litharge, red lead) and carbonate (white lead) as pigments and cosmetics. Lead was also used in Āyurvedic and rasa preparations (nāga bhasma). Lead is a cumulative poison that damages the brain, nerves, blood and kidneys, and is particularly harmful to children and in pregnancy; there is no safe level of exposure.

docs.title: 8.5 Alloys
docs.text:
The principal alloys of Indian metalwork are listed in Table 8.2.

Table 8.2. Principal Alloys in Indian Metalwork Alloy Sanskrit / Indic name Main constituents Uses Bronze kāṃsya Copper, tin (often with lead) Vessels, images, mirrors High-tin bronze kāṃsya, kansa (Hi.) Copper with about 20–33% tin Bells, gongs, vessels, mirrors Brass rīti, pittala Copper, zinc Vessels, lamps, images, instruments Bidri alloy — Mainly zinc, a little copper Inlaid blackened ware “Five metals” pañcaloha Copper alloys of variable composition Images (ritual name) Pewter — Tin, lead Vessels

docs.title: 8.5.1 Bronze and High-Tin Bronze
docs.text: Copper–tin bronze was used in the Harappan period, though less than arsenical copper, and became important in the first millennium BCE. A special South Asian tradition is that of high-tin bronze, with roughly 20–25 per cent tin, which is brittle as cast but can be hot-worked and quenched to make vessels; Sharada Srinivasan and Ian Glover have documented the survival of this craft in Kerala, alongside cast high-tin bronze for bells and mirrors (Srinivasan and Glover 1995). High-tin bronze vessels are also known from early contexts in south India and Southeast Asia.

docs.title: 8.5.2 The Aranmula Mirror
docs.text: The metal mirror (kaṇṇāṭi) made at Aranmula in Kerala is a cast and polished speculum alloy of copper and tin, with about a third tin, which takes a brilliant polish. Its makers keep their recipe within families; Srinivasan and Glover’s analyses confirmed its high-tin composition (Srinivasan and Glover 1995). Aranmula mirrors have a Geographical Indication registration.

docs.title: 8.5.3 Pañcaloha and Aṣṭadhātu
docs.text: Texts on image-making and modern craft practice speak of images made of “five metals” (pañcaloha) or “eight metals” (aṣṭadhātu), lists that may include gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron and zinc, and sometimes mercury. These are ritual and symbolic names. Analyses of South Indian bronze images, including Chola images, generally show copper alloyed with variable amounts of tin and lead (and sometimes zinc), with at most traces of precious metals; there is no evidence that a fixed multi-metal recipe was followed (Dehejia 2002; Biswas and Biswas 1996). Associations of particular metals with particular planets belong to later astrological lore.

docs.title: 8.5.4 Bidri Ware
docs.text: Bidri ware, named after Bidar in the Deccan and made from the Bahmanī or Barīd Shāhī period (15th–16th centuries) onwards, uses an alloy that is mainly zinc. Objects are cast, engraved and inlaid with silver (or brass), and the body is then blackened with a paste traditionally made of soil and sal ammoniac, which darkens the zinc alloy and leaves the inlay bright. Bidri is a good example of a craft that depended on the availability of metallic zinc (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 8.6 Lost-Wax Casting and the Chola Bronzes
docs.text:
The lost-wax (cire perdue) process was used in South Asia from the Harappan period onwards. A model is made in wax, often over a clay core; it is covered with layers of clay; the mould is heated so that the wax runs out; molten metal is poured into the cavity; and the mould is broken to release the casting, which is then chased and finished. The Sanskrit term madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhāna (“method of beeswax”) is the title of the account of the process in the Mānasollāsa, the encyclopaedia compiled about 1130 under the Cālukya king Someśvara III, which is the passage usually cited for it; other texts on image-making describe the method more briefly.

The bronze images made under the Chola dynasty in Tamil Nadu (9th–13th centuries)—Śiva as Naṭarāja, Pārvatī, Viṣṇu, the saints—are among the masterpieces of world metal sculpture. They were cast solid, by the lost-wax method, in copper alloys, and were made to be carried in procession as well as installed in temples (Dehejia 2002). The craft continues among the hereditary image-makers (sthapati) of Swamimalai, who use a modelling wax of beeswax and resin and moulds of fine alluvial clay. The tribal Dhokra metal-casters of eastern and central India use a related lost-wax technique with wax threads. The images as works of art are treated in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa, and the living metal crafts, including the Swamimalai workshops, in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 8.6.1 The Metal of South Indian Images
docs.text:
What the Chola images are made of has been established by analysis rather than from texts. The most extensive study is Sharada Srinivasan’s analysis of more than a hundred South Indian metal images of the Pallava, Chola, Vijayanagara and later periods, which combined the measurement of major and trace elements with lead isotope ratios (Section 4.5) (Srinivasan 1999). Its broad results are consistent with those of earlier, smaller studies. The images are copper alloys, most of them bronzes—copper with some tin and, in many images, a substantial proportion of lead, though some fine images are of bronze low in both tin and lead—and zinc-bearing alloys appear to become more common in the later periods, as metallic zinc and brass became widely available (Chapter 7). Gold and silver, when present at all, are at trace levels. The composition varies from image to image and from workshop to workshop, as one would expect of founders who melted down whatever scrap and ingot metal was at hand. Srinivasan also argued that the combination of composition, trace elements and isotope ratios can help to separate groups of images by period and region, and so to judge whether an image is consistent with the date and origin attributed to it on grounds of style—a matter of practical importance, since South Indian bronzes have long been stolen, copied and traded illicitly.

The choice of a leaded alloy makes sense for casting. Lead does not dissolve in solid copper but remains as fine globules; it lowers the temperature at which the alloy is fully molten and keeps it fluid for longer as it fills the mould, so that thin limbs, fingers and the fine detail of ornament and flame-aureole are reproduced. It also makes the metal softer and easier to chase and file. Its disadvantage is that it weakens the alloy, but a solid image, unlike a sword or a bell, has no need of strength or resonance. The South Indian images were cast solid, which demands much more metal than hollow casting around a clay core, the method preferred in the Himalayan traditions; solid casting avoids the problem of supporting and removing a core but increases the risk of shrinkage cavities as a thick casting cools, and X-radiography of the images reveals such internal flaws as well as old repairs.

The condition of the images also has a chemistry. Many were buried for safety in times of war or upheaval and recovered centuries later, and the surface of buried copper alloys is converted to green and blue corrosion products, mainly copper carbonates. Where chlorides from saline soil or sea air are present, a more damaging form of corrosion (“bronze disease”) can develop, in which unstable copper chlorides continue to react with moisture and oxygen after excavation and eat into the metal; conservators control it by removing chlorides and keeping the objects dry. Images in worship are treated differently: they are bathed, anointed and dressed, and the smooth, dark surfaces of long-worshipped images are the product of centuries of ritual handling.

docs.title: 8.7 The Goldsmith’s Techniques
docs.text: Indian goldsmiths and silversmiths commanded the full range of pre-modern techniques for working precious metals—repoussé and chasing, wire-drawing and filigree, granulation (attested in early historic jewellery, for example at Taxila), and the kundan setting of the Mughal and Rajput courts. The crafts themselves are described in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru; here their chemistry is the point. Granulation depends on fusing tiny gold spheres to a gold surface with a copper-based bonding agent at a carefully controlled temperature. Solders were made by alloying gold with silver and copper to lower its melting point, and the colour of gold objects was improved by surface treatments that removed some of the base metal. Copper and silver were gilded with gold leaf or by fire-gilding with gold amalgam (Chapter 3). Kundan setting, in which stones are held by gold foil pressed around them without claws, needs gold of very high purity to be soft enough—one reason why refining (Section 8.13) mattered to the jeweller as well as to the mint.

docs.title: 8.7.1 Enamelling
docs.text: Enamelling (mīnākārī) fuses powdered coloured glass onto a metal surface. It was practised at the Mughal court and became a speciality of Jaipur, Lucknow, Delhi, Varanasi and other centres; the finest work is champlevé enamel on gold, in which the design is cut into the metal and the hollows filled with enamel, often on the reverse of jewellery set with stones on the front. Enamelling requires glasses of different colours with suitable melting points, applied in order from the most to the least refractory; it is, in effect, a branch of glass chemistry (Chapter 12). Many traditional red and yellow enamels contained lead and other heavy-metal colorants.

docs.title: 8.8 Other Traditions of Metal Images
docs.text:
The Chola bronzes are the most celebrated, but by no means the only, Indian metal images.

Early historic and Gupta images Copper-alloy images of the Buddha and of Hindu and Jain deities were cast from the early centuries CE. The largest surviving early example is the Sultanganj Buddha, a standing figure about 2.3 m high and weighing some 500 kg, cast in copper, found in Bihar in the 1860s and now in Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery; it is usually dated to the 6th–7th centuries. Eastern India Pāla-period workshops in Bihar and Bengal (8th–12th centuries) produced Buddhist and Hindu images in large numbers, which were carried to Tibet, Nepal and Southeast Asia and influenced metal sculpture there. The Himalaya and Kashmir Kashmir, the western Himalaya and Nepal developed their own traditions of cast images, often in brass with inlays of silver and copper; Newar metal-workers of the Kathmandu valley supplied Tibet for centuries. Jain images Jain temples of western India contain many images in brass and other alloys, often inscribed with the date and donor, which make them an important dated series for the history of alloys.

The varied alloys of these images—copper, bronze, leaded bronze, brass—reflect local supplies of tin and zinc as well as workshop traditions; analyses of dated images are one of the best sources for the history of brass in India (Craddock 1998).

docs.title: 8.9 Copper Plates
docs.text: Copper was also a writing material. From about the 4th century CE rulers across India recorded grants of land to Brahmins, temples and monasteries on copper plates (tāmrapaṭṭa, tāmraśāsana), engraved with the text of the grant and often joined by a ring bearing the royal seal. Thousands survive, and they are among the most important sources for the political, economic and social history of early medieval India. Their production required the casting or hammering of sheets of copper, careful engraving, and the casting of seals—a substantial demand for the services of metal-workers. The largest sets, such as the Chola grants from Tamil Nadu, consist of dozens of heavy plates.

docs.title: 8.10 Metal-Working Communities
docs.text: The workers in non-ferrous metals formed distinct communities: goldsmiths (svarṇakāra, Hindi sunār), coppersmiths and brass-workers (tāmrakāra, kaseṛā, ṭhaṭherā), bell-metal workers (kansāri), and in the south the five-craft Viśvakarma groups who worked gold, brass and copper, iron, wood and stone (Mukherjee 1978). Their knowledge was hereditary and their social status ambiguous: indispensable to temple, court and household, they were nonetheless ranked below the priestly and landowning castes in the Brahmanical order, and in the south the Viśvakarma groups engaged in long disputes over their ritual rank. The Arthaśāstra’s detailed lists of goldsmiths’ frauds show the suspicion with which their customers regarded them (Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 8.11 Coinage
docs.text:
South Asia has one of the world’s longest coinage traditions; Table 8.3 gives a brief outline.

Table 8.3. Outline of Indian Coinage Period Coinage Metals and features c. 5th–2nd c. BCE Punch-marked coins Silver, of fixed weight, stamped with symbols c. 2nd c. BCE–3rd c. CE Indo-Greek, Śaka, Kuṣāṇa Silver, copper and (Kuṣāṇa) gold; bilingual legends c. 320–550 CE Gupta Gold dīnāra (the name from the Roman denarius); fine portrait types c. 1200–1550 Delhi Sultanate Silver tanka; billon and copper jital 1540s onwards Sūr and Mughal Silver rupee (introduced by Sher Shāh Sūr), gold mohur, copper dām

The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of the mint was to issue coins of fixed alloy and weight, and its examiner of coins collected fees on coin brought into circulation (Olivelle 2013). The fineness of actual coins varied considerably over time, and periods of debasement—for instance of the later Gupta gold coinage—are visible in modern analyses.

The techniques of coin production changed over time. The early punch-marked coins were made by cutting pieces of silver of the required weight from sheet or bar and stamping them with a number of separate symbol punches. Cast copper coins were also made, in moulds, some of which survive. From the Indo-Greek period onwards most coins were struck between engraved dies, which required dies of hard steel or bronze and skilled engravers; the fine portraiture of Kuṣāṇa and Gupta gold coins reflects the quality of the die-cutters. The Mughal mints, described in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī, refined the bullion brought to them by merchants, tested it, and struck coins of a high and remarkably consistent fineness (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873). The silver rupee of the Mughals and their successors became one of the most widely used currencies of the Indian Ocean world.

docs.title: 8.12 Ṭhakkura Pherū and the Delhi Mint
docs.text:
Nearly three centuries before Abuʾl Faẓl, an official of the Delhi Sultanate wrote down what he knew of coins and metals. Ṭhakkura Pherū was a Jain from Kannāṇa, in present-day Haryana, who served the Khaljī sultans in the treasury and the mint in the early 14th century. He wrote a series of short technical works in Apabhraṃśa, the late literary Prakrit of northern India, on gems, coins, metals, architecture, astrology and arithmetic; his dated works fall between the 1290s and about 1318. His arithmetic, with its units of weight, measure and currency mixing Indian and Persian terms, is discussed in Volume 11, Gaṇita, and his treatise on gems in Chapter 10 (SaKHYa 2009).

Two of his works concern the subject of this chapter. The Dravyaparīkṣā (“Examination of Money”), dated to about 1318, deals first with the testing and refining of gold and silver and with the making of the alloys used for coin, and then catalogues the coins that passed through the Delhi treasury—issues of earlier and regional dynasties as well as of the Delhi sultans themselves—giving for each its weight and its content of fine gold or silver in the units of the mint. The Dhātūtpatti (“The Origin of Metals”) is a short work on the metals and their alloys. Both are practical works, concerned with materials as the mint and the market handled them.

The Dravyaparīkṣā is unusual in three respects. Its author was a working official who wrote from his own experience, not a scholar compiling earlier texts, and he wrote in a vernacular literary language rather than in Sanskrit. It is quantitative: its figures for the fineness of named coins make it, in effect, the earliest Indian assay register, and they allow numismatists to compare the written record with the analysis of surviving coins. And it reflects the mixed world of the Sultanate mint, in which Jain and Hindu bankers, assayers and money-changers worked for Turkish rulers, using Persian names for coins and units alongside Indian ones. Pherū’s works are a reminder that the technical knowledge of medieval India was not held only in Sanskrit, or only by Brahmins, and that the practice of the Delhi mint, like that of Akbar’s described below, was the product of continuous craft traditions that outlasted changes of dynasty.

docs.title: 8.13 The Mughal Mint in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī
docs.text: The fullest pre-modern description of metallurgical practice in India is not a Sanskrit text but the opening chapters of the first book of Abuʾl Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī (completed c. 1598), which describe the imperial mint (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873). Abuʾl Faẓl writes as a courtier and credits many improvements to the emperor himself, but his account of the workmen, their tasks and their fees is detailed and specific, and it records the practice of Akbar’s mints in the late 16th century. The references below are to the āʾīns of Book 1 in Blochmann’s translation.

docs.title: 8.13.1 The Workmen of the Mint
docs.text: The mint was run by a superintendent (dārogha) with an assayer (ṣayrafī), an officer (amīn) who settled disputes, an accountant (mushrif), a merchant who bought bullion, a treasurer and a weighman, and a long series of craftsmen: melters and refiners; the cutter (ẓarrāb) who cut blanks from the ingots; the engraver of the dies; the striker (sikkachī) who stamped the blanks between the dies; and others who recovered precious metal from the mint’s waste (Āʾīn 1.5–9). Abuʾl Faẓl remarks that Indian cutters prepared the blanks so exactly, without an anvil, that they did not differ by a hair, and he names the die-engraver Mawlānā ʿAlī Aḥmad of Delhi, whose lettering cut in steel rivalled the work of calligraphers. The list shows how far coinage depended on a division of skilled labour.

docs.title: 8.13.2 Assaying
docs.text: The assayer judged gold first by its colour and lustre and then by the touchstone (Āʾīn 1.6). To make the test objective, the mint kept a set of touch-needles tipped with gold alloys of known fineness, prepared by melting pure gold with measured amounts of a silver–copper alloy; the streak of the gold under test was compared with the streaks of the needles. Fineness was expressed in degrees (bān). Abuʾl Faẓl notes that the Persians reckoned ten degrees for the purest gold, while Indian assayers used a scale of twelve (bārahbānī). The method is the touchstone assay of the Arthaśāstra, now organised with graded standards. Silver was judged by its colour, by filing and boring, and by heating a sample and plunging it into water: a black colour showed lead, red showed copper, and greyish white showed tin (Āʾīn 1.7).

docs.title: 8.13.3 Refining
docs.text:
The Āʾīn describes the standard pre-modern refining processes (Āʾīn 1.7–9):

  • Refining gold. Gold was refined by cementation. Thin plates of gold were stacked in layers with a mixture of brick dust and a salt, covered with dried cow-dung cakes and heated repeatedly. Silver and base metals passed out of the gold into the cement. The result was checked by the sound of a broken plate, by the touchstone, and by heating a sample alongside pure gold and comparing the weights. The spent cement (sālonī) was kept so that its silver could be recovered.

  • Refining silver. Silver was refined by cupellation, in a shallow hearth of wood ash in which the impure silver was melted with lead under the blast of bellows. The lead and base metals oxidised and soaked into the ash, leaving a disc of refined silver. The lead-rich ash (kharal, a form of litharge) was itself reprocessed.

  • Parting silver from gold. Silver was separated from gold by melting the alloy repeatedly with copper and with sulphur, which carried the silver off as a crust on the surface and left the gold.

  • Recovery from waste. Mint sweepings were washed to concentrate the heavy gold. The residue was rubbed with mercury, which took up the gold as an amalgam, and the mercury was then driven off by heat in a retort. Ashes and slags were smelted with lead and with fluxes such as borax, and the lead was cupelled again. Even the sweepers who carried off the mint’s dust washed it for gold and paid a duty on their profits.

One of the materials named in these chapters, rāsī, is rendered “aqua fortis” in Blochmann’s translation. The text, however, says that it was made from saltpetre and an alkaline salt (ashkhar, which Blochmann renders as natron), and what it actually was is uncertain. The passage is therefore not good evidence for the preparation of mineral acids (Section 13.11).

docs.title: 8.13.4 The Theory of Metals
docs.text:
After describing practice, Abuʾl Faẓl adds two chapters of natural philosophy (Āʾīn 1.13–14). The first follows the theory of the Islamic philosophers and alchemists. The seven metals are formed in the earth from mercury and sulphur, in different proportions and degrees of purity, and mercury is called the “mother” and sulphur the “father” of the metals. The chapter then lists alloys in use in India, with their Indian names: a copper–tin bell metal (kānsī), a copper–lead alloy, brass (pītal) made with zinc (rūḥ-i tūtiyā), and the “eight-metal” alloy (ashtdhāt, Sanskrit aṣṭadhātu). It also mentions a lead-like metal that some identified with zinc and that was mined, it says, in the territory of Jalor in the province of Ajmer. The second chapter discusses the specific gravities of metals and minerals and their measurement by weighing in water and by displacement, and reproduces a table that Abuʾl Faẓl attributes to Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī.

The two kinds of chapter sit side by side. The practical chapters describe processes that a modern metallurgist recognises at once: touchstone assay, cementation, cupellation, parting with sulphur and amalgamation. The theoretical chapters rest on the mercury–sulphur theory that Arabic and Latin alchemy shared, and that Indian rasaśāstra held in its own terms (Chapter 3). As in early modern Europe, practical metallurgy and alchemical theory coexisted in the same culture, and the practice did not derive from the theory.

docs.title: 8.14 Bells
docs.text:
Temple bells, gongs and cymbals are traditionally cast in high-tin bronze (bell metal), whose hardness and elasticity give a long, clear ring. Bell-founders in many regions of India continue to cast bells by traditional methods. The acoustic quality depends on composition, shape, wall thickness and casting quality, which founders control by experience.

The composition of bell metal reflects a balance that founders found empirically and that metallurgy explains. Copper alone is too soft and absorbs vibration; as tin is added, a hard, brittle tin-rich constituent (the delta phase) forms between the grains of copper-rich metal, and the alloy becomes stiffer and rings for longer. With about a fifth to a quarter of tin, as in most Indian bell metal (Table 8.2), the alloy has an excellent ring but is too brittle to be hammered when cold, which is why bells, gongs and the Aranmula mirror are cast to shape and finished by grinding and polishing. Above about a quarter of tin it becomes so brittle that a bell may crack when struck. Lead, which helps the casting of images, is unwelcome in a bell, because the soft lead globules damp the vibration and deaden the tone.

The Kerala vessel-makers documented by Srinivasan and Glover exploit a different property of the same alloy. When high-tin bronze of about the bell-metal composition is heated to a red heat, the brittle constituent dissolves into a phase that can be hot-forged; if the forged vessel is then quenched in water, this phase is retained in a form that is much tougher than the cast metal. The craftsmen therefore hammer their vessels hot and quench them, producing thin, resonant bowls that would shatter if made from the cast alloy (Srinivasan and Glover 1995). Metallography of such vessels shows the needle-like structure of the quenched phase, quite different from the structure of a cast bell (Section 4.5). The same alloy, treated in two ways, thus gives two families of objects: cast bells and mirrors, and wrought and quenched vessels.

docs.title: 8.15 Metals in Medicine
docs.text:
The rasa texts prescribe calcined preparations of gold, silver, copper, tin, lead and other metals (Chapter 9). Calcined copper (tāmra bhasma) and copper sulphate (tuttha) are particularly notable: the texts themselves regard copper as dangerous unless thoroughly processed and list the symptoms of copper poisoning.

The custom of storing drinking water in copper vessels is widespread in India. Copper ions are known to have antimicrobial effects, and some studies have reported reductions in bacterial contamination of water kept in copper pots. That is a different matter from taking copper compounds as medicine. Copper salts are toxic, and copper sulphate in particular has caused serious and fatal poisoning in India.

Health and Safety Note

Copper sulphate, lead compounds and other metal salts are poisonous. No doses or methods are given; see the full note in Section 1.1.

docs.title: 8.16 Metals in Trade
docs.text:
Indian metals and metalwork travelled widely. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records the export of Indian iron and steel and the import of copper, tin and lead into Indian ports in the 1st century CE (Casson 1989). Crucible steel went to Iran and the Arab world (Chapter 6); bronze images went with Buddhism and Hinduism to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and the Himalayas; brass and Bidri ware were exported to the Islamic world and Europe. At the same time India was a major importer of precious metals, especially silver and gold, in exchange for textiles, spices and other goods—a pattern noted with dismay by Roman writers and, much later, by European mercantilist economists.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the refining and assay methods of the Delhi and Mughal mints, recorded by Ṭhakkura Pherū and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī; the high-tin bronze traditions of bells, mirrors and quenched vessels; and the composition of South Indian images, which are copper alloys of variable make-up, mostly leaded bronzes rather than a fixed “five-metal” recipe. Debated or unknown: where the Harappans obtained their copper and tin; how early the Kolar and Hutti reefs were mined; and what the Āʾīn’s rāsī actually was.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Bhasma: Calcined Metals in History and Toxicology
9.1 The Idea of a Bhasma
docs.text:
Bhasma means “ash”. In the rasa literature and in later Āyurveda it denotes a powder obtained from a metal, mineral, gem or shell by a sequence of treatments ending in repeated calcination, after which—according to the texts—the substance has lost its metallic nature and become fit to be taken as a medicine. The texts say that metals in their natural state are poisonous and cause disease, but that “killed” (mṛta, mārita) metals become wholesome and, in the case of gold, mica and iron, powerful rejuvenatives (Ray 1956; Dash 1986).

Health and Safety Note

This chapter gives no doses, proportions, durations, vehicles or step-by-step methods. Many bhasmas are made from lead, mercury, arsenic compounds or copper. Do not prepare or take such products; anyone who has taken them and has symptoms should see a doctor, who can test for heavy-metal poisoning. The evidence is reviewed in Section 9.5; see also the full note in Section 1.1.

Bhasmas are still manufactured on a large scale in India and sold in India and abroad. This chapter treats them in two ways: as a historical tradition of chemical practice, described in the texts; and as a contemporary product whose safety has been examined by modern toxicology.

docs.title: 9.2 The Stages Described in the Texts
docs.text: The rasa texts and the later compendia describe the making of a bhasma in three broad stages: a preliminary “purification” (śodhana), a “killing” (māraṇa) by repeated grinding and heating in sealed vessels, and an examination (parīkṣā) of the product, with the killing repeated until the tests are met. The details vary for each substance and from text to text.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Śodhana
docs.text: “Purification” usually begins with a general treatment in which thin pieces of metal are heated and quenched in a series of liquids—oils, sour gruel, buttermilk, cow’s urine, plant decoctions—followed by treatments specific to each substance. In physical terms, repeated heating and quenching oxidises the metal surface and makes it brittle, so that it can be broken up and ground; some soluble or volatile impurities may also be removed. The texts, however, explain śodhana in terms of removing the “defects” of the substance, and they apply similar procedures to poisons such as aconite and to arsenic sulphides, for which no comparable physical rationale exists.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Māraṇa
docs.text: “Killing” consists, in outline, of grinding the substance with plant juices or with other minerals (often sulphur, mercury or arsenic sulphides) and heating the product in sealed earthen vessels in a puṭa, a cycle that the texts repeat many times. In chemical terms the heating converts most metals to oxides, or, when sulphur is added, to sulphides, and the grinding breaks up the product into a fine powder. Gold behaves differently: it does not oxidise, and modern analyses of gold bhasma find fine particles of metallic gold.

docs.title: 9.2.3 Traditional Tests
docs.text:
The texts give a set of tests that a properly “killed” bhasma must pass (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Traditional Tests for Bhasmas Test What the texts require What it can and cannot show rekhāpūrṇatā The powder fills the lines of the fingers Fineness of the powder vāritara A pinch floats on still water Fineness (surface tension supports fine, light particles) niścandratā No metallic lustre or glitter remains Absence of visible metal or unaltered mica apunarbhava, niruttha Heated with reducing materials, the powder does not revert to metal Absence of easily reducible metal; not absence of the element Colour, taste, texture Specified for each bhasma Consistency with the expected product

These tests are a genuine attempt at quality control, and some correspond to measurable properties such as particle fineness. None of them, however, tests for toxicity. A powder can pass every traditional test and still consist largely of lead oxide or arsenic sulphide; the tests show that a metal has been converted into a compound, not that the compound is safe.

docs.title: 9.3 The Principal Bhasmas and Their Claimed Uses
docs.text:
The following summary describes what the texts claim. It is not a statement that these claims are true.

Gold (svarṇa bhasma). Praised as the supreme rejuvenative, said to strengthen the body, heart and mind and to counter poisons. Analyses find fine particles of metallic gold, sometimes with other metals introduced during processing. Iron (loha or lauha bhasma). Prescribed for pallor (pāṇḍu), enlargement of the liver and spleen, and weakness; analyses find mainly iron oxides. Copper (tāmra bhasma). Prescribed for digestive, liver and skin disorders. The texts themselves warn of its dangers if insufficiently processed. Tin and lead (vaṅga and nāga bhasma). Prescribed especially for urinary and genital disorders and prameha. Lead preparations are inherently toxic. Zinc (yaśada bhasma). A later addition, prescribed for eye diseases and prameha. Mica (abhraka bhasma). One of the most praised rejuvenatives; prepared by especially long processing. Mica is a silicate of aluminium and potassium (with iron and magnesium in dark varieties); the product contains these elements in altered form. Mercurial and arsenical preparations. Discussed in Chapter 3; arsenic sulphides (orpiment, realgar) and white arsenic are also processed into “calcined” or sublimed products.

The texts also prescribe the vehicle (anupāna) with which a medicine is taken—honey, ghee, milk, plant juices—and adjust it to the disease and to the patient’s constitution. This is a characteristic feature of Āyurvedic pharmacology; it does not alter the toxicity of a heavy metal.

docs.title: 9.4 What Modern Analysis Shows
docs.text:
Since the 1990s many studies, mostly in Indian laboratories, have characterised bhasmas with modern methods. An early survey analysed twenty bhasmas for up to eighteen elements by neutron activation and found, among other things, that a sample of the mercurial makaradhvaja was essentially stoichiometric mercuric sulphide (Kumar et al. 2006); a more recent study of a commercial rasasindūra found pure red mercuric sulphide in nanometre-sized particles (Mukhi et al. 2017). Taken together, such studies show that most metal bhasmas consist of oxides of the metal (iron, copper, tin or zinc oxides, for example), or of sulphides when sulphur or mercury has been used in processing, while gold bhasma contains metallic gold. The powders are fine, with primary particles that may be sub-micron in size, usually aggregated into larger clusters. They often contain elements other than the named metal, introduced from the raw material, the processing agents, the crucibles or contamination—including, in a number of studies, lead, mercury and arsenic—and their composition varies between manufacturers and between batches.

Many of the authors of these studies regard their results as confirming that traditional processing yields a well-defined and, in their view, safer product, and some present the fine particle size as the key to the claimed effects (Pal et al. 2014). The analyses certainly show what the products contain and how consistently they are made. Whether a given product is effective or safe is a separate question, which analysis alone cannot answer.

docs.title: 9.4.1 The “Nanomedicine” Argument
docs.text: It has become common to describe bhasmas as “ancient nanomedicine” and to suggest that their fine particle size explains claimed therapeutic effects or reduced toxicity (Pal et al. 2014). This argument should be treated with caution. Fine particle size is a consequence of repeated grinding and calcination; it was not, and could not have been, a goal understood by the authors of the texts. In modern toxicology, smaller particles are often absorbed more readily and can be more, not less, toxic than coarse ones; nanomaterials are subject to particular safety scrutiny for this reason. Finally, describing a product as containing nanoparticles says nothing about whether it works for any disease. The analogy with modern nanomedicine, where particles are designed and tested for specific purposes, is therefore misleading.

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Traditional View
docs.text: The rasa texts knew that metals could be dangerous. They state that improperly prepared metals cause disease and death, list the signs of poisoning by insufficiently “killed” copper or lead, and prescribe remedies for them. Their answer was more thorough processing: a correctly prepared bhasma, they hold, is safe. Modern defenders of rasaśāstra make the same argument in modern language, distinguishing “properly prepared” bhasmas (assumed to be safe) from improperly prepared or adulterated products (acknowledged to be dangerous).

docs.title: 9.5.2 What Toxicology Shows
docs.text:
Toxicology does not support the traditional view as a general rule. The toxicity of lead, mercury and arsenic depends on how much of the element is absorbed, and processing can change that only to a limited degree. Lead oxide, the product of “killing” lead, is absorbed from the gut and is a well-known source of lead poisoning; arsenic sulphides are less soluble than white arsenic but are still toxic; mercuric sulphide is less readily absorbed than mercury salts but accumulates with long use (Liu et al. 2008). The relevant evidence comes from three sources:

  1. Product surveys. Saper and colleagues found lead, mercury or arsenic in about a fifth of Ayurvedic products bought in Boston (2004) and online (2008), with rasaśāstra products the most often affected; if taken as recommended, the metal-containing products could lead to intakes above accepted safety limits (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). Similar results have been reported from other countries (Ernst 2002).

  2. Clinical cases. Lead poisoning, sometimes severe, has been repeatedly reported in people taking Ayurvedic medicines, including pregnant women and children (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004; Kales and Saper 2009).

  3. Experimental studies. Animal studies of individual bhasmas, most of them by Indian Āyurvedic research groups, have produced mixed results. A typical study gave rats copper bhasma for twenty-eight days and found no signs of toxicity at doses corresponding to the therapeutic dose, but mild changes in the liver, kidney, heart and thymus at ten times that dose, and less toxicity in the sample given the traditional final “ambrosial” treatment (amṛtīkaraṇa) (Chaudhari et al. 2016). Reviews of the toxicology of mercury–sulphur preparations, including one by an Indian group, weigh the low solubility of mercuric sulphide against the evidence that it is absorbed and accumulates with long use (Kamath et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2008). Short animal studies of this kind are evidence that a product is not acutely poisonous at the doses tested; they cannot by themselves establish safety for long-term human use.

Defenders of rasaśāstra point to the animal studies and to the texts’ long experience; critics point to the product surveys and the clinical cases. The two bodies of evidence answer different questions—whether a correctly made product is acutely toxic, and whether the products actually sold and taken are safe—and both are needed for a fair judgement.

Table 9.2 sets the main traditional claims beside this evidence.

Table 9.2. Traditional Claims and Toxicological Assessment Claim Source Assessment Śodhana and māraṇa remove the toxicity of metals Rasa texts; modern practitioners Not established; the toxic element remains in the product Passing the traditional tests shows a bhasma is safe Rasa texts The tests measure fineness and non-metallic state, not toxicity Problems arise only from improper preparation or adulteration Modern defenders Contamination is common, but intentional metal content is itself a hazard Fine particle size makes bhasmas safe Modern “nanomedicine” literature Unsupported; fine particles may be absorbed more readily

docs.title: 9.5.3 Regulation
docs.text: In India, Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and classical formulations may be manufactured according to the official Ayurvedic Formulary and Pharmacopoeia. From the mid-2000s India required testing of exported Ayurvedic products for heavy metals, and many countries restrict or prohibit the import of products containing heavy metals. Regulations do not, however, guarantee the safety of products bought informally, over the internet, or from unlicensed practitioners.

docs.title: 9.6 Arsenic and Lead in the Rasa Texts
docs.text: Two groups of substances deserve separate mention because of their toxicity.

docs.title: 9.6.1 Arsenic
docs.text: The rasa texts use three arsenic minerals: orpiment (haritāla, arsenic trisulphide), realgar (manaḥśilā, arsenic sulphide) and a white substance (gaurīpāṣāṇa, śaṅkhiyā) usually identified as white arsenic (arsenic trioxide). The texts classify them among the uparasas and sādhāraṇa rasas, recognise that they are poisons, and prescribe “purifications” before use, followed by calcination or sublimation. Arsenic compounds were also widely used in pre-modern medicine elsewhere—in Europe, for instance, as Fowler’s solution until the 20th century—and arsenic trioxide is today used, under strict control, in the treatment of a particular leukaemia. That modern use, however, depends on precise dosing of a pure compound with careful monitoring; it lends no support to the use of traditional arsenical preparations. Chronic arsenic exposure causes skin lesions, nerve damage and cancers, as the mass poisoning from contaminated groundwater in Bengal and Bangladesh has tragically shown.

docs.title: 9.6.2 Lead
docs.text: Lead (nāga, sīsa) is “killed” in the rasa texts to make nāga bhasma, prescribed especially for urinary disorders and prameha, and litharge and red lead appear in compound medicines and ointments. Lead is the metal most often implicated in poisoning from Ayurvedic products (Saper et al. 2004; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004; Kales and Saper 2009). Lead poisoning can cause anaemia, abdominal pain, kidney damage, nerve damage and, in children and the unborn, lasting harm to the developing brain. There is no level of lead exposure known to be safe.

docs.title: 9.7 Rasaśāstra in Modern Āyurveda
docs.text:
Rasaśāstra became part of the curriculum of the Āyurvedic colleges established from the early 20th century (see also Volume 13, Āyurveda), and today “Rasaśāstra and Bhaiṣajya Kalpanā” is a compulsory subject in the Indian degree in Āyurvedic medicine. Its textbooks, largely based on the Rasaratnasamuccaya, the Āyurvedaprakāśa and the Rasataraṅgiṇī, present the classical procedures as standard methods, and pharmaceutical companies manufacture bhasmas and herbo-mineral compounds on an industrial scale.

Within Āyurveda itself, opinions differ. Some practitioners and researchers regard metallic preparations as the most powerful part of their pharmacy and seek to demonstrate their safety and efficacy by modern methods. Others prefer to avoid them, or reserve them for particular cases, in view of the safety evidence and of the regulations of importing countries (Section 9.5.3). Independent studies continue to find products whose metal content is unacceptable (Saper et al. 2008; Ernst 2002). The debate is not between “tradition” and “modernity” as such, but over what standard of evidence should govern the use of toxic substances as medicines.

docs.title: 9.8 Why Metal Medicines Appealed
docs.text:
If metal medicines were dangerous, why did they become so popular, in India as in early modern Europe? The reasons below are the present author’s suggestions, drawn from the general history of medicine; they have not been tested systematically against the Indian sources.

  • The prestige of metals. Gold, silver and mercury carried enormous symbolic value, and the idea that their imperishability could be transferred to the body was intuitively attractive. The rasa texts made this explicit in their doctrine that what perfects metal will perfect the body.

  • Potency in small quantities. Metal preparations were prescribed in small amounts, and many produced noticeable effects—some of them, in modern terms, toxic effects. In medical cultures that valued strong action, a medicine that “did something” could appear powerful.

  • Stability and portability. Calcined powders keep indefinitely, unlike many herbal preparations, and they are easy to store, transport and sell.

  • Elaborate preparation. The long, costly and secret preparation of a bhasma itself conferred value, and distinguished the learned physician-alchemist from ordinary practitioners.

  • The difficulty of detecting harm. Chronic metal poisoning develops slowly and its symptoms—weakness, anaemia, abdominal pain, nerve damage—resemble those of many diseases. Without modern toxicology, harm caused by a medicine was easily attributed to the disease, to incorrect preparation, or to the patient.

These reasons are historical explanations, not justifications. They help to explain why the European medical tradition also used mercury, antimony and arsenic for centuries, and why it took modern toxicology and controlled trials to change medical practice.

docs.title: 9.9 Siddha Preparations
docs.text: Tamil Siddha medicine (on its texts and history, see Section 2.14) has its own range of metal and mineral preparations, including calcined powders (parpam) and red calcined or sublimed preparations (centūram), as well as preparations of mercury, arsenic and other “poisons” (pāṣāṇam). Its methods and claims parallel those of Sanskrit rasaśāstra, and the same safety concerns apply (Weiss 2009).

docs.title: 9.10 Bhasmas in the History of Chemistry
docs.text:
Seen historically, the bhasma tradition represents a long and sophisticated practice of handling metals and minerals: controlled oxidation and sulphidation, prolonged grinding, sealed-vessel heating graded by fuel, and tests for completeness of reaction. It is one of the richest pre-modern traditions of what would now be called inorganic preparative chemistry, and it is a legitimate subject for historians of science. It is also a reminder that pre-modern medicine, in India as in Europe and China, often gave patients toxic metals. The history of European mercurial and antimonial medicine, and of the Chinese elixirs, belongs to the same story (Chapter 3). Honouring the ingenuity of past practitioners does not require endorsing their therapeutic claims.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: what the texts prescribe; what the traditional tests can and cannot measure; what modern analysis finds in the products—mostly fine oxides and sulphides, often with other elements, of variable composition; and that product surveys and clinical cases have repeatedly found lead, mercury and arsenic in Ayurvedic medicines. Debated: whether correctly prepared bhasmas are safe in long-term use, on which Indian animal studies and international toxicology still disagree; whether particle size matters to their action; and whether any of them is effective, which only properly designed clinical trials could show.

docs.title: 10.1 The Indian Literature on Gems
docs.text:
South Asia was for many centuries a principal source of diamonds, pearls, corundum (ruby and sapphire, especially from Sri Lanka and Burma), beryl, garnet, agate and carnelian, and a centre of gem cutting and trade. A specialised literature on the examination of gems (ratnaparīkṣā) grew up around this trade. Its main texts are (Finot 1896; Bhat 1981–1982):

  • the Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE), whose chapter on articles to be received into the treasury (2.11) describes pearls, gems and diamonds, their sources, qualities and defects (Olivelle 2013);

  • the gem chapters of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century), on gems in general and diamonds, on pearls, on rubies and on emeralds (Bhat 1981–1982);

  • the Ratnaparīkṣā of Buddhabhaṭṭa, the Agastimata and other lapidary treatises, of uncertain date, collected and translated by Louis Finot (Finot 1896); similar material appears in the Garuḍa Purāṇa;

  • the Ratnaparīkṣā of Ṭhakkura Pherū (early 14th century; on its author see Section 8.12);

  • the rasa texts, which treat gems as materials for medicines.

Outside Sanskrit, al-Bīrūnī’s Arabic book on precious stones (Section 10.10) and the 17th-century French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier’s eyewitness account of the diamond mines and markets of the Deccan are the most important sources (Tavernier 1889).

The gem texts are practical manuals for connoisseurs and merchants: they describe the sources of each stone, its colours, its qualities and defects, the methods of distinguishing genuine stones from imitations, and how to value it. They are also full of myth (for instance, of gems formed from the body of a slain demon) and of beliefs about the good or ill fortune that stones bring their owners.

docs.title: 10.2 The Nine Gems
docs.text:
In medieval and modern Indian usage nine gems (navaratna) form a canonical set, associated in astrology with the nine “planets” (navagraha). The association of particular stones with particular planets is a later astrological development; it is not found in the early gem literature, and it has no basis in mineralogy. Table 10.1 gives the usual set.

Table 10.1. The Nine Gems (Navaratna): Mineral Identity and Astrological Association Sanskrit English Mineral Planet (astrological) māṇikya, padmarāga Ruby Corundum (red, coloured by chromium) Sun muktā, mauktika Pearl Calcium carbonate (biogenic) Moon pravāla Coral Calcium carbonate (biogenic) Mars marakata Emerald Beryl (green) Mercury puṣparāga Yellow sapphire or topaz Corundum (yellow) or topaz Jupiter vajra Diamond Carbon Venus nīla, indranīla Blue sapphire Corundum (blue) Saturn gomeda Hessonite Garnet (grossular) Rāhu vaidūrya Cat’s eye Chrysoberyl (chatoyant); earlier texts may mean beryl Ketu

The identifications of several Sanskrit names, especially puṣparāga and vaidūrya, varied over time; vaidūrya in particular is thought to have denoted beryl in early usage before it came to mean cat’s eye.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Sources
docs.text: Until diamonds were discovered in Brazil in the 1720s, India was the world’s principal source of diamonds; smaller quantities came from Borneo. The most famous Indian diamonds came from alluvial deposits along the Krishna river and its tributaries in the eastern Deccan, worked most intensively in the 16th and 17th centuries and marketed through the kingdom of Golconda—hence “Golconda diamonds”. The mines at Kollur, visited by Tavernier, were among the most productive. Diamonds were also obtained in central India around Panna, where the Majhgawan kimberlite pipe is still mined, and in eastern India (Tavernier 1889; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

docs.title: 10.3.2 The Diamond in Indian Thought
docs.text: The Sanskrit word for diamond, vajra, also denotes the thunderbolt of Indra, and the two meanings reinforce each other: the diamond is the hardest of substances, unbreakable and able to cut all others. In Buddhism the vajra became a central symbol of the indestructible nature of enlightenment, giving its name to the Vajrayāna, the “diamond” or “thunderbolt” vehicle of Tantric Buddhism, and to texts such as the Vajracchedikā (“Diamond-Cutter”) sūtra. Poets used the diamond as an image of hardness and brilliance, and the gem texts surrounded it with stories of its divine origin. These associations help to explain the diamond’s prestige, but they are a matter of symbolism rather than of mineralogy.

docs.title: 10.3.3 Tavernier at the Mines
docs.text: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a French gem merchant who made six journeys to the East between 1631 and 1668, visited the diamond mines of the Deccan and described them in his Travels (Tavernier 1889). He describes large numbers of labourers—men, women and children—digging the diamond-bearing gravels, washing and sieving them, and searching the residue under close supervision; the miners’ wages were very low, and the stones belonged to the merchants who rented the ground and to the king, who reserved the largest stones. He also describes the merchants’ methods of bargaining and payment, and the Indian practice of cutting stones to preserve weight. Tavernier’s account is a rare view of the labour behind the gems celebrated in courtly literature, and it shows how the diamond trade linked Golconda with Mughal, Persian and European markets.

docs.title: 10.3.4 Classification and Valuation
docs.text:
The gem texts classify diamonds by colour, transparency, shape, size and defects. The ideal diamond is colourless, transparent, sharp-edged and naturally well-formed (octahedral crystals were prized); defects include spots, lines, cracks, cloudiness and irregular shape. The texts also assign diamonds of different colours to the four social classes (varṇa)—white to the Brahmin, reddish to the Kṣatriya, yellowish to the Vaiśya, dark to the Śūdra—and prescribe that each should wear the diamond of his own class (Finot 1896; Bhat 1981–1982). This classification projects the social hierarchy of the law books onto the mineral world; it tells us more about Brahmanical ideology than about diamonds.

Indian jewellers traditionally preserved weight rather than cutting stones to maximise brilliance, and polished the natural crystal faces; European visitors often criticised Indian cutting for this reason. The modern “brilliant” cut is a European development of the 17th–20th centuries, and the modern grading by colour, clarity, cut and carat weight was codified in the 20th century. The Indian texts’ attention to colour, clarity and weight reflects the practical concerns of any diamond trade rather than an anticipation of modern grading.

docs.title: 10.3.5 Famous Diamonds
docs.text:
Table 10.2 lists some celebrated stones believed to have come from India.

Table 10.2. Some Famous Diamonds Believed to Be of Indian Origin Diamond Weight Notes Koh-i-Noor c. 186 carats before 1852; 105.6 after recutting Mughal and Afghan, then Sikh, possession; taken by the East India Company in 1849; now in the British Crown Jewels Regent c. 410 carats rough; 140.6 cut Found c. 1700; bought by Thomas Pitt; now in the Louvre Hope 45.52 carats Descended, by recutting through the French Blue, from the “Tavernier Blue” bought in India by Tavernier; now in the Smithsonian Institution Orlov c. 190 carats Now in the Kremlin Diamond Fund, Moscow Daria-i-Noor c. 182 carats Pink table-cut diamond, taken by Nādir Shāh from Delhi in 1739; now in the Iranian crown jewels

Historical Note: The Koh-i-Noor

Popular accounts trace the Koh-i-Noor to the Kākatīya kingdom of Warangal and the Kollur mines, and identify it with diamonds mentioned in earlier chronicles. Dalrymple and Anand argue that its history is secure only from the 18th century: it was among the treasures carried off from Delhi by Nādir Shāh in 1739, passed to the Afghan Durrānī rulers and then to Ranjit Singh of the Sikh empire, and was surrendered to the East India Company under the Treaty of Lahore in 1849. Recut in London in 1852, it was set in successive British crowns and is now in the crown made for Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. Its return has been requested by India and by other countries (Dalrymple and Anand 2017).

docs.title: 10.4 Corundum: Ruby and Sapphire
docs.text:
Ruby and sapphire are both corundum (aluminium oxide), coloured respectively by chromium and by iron and titanium. The gem texts discuss rubies (padmarāga, māṇikya) at length, classify them by shade, and distinguish them from red spinel and garnet. Historically, the finest rubies reaching India came from Burma (the Mogok region) and many sapphires and other gem-gravel stones from Sri Lanka; India’s own famous sapphire deposit, in the Paddar area of the Zanskar range in Kashmir, was discovered only in the 1880s. Table 10.3 summarises the corundum gems.

Table 10.3. Corundum Gems Known in India Gem Sanskrit Colouring element Main historical sources Ruby padmarāga, māṇikya Chromium Burma, Sri Lanka; minor Indian sources Blue sapphire nīla, indranīla Iron and titanium Sri Lanka; Kashmir (from 1880s) Yellow sapphire puṣparāga (in part) Iron Sri Lanka Star ruby/sapphire — Rutile inclusions (asterism) Sri Lanka, Burma

docs.title: 10.5 Emerald and Beryl
docs.text: Emerald (marakata) is green beryl coloured by chromium or vanadium. India has only minor emerald deposits, in Rajasthan, which were found in the 20th century. In antiquity emeralds reached India from Egypt; the large emeralds of Mughal jewellery came mainly from Colombia, mined by the Spanish from the 16th century and traded to India through European and Middle Eastern merchants. Mughal craftsmen carved and engraved them, and many famous “Mughal emeralds” are Colombian stones. Aquamarine and other beryls occur in Indian pegmatites.

docs.title: 10.6 Pearls and Coral
