docs.text: The pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar, between south India and Sri Lanka, were among the most important in the world from antiquity: the Periplus mentions them, and Marco Polo described the divers and the royal control of the fishery in the late 13th century (Casson 1989; Yule and Cordier 1903). Pearls also came from the Persian Gulf. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā lists the sources of pearls as including not only oysters but also legendary sources—elephants, serpents, clouds, bamboo, fish, boars and conches—and grades pearls by size, roundness, lustre, colour and weight (Bhat 1981–1982). Coral (pravāla) was imported from the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

docs.title: 10.7 Agate, Carnelian and the Bead Industry
docs.text:
Beyond the nine gems, the texts and the trade recognised many “secondary” stones (uparatna): agate, carnelian, onyx, rock crystal (sphaṭika), garnet, amethyst, lapis lazuli, turquoise and others. Some were local; lapis lazuli came from Badakhshan in Afghanistan, and turquoise from Iran.

The agate and carnelian bead industry is one of the oldest continuous crafts of South Asia. Harappan bead-makers heated carnelian to deepen its red colour—the heat converts iron hydroxides in the stone to red iron oxide—and bored long beads with specially made drills of a hard stone that archaeologists call “Ernestite” (Kenoyer 1998). Their beads reached Mesopotamia. Some carry white lines and patterns made by painting the surface with an alkaline paste and then heating it, which whitens the treated areas; these etched carnelian beads, found in Mesopotamia as well as in the Indus cities, are among the earliest known deliberate chemical treatments of a stone surface, and the technique continued in South Asia long after the Harappan period (Kenoyer 1998). In historical times the centre of the industry has been Khambhat (Cambay) in Gujarat, using stones from the Ratanpur area of the Rajpipla hills, and Khambhat beads were traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries (Francis 2002).

docs.title: 10.8 Shell
docs.text: Shell was one of the most important ornamental materials of South Asia. Harappan craftsmen worked the large marine gastropod Turbinella pyrum (the sacred conch, śaṅkha) and other shells from the coasts of Gujarat and Baluchistan into bangles, beads, inlays and ladles, sawing the heavy shells with bronze saws in specialised workshops at sites such as Nageshwar and Balakot (Kenoyer 1998). The tradition of conch-shell bangles continued through the historical period and survives in Bengal, where white shell bangles (śākhā) are worn by married women. Shell, pearl and coral are chemically similar—mostly calcium carbonate—and the rasa texts treat them together as materials for calcined preparations.

docs.title: 10.9 Testing Gems
docs.text:
The gem texts describe practical tests, some of them effective and some fanciful:

  • examination of colour in different lights and against different backgrounds;

  • hardness, tested by scratching—the diamond scratches every other stone;

  • weight in relation to size (a crude estimate of density);

  • examination of transparency, inclusions and flaws;

  • tests by fire and by water, some of which would damage genuine stones or distinguish them from glass imitations.

The texts also mention optical properties that modern gemology recognises—the “fire” of diamond, the moving line of light on cat’s eye (chatoyancy), the star of some sapphires and rubies—without, of course, explaining them. Claims that a description of diamond as displaying “seven colours” anticipates Newton’s analysis of the spectrum read too much into a conventional poetic number.

docs.title: 10.10 Gem Knowledge at the Sultanate and Mughal Courts
docs.text:
From the 11th century, Arabic and Persian learning added another layer to the knowledge of gems in India. Al-Bīrūnī’s book on precious stones and metals (Kitāb al-jamāhir fī maʿrifat al-jawāhir), written in Ghazna in the 1040s and available in an English translation (al-Bīrūnī, Abū Rayḥān 1989), discusses gems, pearls and metals, their sources, prices, tests and imitations, drawing on Indian as well as Greek, Persian and Arabic informants and recording Indian names and lore. It also records the specific gravities of many stones and metals, which al-Bīrūnī measured himself with remarkable accuracy; the table later reproduced in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī is discussed in Section 8.13. In the early 14th century Ṭhakkura Pherū (Section 8.12) wrote a Ratnaparīkṣā that describes the gems handled in the Delhi treasury, their sources (many outside India) and their prices in contemporary coin.

The Mughal workshops also excelled in carving hardstones. Rock crystal, carved into cups and ornaments, had a long history in India; under Jahāngīr and Shāh Jahān jade (nephrite, imported from Central Asia) was carved into wine cups, dagger hilts and boxes of great delicacy, often inlaid with gold and gems—the wine cup of Shāh Jahān in the Victoria and Albert Museum is the best-known example. Hardstone inlay (pietra dura, Persian parchīnkārī) decorated imperial buildings such as the Tāj Mahal.

The Mughal emperors were among the greatest gem collectors in history. Their treasuries held diamonds from the Deccan, spinels from Badakhshan (often inscribed with the names of successive owners), Burmese rubies, Colombian emeralds and Gulf pearls; the court employed lapidaries who carved and engraved stones and goldsmiths who set them in the kundan technique, using highly refined gold foil. Much of this treasure was carried away by Nādir Shāh after his sack of Delhi in 1739.

docs.title: 10.11 Minerals in the Rasa Texts
docs.text:
The rasa texts’ classes of minerals were introduced in Chapter 1. Three minerals deserve brief further mention.

Śilājatu (shilajit) A dark, tarry exudate found on rocks in the Himalaya and other mountains, formed from decomposed plant matter. The rasa texts class it among the mahārasas and praise it as a rejuvenative. It contains humic and fulvic substances and minerals. Commercial shilajit products have been found to contain heavy metals, and raw or poorly processed material may be contaminated. Gandhaka (sulphur) Second only to mercury in rasaśāstra, as the “female” partner of mercury in the formation of mercuric sulphide. India has few deposits of native sulphur, and much of the sulphur used must have been imported. Abhraka (mica) Mica, abundant in Indian pegmatites (Bihar and Jharkhand later became the world’s leading producers), is classed by the texts into varieties by colour and by its behaviour in fire. Black mica (biotite) is preferred for medicine. Mica dust is a respiratory hazard to miners.

docs.title: 10.12 Gems in Medicine and Astrology
docs.text:
The rasa and later Āyurvedic texts prescribe preparations of pearl, coral, shell and gems: fine pastes ground with rose water or other liquids (piṣṭi) and calcined powders (bhasma). Pearl, coral and shell preparations consist essentially of calcium carbonate, which is an antacid; other claimed effects, for example on the heart, have not been established. Calcined diamond and ruby preparations are prescribed by the texts as rejuvenatives; they consist of carbon residues or aluminium oxide together with whatever other materials were used in processing.

The wearing of gems to counteract the influence of planets (ratna remedies in jyotiṣa) is a widespread practice in India. It is a matter of belief; there is no evidence that gems worn on the body have physical effects on health or fortune. Claims that gems “absorb and transmit planetary vibrations” are pseudo-scientific.

Health and Safety Note

Gem and mineral preparations are often processed with mercury, sulphur or arsenic compounds. No doses or methods are given, and no therapeutic claim here is established; see the full note in Section 1.1.

docs.title: 10.13 Minerals and the State in the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s treatment of gems belongs to its larger concern with state revenue. The superintendent of the treasury was to receive gems, pearls and diamonds only after examination by experts, and the text lists the sources (rivers, mines, seas and named regions), types and qualities of each kind, with an emphasis on detecting inferior or false stones (Olivelle 2013). The superintendent of mines controlled the extraction of metal ores and gems, and the state claimed a share of all mineral production. These chapters are among the earliest systematic descriptions of gems in any literature, alongside the Greek and Roman lapidary tradition of Theophrastus and Pliny.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: India was the main source of diamonds until the 1720s, from the alluvial mines of the Krishna valley; many gems prized in India came from Burma, Sri Lanka, Badakhshan and Colombia; the gem texts are practical manuals mixed with myth and social ideology; and the bead industry runs from the Harappan cities to Khambhat. Debated: the dates of most Sanskrit lapidaries; the identification of terms such as puṣparāga and vaidūrya; and the early history of famous stones such as the Koh-i-Noor.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Raṅga: Dyes, Mordants, Pigments and Inks
11.1 Dyeing as Chemistry
docs.text:
Dyeing cotton is chemically difficult. Most natural dyes do not bond to cellulose fibres by themselves; they wash out or fade. Indian dyers solved the problem with two techniques that they brought to a high level: vat dyeing with indigo, which depends on a reduction–oxidation cycle, and mordant dyeing, in which metal salts fixed to the fibre bind the dye and determine its colour. With these, combined with resists of wax, mud or tied thread, Indian craftsmen produced the fast, brilliantly coloured cottons—chintzes, calicoes, kalamkari, ajrakh, bandhani—that were traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries and, from the 17th century, transformed European taste (Riello 2013; Balfour-Paul 1998). This chapter is concerned with the chemistry; the textile traditions themselves are described in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru, and their trade in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra.

As with metallurgy, this was craft knowledge, held by dyers’, printers’ and painters’ communities and passed on within families. Sanskrit literature mentions dyes and dyed cloth, but the detailed knowledge of the processes comes mainly from the products themselves, from European observers of the 17th–19th centuries, who were trying to learn the secrets of Indian dyeing, and from surviving craft practice.

docs.title: 11.2 Cotton
docs.text:
The history of Indian dyeing is bound up with that of cotton. Mineralised cotton fibres preserved in the corrosion of a copper bead from Mehrgarh, of the 6th millennium BCE, are among the earliest evidence for the use of cotton anywhere, and the Harappans grew and wove cotton; fragments of cotton cloth survived at Mohenjo-daro in contact with a silver vessel. Cotton was domesticated independently in South Asia and in the Americas. Greek writers from Herodotus onwards knew of Indian “wool that grows on trees”, and Indian cotton cloth was a major export for some two thousand years (Riello 2013; Kenoyer 1998).

Cotton’s importance for chemistry is that it is hard to dye. Wool and silk, being protein fibres, take many dyes readily; cellulose does not. The mordanting and vat-dyeing techniques described in this chapter were developed above all to colour cotton fast, and their success was one reason why Indian cottons dominated world markets until the industrial revolution.

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Plant and the Dye
docs.text:
Indigo is obtained in India mainly from Indigofera tinctoria (Sanskrit nīlī). The leaves do not contain the blue dye as such but a colourless compound, indican. When the leaves are steeped in water, indican is broken down to indoxyl; when the liquid is beaten to aerate it, indoxyl is oxidised to the insoluble blue pigment indigotin, which settles and is collected, pressed and dried into cakes (Figure 11.1). Similar blue dyes were obtained elsewhere from woad (Europe), from Polygonum and Strobilanthes (East and Southeast Asia) and from other plants; the oldest known indigo-dyed textiles come from Peru. What distinguished India was the scale and quality of its indigo production and its long role as an exporter (Balfour-Paul 1998).

Figure 11.1. Simplified indigo extraction, with the chemical changes involved

docs.title: 11.3.2 The Indigo Vat
docs.text:
Indigotin is insoluble in water and cannot dye fibres directly. The dyer therefore reduces it, in an alkaline vat, to a soluble yellowish form (leuco-indigo, “indigo white”). Fibres immersed in the vat absorb leuco-indigo; on exposure to air it is oxidised back to blue indigotin, now trapped within the fibres:

\[\begin{gather*} \text{indigotin (blue, insoluble)} \ \xrightarrow{\text{reduction, alkali}}\ \text{leuco-indigo (soluble)},\\ \text{leuco-indigo in the fibre} \ \xrightarrow{\text{air}}\ \text{indigotin fixed in the fibre}. \end{gather*}\]

Traditional vats were made alkaline with lime or plant ashes and reduced by fermentation, with additions such as molasses, bran or seeds that fed the bacteria responsible. Managing a fermentation vat requires close attention to its smell, colour and surface; dyers judged its condition by experience. Repeated dips build up deeper shades.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Indigo in Trade and Colonial History
docs.text:
The Periplus lists “Indian black” (indikon melan), generally taken to be indigo, among the exports of Barbarikon at the mouth of the Indus, and Roman writers knew indicum as a costly pigment (Casson 1989). The English word “indigo” derives, through Spanish or Portuguese and Latin, from Greek indikon, “Indian (substance)”. From the 16th century indigo from Gujarat and the Indo-Gangetic plain was exported to Europe in quantity, and it gradually displaced woad there. In the 17th century the most prized grades came from Bayana, near Agra, and from Sarkhej, near Ahmedabad; Dutch and English factors bought them in competition with Persian and Armenian merchants, and the Mughal state and nobility took a close interest in the trade. Later in the century Indian indigo for Europe faced competition from plantations in the Caribbean and the American colonies, and the centre of Indian production shifted to Bengal and Bihar.

From the late 18th century European planters, with East India Company support, organised indigo production in Bengal and Bihar, often by compelling peasants to grow indigo on unfavourable terms. Resistance culminated in the “Blue Mutiny” of 1859–1862 in Bengal (Kling 1966), and the grievances of indigo cultivators in Champaran (Bihar) were the occasion of Gandhi’s first campaign in India in 1917. Adolf von Baeyer’s research on the structure and synthesis of indigo (from the 1870s) led to its industrial synthesis, and from 1897 the German firm BASF marketed synthetic indigo, which within two decades largely destroyed the natural indigo trade (Balfour-Paul 1998).

docs.title: 11.4 Other Natural Dyes
docs.text:
The principal natural dyes used in India besides indigo are listed in Table 11.1.

Table 11.1. Principal Natural Dyes Used in India Dye Sanskrit Source Colour Main colorant Indigo nīlī Indigofera tinctoria Blue Indigotin Indian madder mañjiṣṭhā Rubia cordifolia root Red Purpurin, related anthraquinones Chay root — (Ta. cāyavēr) Oldenlandia umbellata root Red Alizarin and related anthraquinones Lac lākṣā Secretion of the lac insect (Kerria lacca) Red, crimson Laccaic acids Safflower kusumbha Carthamus tinctorius flowers Yellow, red Carthamin Turmeric haridrā Curcuma longa rhizome Yellow (fugitive) Curcumin Kamala kampillaka Mallotus philippensis fruit hairs Orange Rottlerin and related compounds Sappanwood pattaṅga Caesalpinia sappan wood Red Brazilin Myrobalan, pomegranate rind harītakī, dāḍima Fruits and rind Yellow, brown; black with iron Tannins Henna — (Hi. mehndī) Lawsonia inermis leaves Orange-red Lawsone

Some dyes now associated with India are later introductions: annatto (Bixa orellana), for example, is an American plant brought to Asia after 1500.

docs.title: 11.5 Mordants
docs.text:
A mordant (from French mordre, “to bite”) is a metal salt that is fixed to the fibre and forms an insoluble complex (a “lake”) with the dye. With anthraquinone dyes such as madder, chay and lac, the metal of the mordant largely determines the colour: aluminium gives red, iron gives purple to black, and mixtures give intermediate shades. The mordants and auxiliaries used by Indian dyers are listed in Table 11.2.

Table 11.2. Mordants and Auxiliaries in Indian Dyeing Agent Indic names Function Alum sphaṭikā, kāṅkṣī; Hi. phiṭkarī Aluminium mordant: reds with madder, chay and lac Iron kāsīsa (ferrous sulphate); iron liquor from rusty iron and jaggery or sour gruel (Te. kasimi) Iron mordant: purples and blacks; black outlines in kalamkari Tannins harītakī (myrobalan) and other barks and fruits Pre-treatment of cotton, helping metal salts bind to it; black with iron Alkalis Plant ashes, lime, sajjī Scouring cotton; alkaline indigo vats Dung — Bleaching and clearing the ground of printed cloth

The key technique of Indian cotton printing was to apply different mordants to different parts of the cloth—by pen, by block or under resist—and then to dye the whole cloth in a single red dye bath. Where alum had been applied the cloth turned red, where iron had been applied black or purple, and where there was no mordant the dye washed out in the subsequent clearing. Combined with indigo dyeing under a wax resist, this allowed multicoloured, wash-fast designs on cotton.

docs.title: 11.6 Resist and Mordant Techniques
docs.text: Patterns were produced by keeping the dye or mordant away from parts of the cloth or yarn. In bandhani (tie-dyeing; Sanskrit bandha, “binding”) and ikat, thread bound tightly round the cloth or the yarn physically excludes the dye; in the double ikat of Patan (paṭolā) both warp and weft are resist-dyed before weaving. Pastes of wax, or of mud with gum and lime (the dabu of Bagru in Rajasthan), protect areas of cloth from the cold indigo vat, and wood blocks were used to print both resists and mordants, as in the ajrakh of Sindh and Kutch, printed on both sides of the cloth in a long sequence of resisting, mordanting, dyeing with indigo and madder, and washing. The regional traditions, their makers and their designs are described in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru; kalamkari is taken here as the best-documented example of the chemistry.

docs.title: 11.6.1 Kalamkari
docs.text:
Kalamkari (“pen-work”) is the hand-painted and printed mordant-dyed cotton of the Coromandel coast, the “chintz” of European trade. The two best-known centres today are Srikalahasti, where narrative temple cloths are drawn freehand, and Machilipatnam, where block printing is used. A simplified outline of the traditional sequence is given in Table 11.3.

Table 11.3. Outline of the Kalamkari Sequence (simplified) Stage Process and chemical role Preparation Cotton scoured and treated with myrobalan (tannin) and milk, preparing it to take metal salts Black outlines Drawn with iron liquor, which reacts with the tannin to give black Red areas Alum mordant painted or printed where red is wanted Red dyeing Cloth boiled with chay root or madder; colour fixes where alum (red) and iron (black) are present Blue areas Areas not to be blue are covered with wax; cloth dipped in the indigo vat; wax removed Further colours Yellow (often fugitive) painted over blue for green, or over red for orange Clearing Repeated washing, dung baths and bleaching in the sun to whiten the ground

Kalamkari demands precise control of many steps, and its products were highly prized. It is reasonable to call it one of the most sophisticated applications of practical chemistry in pre-industrial textile production. European observers, notably the French in Pondicherry in the 1730s, wrote detailed accounts of the process in order to imitate it (Riello 2013).

docs.title: 11.7 Indian Cottons and Europe
docs.text: Indian dyed and printed cottons were traded across the Indian Ocean from early times—medieval Gujarati block-printed fragments survive at Fustat in Egypt—and from the 17th century the English and Dutch companies shipped them to Europe in huge quantities, provoking the French ban (1686–1759) and the English Calico Acts (1700, 1721). The trade and its protectionist response are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru, and Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra. For the history of chemistry the important consequence is that European printers set out to imitate Indian mordant methods, and the resulting industry of printed cottons was one of the foundations of the European chemical and textile industries (Riello 2013).

docs.title: 11.8 Red Dyes: Chay and Turkey Red
docs.text: The brilliant, fast reds of Coromandel chintz depended on chay root (Oldenlandia umbellata), a small plant growing wild and cultivated in sandy coastal soils of the south-east. Its roots contain alizarin and related anthraquinones and give, on an alum mordant, a red that dyers and European buyers considered superior to that of madder. Chay was collected and cultivated by specialist communities, and its supply was a matter of concern to the European companies trading on the Coromandel coast; it was also exported. The particular qualities of Coromandel reds were often attributed by contemporaries to the water of particular places, a belief that reflects the dyers’ attention to the mineral content of water, which affects mordant dyeing.

docs.title: 11.8.1 Turkey Red
docs.text: “Turkey red” was a brilliant, very fast red produced on cotton by a long and complex process in which the cloth was repeatedly treated with oil, alkali, dung and mordants before dyeing with madder. The process was practised in India and the Ottoman lands, reached France in the mid-18th century through Greek and Ottoman dyers, and then spread to Britain, where Glasgow became a major centre. Its chemistry—the formation of a complex of alizarin with aluminium and calcium in an oil-treated fibre—was only gradually understood. Turkey red is a good example of a process from the Indian Ocean world that European industry adopted and industrialised.

docs.title: 11.9 Dyers and Printers
docs.text: Dyeing and printing were the hereditary work of specialised communities, Hindu and Muslim—rangrez dyers, chhīpā printers, the largely Muslim Khatri ajrakh printers of Kutch and Sindh, and the Hindu and Muslim kalamkari painters of the Coromandel coast—and women did much of the work, especially the tying of bandhani (see Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru). Their knowledge of the behaviour of mordants, dyes, water, temperature and weather was empirical, closely guarded and never written down by the dyers themselves. When European companies and colonial officials sought to learn it, they did so by observing and questioning dyers; the resulting accounts, such as those from Pondicherry in the 18th century, are among the best sources for the techniques, but the dyers’ own perspective is largely absent from the written record (Riello 2013).

docs.title: 11.10 Lac
docs.text: Lac (lākṣā) is the resinous secretion of the lac insect (Kerria lacca), which infests the branches of host trees such as kusum, palāśa and ber. The encrusted twigs (stick-lac) yield a water-soluble red dye, consisting of laccaic acids (anthraquinone compounds), and a resin, refined as shellac. Lac dye was used for textiles, leather and cosmetics (alaktaka, the red colour with which women painted their feet), and lac resin for lacquer, sealing wax, ornaments, varnishes and, from the late 19th century until the coming of vinyl, gramophone records. India has long been the world’s largest producer of lac.

docs.title: 11.11 Pigments and Cosmetics
docs.text:
Indian painters and cosmeticians used a range of mineral and organic pigments: red and yellow ochres, lamp-black, chalk and lime, orpiment (yellow arsenic sulphide), vermilion (red mercuric sulphide), red lead, lapis lazuli (imported ultramarine), indigo, lac and plant colours. Some of these, and their hazards, are listed in Table 11.4.

Table 11.4. Some Traditional Pigments and Cosmetics Material Indic name Composition Hazard Vermilion sindūra, hiṅgula Mercuric sulphide (or, in modern products, often red lead or synthetic dyes) Mercury; lead Red lead sindūra (in part) Lead tetroxide Lead Orpiment haritāla Arsenic trisulphide Arsenic Kohl añjana, kājal, surmā Lamp-black in fat; or ground galena (lead sulphide) or stibnite Lead (galena-based) Alaktaka alaktaka Lac dye —

docs.title: 11.11.1 Pigments in Painting
docs.text:
Scientific study of Indian paintings has begun to identify the pigments painters actually used. The mural paintings of Ajanta (5th century CE) were painted on a ground of mud plaster and lime with earth pigments (red and yellow ochres, green earth), lamp-black, lime white and, for blue, lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan. Later manuscript and album painters, especially at the Mughal and Rajput courts, used a wider range: vermilion, red lead, orpiment, indigo, lac, lapis, malachite and verdigris, lead white, gold and silver. Painters prepared their own colours, grinding minerals, washing and levigating them to separate the finest particles, and binding them with gum.

One pigment has a curious history. “Indian yellow” (peori), used in Rajput and Mughal painting and exported to Europe, was reported in 1883 by an Indian official, T. N. Mukharji, replying to an enquiry from Kew, to be made in Bihar from the urine of cows fed on mango leaves. The account has often been doubted, but laboratory analysis has shown that the pigment consists mainly of the magnesium salt of euxanthic acid, a compound formed in the animal body, which is consistent with Mukharji’s report of an animal source (Baer et al. 1986). Production is said to have ceased in the early 20th century, and the modern paints sold under the name are synthetic.

docs.title: 11.11.2 Ink and Writing Materials
docs.text:
The earliest Indian manuscripts were written on birch bark in the north-west and on palm leaf in most of the subcontinent, with inks made largely from lamp-black (carbon) bound with gums; in the palm-leaf tradition of the south and east, letters were often incised with a stylus and then rubbed with lamp-black. Paper-making reached India from the Islamic world and became established from about the 13th century, with Kashmir, Sialkot, Kalpi and other centres becoming famous for fine paper; the iron-gall inks of the Persianate tradition, and the damage they do to paper, are described in Section 13.7. Some of the painters’ pigments—orpiment, vermilion, lead white—were toxic, both to the painters who prepared them and to the manuscripts they eventually corroded.

Health and Safety Note

Several traditional pigments and cosmetics are toxic. Galena-based surmā and kohl and lead-based sindūr are recognised causes of lead poisoning, especially in young children, and health authorities in several countries have warned against them. Vermilion contains mercury and orpiment contains arsenic. Lamp-black kajal made without lead compounds does not carry the same risk, but commercial products should not be assumed to be lead-free.

docs.title: 11.12 Turmeric
docs.text: Turmeric (haridrā) is a bright yellow dye for cotton and silk, but a fugitive one: it fades quickly in light and changes colour with alkali. It was therefore used mainly where brilliance mattered more than permanence—ritual cloths, cosmetics, food—and, in combination with indigo, for greens. Its colouring compound, curcumin, has been intensively studied for possible pharmacological effects, with mostly disappointing results in clinical trials; these modern investigations should not be read back as “validating” traditional uses.

docs.title: 11.13 The End and Revival of Natural Dyeing
docs.text:
William Henry Perkin’s synthesis of mauve (1856), the industrial synthesis of alizarin (1869) and that of indigo (1897) transformed the dye industry. Within a few decades synthetic dyes had largely replaced natural ones in India as elsewhere, with devastating effects on indigo cultivators and on many dyers (Balfour-Paul 1998).

Since the later 20th century there has been a revival of natural dyeing, encouraged by craft organisations, designers and the market for handmade textiles, and by concern over the pollution caused by synthetic dyeing. Several Indian dyed textile traditions—among them Pochampally ikat, the kalamkari of Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam, Bagh prints, Sanganeri block printing and Patan paṭolā—are registered as Geographical Indications. Natural dyeing is not automatically “green”: mordants and dyeing effluents also need careful handling, and the demand for land and water for dye plants is considerable. Its value lies in the skills and designs it preserves as well as in its environmental advantages.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the chemistry of the indigo vat and of mordant dyeing with alum and iron, and the sequence of operations in kalamkari; the scale of the indigo and cotton trades and the coercion of the colonial indigo system; and the toxicity of lead- and mercury-based pigments and cosmetics. Debated: when mordant dyeing of cotton began; how far European printers learned directly from Indian practice; and the origins of particular reds and of pigments such as Indian yellow.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Kāca and Mṛttikā: Glass, Ceramics and Building Materials
12.1 Vitreous Materials before Glass
docs.text: Glass (Sanskrit kāca) was preceded in South Asia, as in Egypt and Mesopotamia, by other vitreous materials. The Harappans made faience on a large scale: a body of crushed quartz, bound with a little alkali and colourant, shaped into beads, bangles, small vessels and figurines and fired so that a glassy surface formed, usually blue or green from copper. They also made high-fired “stoneware” bangles, fired in sealed containers until partly vitrified, and they glazed steatite beads (Kenoyer 1998). These crafts, which have been studied through workshop debris, experimental replication and laboratory analysis, are the earliest body of chemical technology in South Asia, and they deserve a closer look (Kenoyer 1998; Vidale 2000).

docs.title: 12.1.1 Faience
docs.text: Faience is not a glass and not a pottery, but a material between the two. Its body is made of finely ground quartz, mixed with a small proportion of alkali—from plant ash or natural soda—and usually some lime, moistened, shaped by hand or in moulds, and fired. During firing the alkali reacts with the surfaces of the quartz grains to form a little glass, which binds the grains together, and a glassy layer forms on the surface. Copper compounds added to the body or to the glazing mixture give the characteristic turquoise and blue-green colours. Studies of Egyptian and Near Eastern faience have identified three ways of producing the surface glaze: applying a glazing slurry; “efflorescence”, in which soluble alkali salts in the moist body migrate to the surface as it dries and form the glaze on firing; and “cementation”, in which the object is fired buried in a glazing powder. Which of these the Harappans used, and in what combination, is still being investigated. Much Harappan faience is dense and contains a high proportion of glassy phase through its body, more than is usual in Egyptian faience, and some archaeologists have preferred to call it a vitreous paste. Harappan craftsmen made from it beads, bangles, small vessels, inlays, figurines of animals and moulded tablets bearing short inscriptions in the Indus script (Kenoyer 1998).

docs.title: 12.1.2 Fired and Glazed Steatite
docs.text: Steatite (soapstone), a rock composed largely of talc, is so soft that it can be carved with copper tools. When it is heated to about 900–1000 °C it loses its water and recrystallises into a white, much harder material composed largely of a magnesium silicate (enstatite) and silica. Harappan seal-cutters exploited this transformation: they carved the square stamp seals in the soft stone and then fired them, and many seals and beads were coated with an alkaline glaze before firing, which gave them a white or bluish surface. The crisp edges of many Indus seals have survived for four thousand years largely because of this treatment. Steatite was also made into enormous numbers of tiny disc beads, some only about a millimetre across; whether some of these “microbeads” were made from a paste of powdered steatite rather than cut from the stone has been debated (Kenoyer 1998; Vidale 2000).

docs.title: 12.1.3 Stoneware Bangles
docs.text: The most demanding Harappan ceramic was the stoneware bangle, found mainly at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. These thin bangles, dark grey to black and highly polished, were made of an extremely fine, carefully prepared clay and fired at temperatures well above those of ordinary Harappan pottery, so that the body partly vitrified and became dense and hard. They were fired stacked inside closed clay containers (saggars) sealed with clay, which protected them from the fuel and created the reducing atmosphere that produced their dark colour; the containers were broken open after firing. Many bangles bear tiny inscriptions in the Indus script, and the sealed containers were sometimes stamped. The difficulty of the process, the limited number of places where its debris has been found, and the inscriptions suggest that production was controlled by a small group, perhaps under some form of civic or elite supervision (Kenoyer 1998; Vidale 2000).

docs.title: 12.1.4 A Shared Pyrotechnology
docs.text: Faience, fired steatite and stoneware, together with the heat-treatment of carnelian and the alkaline etching of carnelian beads (Section 10.7), depended on a common stock of skills: grinding and mixing minerals, the use of alkalis as fluxes and of copper as a colourant, and above all the control of temperature and atmosphere in kilns and sealed containers. Kenoyer and Vidale have emphasised that these crafts were technically interlinked and that techniques passed between them—alkaline glazes between steatite and faience, sealed firing between stoneware and other products (Kenoyer 1998; Vidale 2000). There is no convincing evidence that the Harappans made glass in the strict sense, and glass-making proper appears in South Asia only in the first millennium BCE (below); but the Harappan vitreous crafts show a command of high-temperature chemistry that is remarkable for its date.

docs.title: 12.2 Glass in South Asia
docs.text:
The earliest glass objects from South Asia are beads and small ornaments from sites of the early first millennium BCE in the north and the megalithic sites of the south. By the last centuries BCE glass was being made and worked on a large scale, and South Asia became one of the major glass-producing regions of the ancient world (Henderson 2013; Francis 2002). Table 12.1 gives an outline.

Table 12.1. Outline of Glass in South Asia (approximate) Period Sites (examples) Evidence c. 2600–1900 BCE Harappan cities Faience; glazed steatite; stoneware bangles early 1st mill. BCE Painted Grey Ware and megalithic sites Early glass beads c. 3rd c. BCE–3rd c. CE Arikamedu, Taxila, Kodumanal, Mantai (Sri Lanka) Drawn glass beads in quantity; glass working; Roman vessel glass imported medieval Many urban sites Glass bangles; vessels; window glass in some buildings early modern Kapadvanj, Patna, Firozabad Glass vessels, bottles, huqqa bases, bangles

docs.title: 12.2.1 Arikamedu and the Indo-Pacific Beads
docs.text: Arikamedu, on the coast near Puducherry, was excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 and by Vimala Begley’s team in 1989–1992. It was a port in contact with the Roman world in the early centuries CE: Wheeler found Mediterranean amphorae and Italian red-gloss pottery (Arretine ware), which allowed him to date the site, and Begley’s excavations showed that the settlement began before the Roman contact and continued after it. It was also a major centre for making small, monochrome glass beads drawn from glass tubes, and for working semi-precious stones (Begley et al. 1996). These “Indo-Pacific” beads, as Peter Francis called them, were made at several South Asian and later Southeast Asian sites and traded from East Africa to Korea; they are among the most widely distributed artefacts of the ancient world (Francis 2002). At Papanaidupet in Andhra Pradesh drawn glass beads were still made by related methods in the 20th century.

docs.title: 12.2.2 Composition
docs.text: Laboratory analyses show that much South Asian glass belongs to a distinctive type known as mineral-soda-alumina glass: a soda glass with a relatively high alumina content, probably made from local sands rich in feldspar and from a mineral (not plant-ash) source of soda, such as the alkaline efflorescences (Hindi reh) of north Indian soils. This glass differs from the natron glass of the Roman Mediterranean and from the plant-ash glasses of western Asia, and its distinctive composition allows Indian glass to be identified at distant sites (Dussubieux et al. 2010; Henderson 2013). Potash glasses and plant-ash soda glasses also occur in South and Southeast Asia, and the picture is still being refined by new analyses.

docs.title: 12.2.3 Colour
docs.text: South Asian glass-makers coloured glass with metal oxides: copper for turquoise and green (and, under reducing conditions, for opaque red), cobalt for deep blue, iron for greens and browns, manganese for purple and black, and lead–tin compounds for opaque yellow. The orange-red opaque glass beads of the Indo-Pacific type, coloured with cuprite, required careful control of the furnace atmosphere (Francis 2002; Henderson 2013).

docs.title: 12.2.4 Bead-Making Techniques
docs.text:
1. Drawing: a hollow tube of glass is drawn from a gather on a pointed tool; the tube is cut into short segments and reheated to round the edges. This allowed mass production of small beads.

  2. Winding: glass is wound round a wire or rod to form individual beads.

  3. Folding, moulding and drilling: used for larger or special beads.

docs.title: 12.3 Glass at the Mughal and Rajput Courts
docs.text: Glass vessels, though less common in India than in the Islamic Middle East or Europe, were made and used at the courts and in the cities of medieval and early modern India. Mughal and Deccani glass includes huqqa bases, bottles, flasks and cups, sometimes gilded or enamelled; some were imported from Iran, Venice or later Britain, and some were made locally, at centres such as Patna and Kapadvanj in Gujarat. Mirror glass was used for decoration in the “mirror palaces” (shīsh maḥal) of the Mughal and Rajput courts, such as those of the Agra fort and of Amber, whose walls and ceilings are set with countless small pieces of convex mirror in stucco. In the 18th and 19th centuries, imported European glass, including chandeliers and coloured glass, became fashionable among Indian elites and gradually displaced local production of fine glassware.

docs.title: 12.4 Glass Bangles
docs.text: Glass bangles have been worn in South Asia since at least the early historic period and carry social meanings—in many communities they mark married status, and their breaking marks widowhood. In medieval and modern times bangle-making became concentrated in a few centres, above all Firozabad in Uttar Pradesh, where the industry grew from the late 19th century. Glass is melted in furnaces, drawn into coils on rotating rods, cut, joined and decorated, largely in small workshops and homes. The industry has long been associated with hazardous working conditions—heat, fumes and burns—and with the use of child labour, which has been the subject of repeated official and non-governmental intervention.

docs.title: 12.5 Pottery
docs.text:
Pottery is among the oldest crafts of South Asia. At Mehrgarh in Baluchistan pottery appears in the later Neolithic levels, after an earlier aceramic phase. Table 12.2 gives a very brief outline of some of the principal wares.

Table 12.2. Some Major Ceramic Traditions of South Asia Period Ware Characteristics c. 6th mill. BCE onwards Mehrgarh and early village pottery Hand-made, later wheel-made painted wares c. 2600–1900 BCE Harappan Wheel-thrown red ware with black painting; standardised forms; kilns c. 1200–600 BCE Painted Grey Ware Fine grey ware with black painting, Ganga–Yamuna plain c. 700–200 BCE Northern Black Polished Ware Fine ware with a glossy black (or other coloured) surface early centuries CE Rouletted Ware, Red Polished Ware Fine wares, partly connected with maritime trade from c. 13th c. CE Glazed wares and tiles Lead- and alkali-glazed pottery and tiles under the Sultanates and Mughals

docs.title: 12.5.1 Northern Black Polished Ware
docs.text: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), the fine ware of the early historic cities of the Ganga plain, has a thin, lustrous surface, usually black but sometimes golden, red or steel-blue. Its surface appears to be a very fine slip, fired in a reducing atmosphere and then cooled in a way that preserved its dark colour and sheen; the exact technique is still debated. NBPW is a technically demanding ware, comparable in fineness to the best Mediterranean wares of the period.

docs.title: 12.5.2 Terracotta
docs.text: Terracotta, low-fired unglazed clay, has been used in South Asia for figurines from the Harappan period, for the moulded plaques and figures of the early historic period, and for architectural decoration. The brick temples of Bengal, especially those of Bishnupur (17th–18th centuries), are covered with terracotta panels showing scenes from the epics, the Kṛṣṇa legend and contemporary life.

docs.title: 12.5.3 Glazes and Tiles
docs.text: True glazes on pottery appear in South Asia mainly with the Islamic period. Glazed tiles adorn the tombs and mosques of Multan, Uch and Thatta in the Indus valley (14th–18th centuries), the monuments of the Delhi Sultanate, and Mughal buildings such as the Lahore Fort, where mosaics and painted tiles (kāshīkārī) in Persian style were used on a large scale. The “blue pottery” of Jaipur, made from a body of ground quartz and glass with very little clay and painted in cobalt and copper colours, is a 19th-century development of Persianate traditions.

docs.title: 12.5.4 Kilns
docs.text: Indian potters used open firings (pots stacked with fuel in the open or in a shallow pit) for much everyday ware, and updraught kilns of various kinds for higher-quality ware and bricks. Controlling the atmosphere (oxidising or reducing) and the cooling, as much as the maximum temperature, determined the colour and finish of the product.

docs.title: 12.6 Bricks
docs.text:
Fired brick is one of the great ceramic achievements of the Harappan civilisation. The Harappan cities used sun-dried and kiln-fired bricks on a huge scale, made in moulds to standard proportions—the length, breadth and thickness of most bricks are in the ratio 4:2:1, whatever their absolute size—and laid in bonds that are still standard today. Fired bricks were used where durability against water mattered: for drains, wells, bathing platforms and the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, which was made watertight with carefully fitted bricks, gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002).

Fired brick returned to large-scale use in the cities of the early historic period and remained the main building material of the Ganga plain, where stone is scarce, through the Buddhist stūpas and monasteries, the brick temples of the Gupta period (such as Bhitargaon) and of Bengal, and the Sultanate and Mughal buildings of the north. Brick-making requires the selection and preparation of clay, the control of shrinkage in drying, and the firing of very large quantities in clamps or kilns—a major consumer of fuel and of labour.

docs.title: 12.7 Crucibles and Refractories
docs.text: Some of the most demanding ceramics were made not for use in the home but for metallurgy: the crucibles of crucible steel production (Chapter 6), the retorts and furnace plates of Zawar (Chapter 7), the clay tuyères of iron-smelting furnaces, the cupels used for refining silver and gold, and the sealed earthen dishes of the rasa laboratory. These had to withstand high temperatures for long periods, resist thermal shock and chemical attack, and be cheap enough to be discarded after one use. Potters achieved these properties by selecting refractory clays and adding temper—rice husk, sand, crushed potsherd—whose combination of porosity and refractoriness suited each purpose (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Rehren and Papachristou 2003; Craddock 2017). These utilitarian ceramics are a little-noticed but essential part of the history of Indian technology.

docs.title: 12.8 Lime, Mortars and Plasters
docs.text:
Indian builders used a variety of binding materials, the main ones of which are listed in Table 12.3.

Table 12.3. Some Traditional Binding Materials Material Names Composition Uses Mud mortar — Clay and silt Common walling Lime mortar sudhā, cūnā Lime with sand Masonry, plaster Surkhī mortar surkhī Lime with crushed burnt brick (a hydraulic additive) Masonry, waterworks Shell lime — Lime burnt from shells Coastal building, plaster Polished lime plaster ārāish (Rajasthan) Fine lime, polished, sometimes with additives Wall surfaces with a marble-like finish Vajralepa vajralepa Plant materials and resins boiled to a glue (Bṛhatsaṃhitā) Adhesive and coating

Lime mortars set by reacting with carbon dioxide from the air; the addition of crushed brick (surkhī) makes them partly hydraulic, able to set in damp conditions, which made surkhī mortar valuable for tanks, wells and bridges. Many Indian builders also added organic materials to lime—jaggery, plant gums, fruit pulps, pulses—and modern studies suggest that some of these modify the setting and workability of the mortar.

The Bṛhatsaṃhitā has a short chapter on vajralepa, “adamantine plaster”, a glue made by boiling various fruits, barks, resins and other substances, which it recommends for temples, images, walls and wells (Bhat 1981–1982). Popular claims that vajralepa was a “super-cement” stronger than modern concrete have no basis in tests of the recipes; it was an adhesive and coating rather than a structural cement.

docs.title: 12.8.1 Gypsum
docs.text:
The second mineral binder of South Asia is gypsum, hydrated calcium sulphate, which occurs in large beds in the arid north-west; Rajasthan supplies most of India’s gypsum today. Its chemistry is simpler than that of lime. Heated gently, to little more than the boiling point of water, gypsum loses three-quarters of its water and becomes a fine white powder, the hemihydrate known as plaster of Paris:

\[\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{CaSO}_4\cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{H}_2\text{O} .\]

Mixed with water, the powder takes it up again and sets within minutes as a mass of interlocking gypsum crystals, expanding slightly as it does so. Overheated, it loses all its water and becomes “dead-burnt” anhydrite, which sets only very slowly. Because it sets quickly and fills fine detail, plaster is ideal for moulds and casts; because gypsum is appreciably soluble in water, it is less durable than lime in exposed walls, and was used mainly where it could be kept dry. The Harappan builders used gypsum mortar in the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro (Section 12.6).

Gypsum has two modern uses in India that connect with other chapters of this volume. It is the standard amendment for reclaiming sodic soils, the barren ūsar lands of the Ganga plain whose alkaline salts were once collected as reh (Section 13.3): calcium from the gypsum displaces the sodium held by the clay, and the sodium is washed out as soluble sulphate (Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna). And plaster of Paris has largely replaced clay for the festival images immersed in rivers and lakes, with consequences for water quality discussed in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 12.9 Stone: Weathering, Polish and Conservation
docs.text: Mortars and plasters were applied to stone and brick, and the chemistry of the stone itself—how it was chosen, finished and preserved, and how it decays—belongs in the same story. The architecture and sculpture made from stone are the subject of Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; this section is concerned with the materials.

docs.title: 12.9.1 Building Stones
docs.text:
India’s builders and sculptors used the stone of their regions, and the chemistry of each stone shaped what could be done with it. The sandstones of the Vindhyan ranges—the buff stone of Chunar near Varanasi used for the Mauryan pillars, the red stone of the Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and Dholpur region used for Mughal buildings—consist of grains of quartz bound by a natural cement, and their durability depends on that cement: sandstones bound by silica are hard and lasting, those bound by calcite are vulnerable to acid, and those rich in clay swell and flake with repeated wetting and drying. Marble, such as the white marble of Makrana in Rajasthan used for the Taj Mahal, is recrystallised calcium carbonate: it takes a fine polish and can be carved in great detail, but it is attacked by acids. The granites and charnockites of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, made of quartz, feldspars and dark silicate minerals, are among the most durable building stones, though hard to carve; they weather slowly as the feldspars are converted to clay. The basalt of the Deccan Traps, into which the caves of Ellora were cut, and the soft schists of the Hoysaḷa temples and of Gandhāra each had their own working properties.

The colours that give Indian buildings much of their character are also chemical. The red of the Mughal sandstones comes from thin films of iron oxide (haematite) coating the quartz grains; where the iron was removed by ground water, or reduced to its paler ferrous state around decaying organic matter, the stone is buff, white or greenish, and the spotted and banded stones prized by builders record such differences in the rock. The black of the polished basalt and of the dark chloritic stones used for images comes from iron- and magnesium-rich silicate minerals, and the green and grey tones of many schists from chlorite. Builders exploited these differences deliberately, as in the inlay of white marble into red sandstone that distinguishes the façades of Mughal Delhi and Agra (Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa). The same iron oxides that colour the stone are responsible for the rusty stains that disfigure pale marble and sandstone when iron in or near the surface weathers.

Laterite, the red, iron-rich rock of the Western Ghats, the Konkan, Kerala and Odisha, is a product of tropical weathering, in which rain leaches silica and other soluble components from the parent rock and leaves a residue rich in the oxides and hydroxides of iron and aluminium. Fresh laterite is soft enough to be cut into blocks with a pick, and it hardens on exposure to the air as it dries out and its iron compounds crystallise. Francis Buchanan, travelling in Malabar in 1800–1801, described this property and gave the rock its name, from the Latin later, “brick”, in the account he published in 1807. Laterite blocks, often plastered with lime, are the traditional walling material of coastal Karnataka, Goa and Kerala.

docs.title: 12.9.2 The Mauryan Polish
docs.text: The pillars and animal capitals set up in the reign of Aśoka (3rd century BCE), and the interiors of the rock-cut Barabar caves in Bihar, have a lustrous, almost glassy polish that has impressed observers since they were first described. How it was produced is not known with certainty. The usual view is that it was obtained by prolonged grinding and burnishing with progressively finer abrasives; others have proposed that a coating or surface treatment was applied. The few published scientific examinations have not settled the question, and the polish remains one of the open problems of early Indian stone technology. Claims that the Mauryan craftsmen possessed a lost chemical secret go well beyond the evidence.

docs.title: 12.9.3 Decay and Repair
docs.text: Stone decays by physical, chemical and biological processes acting together. Rain made weakly acid by carbon dioxide slowly dissolves marble and calcareous sandstone, and sulphur dioxide from burning coal and oil turns calcite into the more soluble gypsum, which washes away or forms blackened crusts; soluble salts carried in by ground water crystallise in the pores and break the stone from within; and iron cramps rust and swell, cracking the blocks they were meant to hold. The best-known Indian case is the Taj Mahal. A Supreme Court order of 1996 moved or converted polluting industries in the Taj Trapezium Zone around it, but the marble has continued to discolour, and a study published in 2015 attributed the discoloration mainly to deposited black and brown carbon particles and dust rather than to chemical attack on the stone (Bergin et al. 2015). The chemical lesson of 20th-century conservation, learned at some cost with Portland cement, is that repairs should be softer and more permeable than the stone they protect, as traditional lime plasters were.

docs.title: 12.10 Living Traditions
docs.text:
Many of the crafts discussed in this chapter survive: village potters work in every region of India; terracotta figures are made for shrines and festivals; Khurja in Uttar Pradesh and Jaipur produce glazed wares; and Firozabad remains the centre of glass bangles. These traditions are under pressure from industrial products and changing tastes, and many of their practitioners are poor. Their history is part of the history of Indian chemistry: the control of materials, temperature and atmosphere in kilns and furnaces was as much an empirical chemical skill as anything practised in the alchemist’s laboratory.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the Harappan vitreous crafts formed an interlinked high-temperature technology; South Asian mineral-soda-alumina glass and the drawn Indo-Pacific beads were traded from East Africa to Korea; and the chemistry of lime, gypsum and the common building stones is well understood. Debated: which glazing methods the Harappans used; when glass proper was first made in South Asia; how the Northern Black Polished Ware surface and the Mauryan polish were produced; and the composition and purpose of vajralepa.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Kṣāra and Lavaṇa: Salts, Alkalis, Acids and Sugar
13.1 The Reagents of Pre-Modern Chemistry
docs.text:
Metals and gems attract the attention of historians because they survive and because they are beautiful. The everyday work of pre-modern chemistry, however, was done with salts. Washermen scoured cloth with alkaline earth, dyers made their indigo vats alkaline and fixed their reds with alum, glass-makers fluxed sand with soda, goldsmiths cleaned and joined metal with borax and sal ammoniac, tinsmiths coated copper pots with the help of sal ammoniac, surgeons cauterised with caustic alkali, refiners parted gold from silver with common salt, and the makers of gunpowder depended on saltpetre. The rasa texts, too, are full of salts: their lists of reagents include the “five salts”, the “three alkalis”, alum, the vitriols, borax and sal ammoniac, and many of their operations on mercury and metals are carried out in the presence of one or more of them.

Health and Safety Note

This chapter describes historical methods in outline only, and gives no quantities or procedures. Caustic alkalis cause severe chemical burns, especially to the eyes; the vitriols, particularly copper sulphate, are poisonous if swallowed; mineral acids are corrosive and give off toxic fumes; and saltpetre mixtures are fire and explosion hazards. Nothing here should be attempted outside a properly equipped and supervised laboratory. Medical uses of kṣāra and of mineral salts are described as history and are not recommendations (see also Section 1.1).

This chapter describes these substances: what they were, how they were obtained or made, how they were named and classified, and what they were used for. Several of them have been mentioned in earlier chapters, in connection with medicine (Chapter 1), the mint (Chapter 8), dyeing (Chapter 11) and glass (Chapter 12); here they are treated together, as a chemical industry in their own right. The social and fiscal history of salt, which in India is a large subject, belongs to Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra, and gunpowder as a weapon to Volume 20, Yuddha. This chapter is concerned with the chemistry.

Pre-modern writers had no concept of a “salt” as the product of an acid and a base. Sanskrit distinguishes lavaṇa, a salty substance (above all common salt), from kṣāra, a caustic or alkaline one, and names many other substances individually. Arabic and Persian likewise distinguish milḥ (salt) from qily, the alkaline ash of certain plants, from which, through medieval Latin, comes the English word “alkali”. Table 13.1 lists the principal substances discussed in this chapter, with their usual modern identifications. As with the minerals of the rasa texts (Table 1.2), the same name can denote different substances in different texts and regions, and identifications based on modern usage may not hold for early texts.
