docs.title: 14.4.1 Sal Ammoniac and the Rasa Texts
docs.text: Sal ammoniac is the clearest case. It was a central reagent in Arabic alchemy from the late 9th century, it was traded from Central Asia, and its Arabic and Persian names have a plausible derivative in Sanskrit navasāra. The substance does not appear in the classical medical compendia; in the rasa texts it appears among the “common” minerals (sādhāraṇa rasa) of the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Table 1.2). This does not prove that the rasa alchemists learned its use from Muslim practitioners—the substance could have been obtained from kiln soot locally—but it is consistent with the movement of a material and its name from the Persianate world into Sanskrit.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Tutty and Zinc
docs.text: The Persian tūtiyā illustrates how the two traditions approached the same material from different directions. In Iran and the Islamic world, tutty was the zinc oxide that collects as a white crust on the upper parts of furnaces in which zinc-bearing ores are roasted or brass is made, and it was prized as an eye medicine. Marco Polo describes its manufacture at Cobinan (Kuhbanan) in the province of Kerman in the late 13th century: an ore was heated in a furnace with an iron grating above it, and the vapour rising from it condensed on the grating as tutty, while the residue left below was sold as “spodium” (Yule and Cordier 1903). This is the deliberate collection of a sublimate, but the product is an oxide; the metal itself escaped. The Indian achievement, at Zawar and in the rasa texts’ extraction of the “essence” (sattva) of calamine, was to condense the zinc vapour as metal by excluding air (Chapter 7). When the Āʾīn-i Akbarī calls metallic zinc rūḥ-i tūtiyā, “the spirit of tutty”, it uses Persian vocabulary for an Indian product. Whether the Persian word itself derives from Sanskrit tuttha, as has been suggested, is uncertain; the substances the two words denote are different.

docs.title: 14.4.3 New Diseases and New Medicines
docs.text:
The later rasa literature also shows how the tradition absorbed new knowledge from outside. Bhāvamiśra’s Bhāvaprakāśa (16th century) describes a disease it calls phiraṅgaroga, “the Frankish disease”, which is syphilis, brought to India in the wake of the Portuguese; it prescribes mercurial preparations for it, as did contemporary European and Islamic physicians, along with the newly imported China root (copacīnī, the rhizome of a Smilax species) that the Portuguese also promoted as a remedy (Volume 13). Among the mercurials used for the disease was rasakarpūra, “mercury-camphor”, a white sublimate usually identified as a mercury chloride, made by heating mercury with salts. Its preparation depends on the same chemistry of chlorides and sublimation that Arabic alchemists exploited with sal ammoniac and common salt. Like all mercury compounds it is highly toxic; mercurous chloride (calomel) remained a standard European medicine into the 20th century, with well-documented harmful effects (Chapter 3).

The overall picture is of two traditions that developed largely independently, each with its own theory and goals, which came into contact from the 11th century onwards and exchanged materials, names and techniques—above all in pharmacy, metallurgy and distillation—more readily than ideas.

docs.title: 14.5 The Still: Distillation in India
docs.text: Distillation—heating a liquid and condensing its vapour—underlies the rasa texts’ operations on mercury (Chapter 3), the zinc retorts of Zawar (Chapter 7) and, in other traditions, the making of spirits and perfumes.

docs.title: 14.5.1 Gandhāra
docs.text: F. R. Allchin argued in 1979 that pottery vessels found at Shaikhan Dheri in Gandhara and at Taxila, of the last centuries BCE and early centuries CE, were parts of stills used to distil alcoholic spirits, and that India might be “the ancient home of distillation” (Allchin 1979). The interpretation is plausible but not universally accepted; the vessels could have had other uses, and the textual evidence for distilled spirits in early India is uncertain. Fermented liquors (surā, āsava, ariṣṭa), by contrast, are amply documented (Chapter 1, and Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna). In Allchin’s reconstruction the Gandhāran still consisted of a large globular pot heated over a fire, a head or condenser, and a tube leading the vapour sideways and down into a separate receiving vessel that could be cooled—an arrangement with an external receiver, in contrast to stills in which the condensate is caught inside the heated vessel.

docs.title: 14.5.2 The Rasa Laboratory
docs.text: The rasa texts describe apparatus for upward, downward and sideways “falling” (ūrdhvapātana, adhaḥpātana, tiryakpātana) of mercury, and the vidyādharayantra and related devices in which a vessel with a cooled upper part receives a sublimate or distillate (Chapter 2). These are distillation and sublimation in the technical sense, but their purpose was to separate or recover mercury, not to make spirits or perfumes. The downward variant—in which the charge is heated from above and the vapour driven down into a cooler vessel below—corresponds to the method used on an industrial scale for zinc at Zawar (Chapter 7). The upward apparatus has a close functional parallel in the Arabic aludel, a vessel for sublimation in which the vapour of a heated substance rises into one or more heads and condenses on their cooler walls. In the vidyādharayantra, as the texts describe it, the cooling is made more effective by keeping water on top of the upper vessel, the same device that the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes for distilling spirits (below). Such parallels show how a few physical principles—heat below, a cooled surface above, a sealed joint between them—were applied independently or by borrowing across many traditions, and they make the direction of any borrowing hard to establish.

docs.title: 14.5.3 The Alembic
docs.text: The Arabic qarʿ and anbīq—a cucurbit or boiling vessel surmounted by a head with a channel round its inner rim and a spout to carry the condensate to an external receiver—were the standard stills of Islamic alchemy, pharmacy and perfumery. In Iran, especially in the province of Fars, rose-water was distilled on a commercial scale by the 10th century and exported widely, including to India and China (al-Hassan and Hill 1986; Forbes 1948). With the Persianate courts of the Sultanate and Mughal periods, the alembic, the distilled waters of Islamic pharmacy and the distillation of spirits became part of north Indian urban life (Habib 2008).

docs.title: 14.5.4 Spirits in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī
docs.text:
For the late 16th century the evidence is explicit. In its account of the sugar-cane, the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the fermentation of a liquor from cane or brown sugar and three ways of distilling it into arrack (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873). In the first, the liquor was heated in a brass vessel with a cup fixed inside it; the vessel was closed with an inverted lid sealed with clay, cold water was poured on the lid and changed as it grew warm, and the vapour condensed on the lid and dripped into the cup. In the second, the vessel was closed with an earthen pot from which two pipes led to receiving jars standing in cold water. In the third, a hollow-handled ladle fixed inside the pot carried the condensate out through a pipe into a jar, while the lid was kept full of cold water. Some distillers, it adds, distilled the spirit twice to make it stronger. Distilled spirits were thus well established in Mughal India, and the colonial authorities later taxed country liquor heavily.

The three methods correspond to the principal types of pre-modern still (Figure 14.1). In Joseph Needham’s comparative study of chemical apparatus, stills in which the vapour condenses on a cooled, concave lid and drips into a catch-cup inside the vessel are characteristic of East and Central Asia, whereas the Hellenistic and Arabic alembic, like Allchin’s Gandhāran still, leads the condensate to an external receiver (Needham et al. 1980). The Āʾīn’s first method is of the inner-cup type; its second and third, with their pipes and cooled receivers, are of the external type. Mughal India thus used both traditions side by side.

Figure 14.1. Schematic types of still used in India: (a) the vapour condenses on a lid cooled with water and drips into a cup inside the vessel; (b) it is led through a pipe to a cooled receiver outside; (c) it is driven downwards, away from the heat, into a receiver below. Proportions are not to scale; the vessels and their arrangements varied widely.

docs.title: 14.5.5 Country Spirits under Colonial Rule
docs.text: Village distillation of spirits from sugar, molasses, palm sap and, in central India, the flowers of the mahua tree (Madhuca longifolia) continued throughout the colonial period, using simple pot stills of earthenware or copper with external receivers. The colonial excise systems alternated between licensing such “outstills” and concentrating production in central distilleries that were easier to supervise and tax. Restrictions on home distillation, especially of mahua spirit, bore heavily on Adivasi communities for whom it had ritual and social importance (Volume 23, Jana–Jāti). On the west coast, Portuguese Goa developed its own distilled spirit, feni, made from fermented coconut-palm sap and, after the Portuguese introduced the cashew tree from Brazil in the 16th century, from the juice of the cashew apple; it is still distilled in small pot stills, and cashew feni has been registered as a geographical indication. The Portuguese introduction of the cashew is a reminder that the raw materials of Indian chemistry, like its techniques, were enlarged by exchange across the oceans after 1500.

docs.title: 14.6 ʿAraq and Arka: Distilled Waters and Perfumes
14.6.1 Distilled Waters
docs.text: Arabic ʿaraq, “sweat”, the drops that form on the head of a still, gave its name both to distilled waters and to distilled spirits (whence “arrack”). Unani pharmacy uses many distilled waters (ʿaraqiyāt) of flowers, seeds and herbs, among them rose-water and the water of fennel (Volume 13). Later Sanskrit adopted arka in the same sense, a usage that appears to follow the Arabic and that is distinct from the older meaning of arka as the sun or as the plant Calotropis. A work devoted to such distillates, the Arkaprakāśa, attributed to Rāvaṇa, belongs to the late period of the medical literature (Meulenbeld 1999–2002), and modern Āyurvedic pharmacy recognises arka as a class of preparations made by distilling plant materials with water.

docs.title: 14.6.2 Perfumery
docs.text:
Indian perfumery has a long literary history, from the chapter on compounding perfumes (gandhayukti) in Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā to the later Sanskrit works on perfume-making surveyed by James McHugh (Bhat 1981–1982; McHugh 2012). The aromatic materials, their trade, and the history of perfumery as a craft and a courtly art are treated in Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna. The classical Sanskrit perfumer worked mainly by blending, steeping, cooking and fumigating aromatic materials; distillation became important only later, and largely through the Persianate tradition.

The Mughal court, as described in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī, consumed perfumes on a lavish scale. Its chapter on perfumes gives recipes for compound perfumes and incenses based on ambergris, aloewood, sandalwood, musk and rose-water, lists perfumes with their prices, and describes the preparation of some of them (Āʾīn 1.30) (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873). One of these preparations is a distillation per descensum. To obtain the oil of aloewood (chūwa), a small bottle coated with clay was filled with chips of the wood and set upside down, its neck passing through a hole in a vessel to rest just above a cup of water; a gentle fire of dried dung was lit on top, and the oil that ran down from the heated wood gathered on the surface of the water, from which it was collected and washed. The principle is that of the rasa texts’ downward distillation (adhaḥpātana) and of the Zawar zinc retorts (Chapter 7), applied here to a perfume.

Jahāngīr records in his memoirs that the attar (ʿiṭr) of roses was discovered in his reign by the mother of Nūr Jahān, who noticed an oily film forming on rose-water and collected it; he named the perfume after himself (Thackston 1999). The account shows that the separation of rose oil was claimed and celebrated at his court; it does not show that rose oil had never been obtained before elsewhere, and the story is discussed in Volume 15.

docs.title: 14.6.3 The Kannauj Method
docs.text: The distilled perfume oils known as ʿiṭr or attar are made today, especially at Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh, by a method of hydrodistillation: flowers or other aromatic materials are heated with water in a large copper still (deg), and the vapour is led through a bamboo pipe into a receiving vessel (bhapkā) containing sandalwood oil, which absorbs the fragrant components; the process is repeated with fresh flowers until the oil is saturated. The method, described more fully in Volume 15, is an external-receiver still (Figure 14.1b) with an unusual feature: the receiver contains an oil that dissolves the volatile aromatic compounds as they condense, while the water that condenses with them settles out and is drawn off. Sandalwood oil, itself only slightly volatile, serves as solvent and fixative, slowing the evaporation of the lighter scents. The “earth” attar (miṭṭī) is distilled from discs of baked clay and captures the smell of rain on dry earth, a smell that modern chemistry attributes largely to compounds produced by soil micro-organisms.

docs.title: 14.7 The Physical Chemistry of Distillation
docs.text:
Distillation works because the components of a mixture differ in volatility. When a fermented liquor containing a few per cent of ethanol is heated, the vapour that rises is richer in ethanol than the liquid, because ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) is more volatile than water; condensed, it gives a liquid much stronger than the original. One distillation in a simple pot still with a cooled receiver yields a spirit of moderate strength, and a second distillation of that spirit—the “double distilling” that the Āʾīn-i Akbarī mentions—yields a stronger one. Even repeated distillation cannot remove all the water, because ethanol and water form a constant-boiling mixture (an azeotrope) containing about 95–96 per cent ethanol by weight; absolute alcohol requires other methods. A simple still also concentrates other volatile substances present in the liquor, among them small amounts of methanol and higher alcohols, which is why skilled distillers discarded the first and last portions of a run.

Perfume distillation rests on a different principle. Most of the aromatic compounds of flowers, woods and roots—terpenes, aromatic alcohols and esters—boil at temperatures well above that of water, often between 150 and 300 °C. But when such compounds are heated together with water, the mixture boils when the combined vapour pressures of water and oil equal the pressure of the atmosphere, which happens below 100 °C; the steam therefore carries the oils over at a temperature at which they are not decomposed. This is the principle of steam distillation and of the Kannauj deg. Because the oils are only slightly soluble in water, they separate from the condensed water as a film or are captured by an absorbent oil.

The distillation and sublimation of metals and their compounds follow the same physics at higher temperatures. Mercury boils at 357 °C and is readily distilled from its ores or amalgams; zinc boils at 907 °C, below the temperature at which its oxide is reduced, so that it can be won only as a vapour and condensed out of contact with air (Chapter 7); sal ammoniac and calomel (mercurous chloride) sublime without melting. The rasa alchemists, the zinc smelters of Zawar and the perfumers of the Mughal court were exploiting the same property of matter with very different apparatus and purposes.

docs.title: 14.8 From Kīmiyā to Chemistry
docs.text:
When modern chemistry was taught in Indian schools and colleges in the 19th century, the old words were given new meanings. In Urdu, as in modern Arabic, kīmiyā came to mean chemistry; in Hindi and several other Indian languages the Sanskrit rasāyana (Hindi rasāyan, rasāyan-vijñān) was adopted instead, a choice that linked the new science to the old alchemical and medical tradition. P. C. Ray’s decision to call his history of the Sanskrit sources “Hindu chemistry” belongs to the same moment (Chapter 15). In both cases a word for alchemy, with its hopes of gold and immortality, became the name of a laboratory science that had renounced those hopes, and the persistence of the old words has contributed to the modern habit of reading the alchemical texts as early chemistry.

Health and Safety Note

Mercury compounds, including rasakarpūra and calomel, are highly toxic, and metal-based kushtas raise the same concerns as bhasmas (Section 1.1). Distilling spirits outside licensed premises is illegal in India and dangerous: mass poisonings from illicit liquor have been caused mainly by methanol, usually added as an adulterant. No procedures or proportions are given.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: Arabic and Persian kīmiyā reached India with the Persianate courts from the 11th century; al-Bīrūnī knew and described Indian rasāyana about 1030; materials and words—sal ammoniac, borax, tutty, kushta, arka—passed between the traditions; and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes stills of both the inner-cup and the external-receiver types. Debated: whether either alchemy influenced the theory of the other; whether Allchin’s Gandhāran vessels were stills; and the history of the Indo-Persian alchemical literature, which has hardly been studied.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Legacy: From Rasāyana to Modern Chemistry
15.1 Taking Stock
docs.text:
The preceding chapters have described a long and varied history. Its most secure achievements, established by archaeology and laboratory analysis, are practical ones:

  • the copper, bronze, faience, stoneware and bead technologies of the Harappan cities;

  • an early, probably independent, iron industry, and the forge-welding of massive iron objects such as the Delhi pillar, whose slow corrosion is now well understood;

  • crucible steel, made in south India from at least the last centuries BCE, and later in Sri Lanka, and traded across western Asia;

  • the earliest known industrial-scale distillation of zinc, at Zawar;

  • high-tin bronzes, lost-wax casting and the Chola bronzes;

  • mineral-soda-alumina glass and the Indo-Pacific bead industry;

  • indigo vat dyeing and mordant printing and painting of cotton, which shaped world trade in textiles;

  • the production and refining of salts—saltpetre above all, but also alkalis, alum, sal ammoniac and salt itself—on which much of the craft economy, and for two centuries much of Europe’s gunpowder, depended.

Alongside these stands the Sanskrit literature of rasaśāstra, with its laboratory, apparatus, classifications of minerals and long sequences of operations on mercury and metals. It is an important chapter in the global history of alchemy, comparable to the Chinese and Arabic traditions. Its theoretical goals—transmutation and bodily immortality—were unattainable, and its medical legacy is, as earlier chapters have shown, a serious contemporary safety problem.

Two cautions follow. First, the achievements were mostly those of craft communities, not of textual scholars; the people who smelted the iron and dyed the cloth were often of low social status and left no writings. Second, much popular writing on these subjects is marred by exaggeration—claims of absolute priority, of anticipations of modern science, of “lost” secrets. The record is impressive enough without them.

docs.title: 15.2 P. C. Ray and the Historiography of Indian Chemistry
docs.text:
The modern study of Indian chemistry began with Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861–1944), a chemist at Presidency College, Calcutta, who founded the firm that became Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (incorporated 1901) and is remembered in chemistry for his work on mercurous nitrite and related compounds. His History of Hindu Chemistry (two volumes, 1902 and 1909) surveyed Sanskrit medical and alchemical literature, with extracts and translations, and argued that India had possessed a genuine chemical tradition (Ray 1902–1909). A revised edition, edited by Priyadaranjan Ray, appeared in 1956 (Ray 1956).

Ray’s work was written in a nationalist spirit, but it was not uncritical. He attributed the decline of Indian chemistry in part to the caste system, which separated learning from manual work and left practical knowledge to groups whom the learned despised, and to philosophical attitudes that devalued the study of the material world. Some of his datings of rasa texts were too early and have since been revised, and some of his attributions (notably of a Rasaratnākara to Nāgārjuna) have been shown to be mistaken (Wujastyk 1984; Meulenbeld 1999–2002). His work nevertheless remains the starting point for the subject, and his insistence on the social conditions of science is as relevant now as it was then.

Later scholarship has moved in several directions: the bibliographical and philological work of Meulenbeld and others on the rasa texts (Meulenbeld 1999–2002); the study of rasaśāstra as part of Tantric religion, above all by David Gordon White (White 1996); the archaeometallurgical work of D. P. Agrawal, R. Balasubramaniam, Sharada Srinivasan, S. Ranganathan, Paul Craddock, Gill Juleff, Thilo Rehren and many others (Agrawal 2000; Balasubramaniam 2002; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Craddock 2017; Juleff 1998); and the economic and social history of Indian crafts and trade (Riello 2013).

docs.title: 15.3 Modern Chemistry and Metallurgy in India
docs.text:
Modern chemistry came to India in the 19th century through colonial education and administration: chemistry was taught at the medical colleges and the new universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (founded 1857), and the Geological Survey of India (1851) and the colonial mints and arsenals employed European chemists and metallurgists. Indian chemists of the first generation, P. C. Ray foremost among them, combined research with the conviction that chemistry should serve Indian industry; Ray’s Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works was one of the first Indian-owned chemical firms.

The early 20th century saw the foundation of the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore (1909), whose creation owed much to the initiative of J. N. Tata, and of the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur, which began production in 1912 (Chapter 5). Indian chemists such as Nil Ratan Dhar, Jnan Chandra Ghosh, Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar and T. R. Seshadri built research schools; Bhatnagar became the first director-general of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), founded in 1942, whose national laboratories—among them the National Metallurgical Laboratory at Jamshedpur and the National Chemical Laboratory at Pune—shaped the post-independence development of chemistry and materials science.

docs.title: 15.3.1 Ray’s Laboratory and the Calcutta School
docs.text:
Ray’s own career shows how the new science was made Indian. Born in 1861 in a landholding family of Khulna district in eastern Bengal, he studied in Calcutta and then, with a scholarship, at the University of Edinburgh, where he took his doctorate in chemistry in 1887. On his return he found the senior grade of the Indian Educational Service effectively closed to Indians, and he joined Presidency College in 1889 in a junior post, an experience of discrimination that he recalled with some bitterness in his autobiography (Ray 1932; Arnold 2000). At Presidency College he built up a research laboratory with very limited means. His work on the nitrites, beginning with the preparation of mercurous nitrite in 1896, was published in Calcutta and in London and gave him an international reputation.

Ray also set out to show that Indians could manufacture the chemicals and medicines that India imported. In 1892 he began making pharmaceutical preparations, with a small capital, in his own lodgings in Calcutta; the venture was incorporated in 1901 as the Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, which moved to a factory in the suburbs and grew rapidly in the years of the Swadeshi movement after 1905, when Indian-made goods were deliberately preferred. It made medicines from Indian plants as well as standard pharmacopoeial preparations, laboratory chemicals and household products. Ray’s purpose was as much social as commercial: he repeatedly urged the educated Bengali middle class to turn from government service and the law to industry, and he saw the firm as a demonstration that chemistry could be the basis of Indian enterprise (Ray 1932).

His most lasting creation was a school of chemists. Among his students at Presidency College and, after 1916, at the new University College of Science in Calcutta, where he became the first Palit Professor of Chemistry, were Nil Ratan Dhar, Jnan Chandra Ghosh, Jnanendra Nath Mukherjee and Priyadaranjan Ray, who between them founded research traditions in physical, colloid and inorganic chemistry at Calcutta, Dacca, Allahabad and Bangalore; the physicist Meghnad Saha also attended his lectures. In 1924 Ray became the first president of the Indian Chemical Society, whose journal gave Indian chemists a forum of their own. The History of Hindu Chemistry belongs to the same project. It was written, in part, to give Indian students of a European science a history of their own, and it presented the Sanskrit tradition both as evidence of past achievement and, through its account of caste and the contempt for manual work, as an explanation of later decline (Ray 1902–1909; Prakash 1999).

The Calcutta school shaped the teaching of chemistry in India for half a century. Its graduates staffed the chemistry departments of the new universities, and the institutions in which they worked—the University College of Science, the Indian Institute of Science, the national laboratories of the CSIR—trained the chemists and metallurgists who, after 1947, carried out much of the analytical work on Indian iron, steel, zinc, glass and medicines on which this volume relies (Kumar 1995; Arnold 2000).

This modern history is linked to the older one in two ways. Some of the earliest work in the history of Indian chemistry was done by modern Indian chemists, notably Ray, who saw it as part of a national scientific revival. And it was modern laboratory science, including Indian laboratories, that made possible the archaeometallurgical research on which much of this volume depends.

docs.title: 15.4 From Salts to Soda Ash: The Modern Chemical Industry
docs.text:
The substances discussed in Chapter 13—saltpetre, borax, alum, alkalis, salt—were, in the 19th century, among India’s exports of raw materials, along with indigo, lac and the myrobalans used in European tanning. Manufactured chemicals, by contrast, were largely imported: soda ash, caustic soda, acids, synthetic dyes, drugs and fine chemicals came from Britain and, increasingly, Germany. Indian chemical manufacture in the modern sense began on a small scale at the end of the century, with ventures such as Ray’s Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, and with government laboratories that made vaccines and sera, such as the Plague Research Laboratory set up in Bombay in 1899 under Waldemar Haffkine (Arnold 2000).

The modern successors of the old salt economy grew out of this dependence. The First World War, which cut off German dyes and drugs, led the Indian Industrial Commission (1916–1918) to recommend government support for industrial research (Arnold 2000; Kumar 1995), and the inter-war decades saw the first Indian firms in several branches of the industry: factory soap made from vegetable oils and caustic soda gradually replaced the washermen’s sajjī, reh and soapnut (Chapter 13). From 1939 Tata Chemicals built a works at Mithapur in Gujarat to make soda ash by the ammonia–soda (Solvay) process from the two cheapest raw materials of the old salt economy, brine and limestone. The successor of Bihar saltpetre was synthetic nitrogen: the public-sector fertiliser factory at Sindri, producing from 1951, was a showpiece of the first Five-Year Plans, and synthetic ammonia later underpinned the Green Revolution (Volume 15). The pharmaceutical industry that grew after Independence, and the generic manufacturing made possible by the Patents Act of 1970, belong to the economic history of modern India rather than to this volume.

The modern industry also inherited, on a far larger scale, the dangers that run through this volume. The release of methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide pesticide plant at Bhopal on the night of 2–3 December 1984, which killed thousands within days, remains the worst disaster in the history of the chemical industry; less dramatic, but widespread, are chromium from tannery effluents, mercury from older chlor-alkali plants and pesticide residues. From the mercury of the rasa laboratory and the lead of the cupelling hearth to Bhopal, the history of Indian chemistry is also a history of the people who bore its costs.

docs.title: 15.5 The Evidence and How It Is Weighed
docs.text:
The kinds of evidence used in this volume, and what each can show, are summarised in Table 15.1.

Table 15.1. Kinds of Evidence for the History of Indian Chemistry and Metallurgy Kind Examples What it can show Artefacts Iron pillars, steel ingots, bronzes, beads, textiles What could be made; composition and structure Production debris Slag, crucibles, retorts, kiln remains How and on what scale things were made; dates Mining remains Workings at Zawar, Rajpura–Dariba, Khetri, Hutti Sources of raw materials; dates Texts Arthaśāstra, gem treatises, rasa texts Classifications, terminology, some processes, ideas Observers’ accounts Xuanzang, al-Bīrūnī, Tavernier, Buchanan, Voysey Practices at particular times and places Ethnography Elwin on the Agaria; studies of living crafts Practices surviving into modern times Laboratory analysis Metallography, chemical and isotopic analysis Composition, microstructure, provenance, date

The methods by which production debris, mine workings and objects are analysed are explained in Section 4.5. The strongest conclusions come where several kinds of evidence agree—for example, where travellers’ descriptions of crucible steel making, excavated crucibles and the analysis of steel ingots tell the same story. Texts alone are a weak guide to practice, and analysis alone cannot recover the meanings that materials had for their makers.

docs.title: 15.6 Connections to Modern Chemistry
docs.text:
Did Indian chemical knowledge contribute to modern chemistry? The honest answer is: in specific ways, and mostly indirectly.

  • European study of wootz in the early 19th century contributed to the understanding of carbon in steel (Chapter 6).

  • European attempts to reproduce Indian mordant-dyed cottons stimulated the growth of textile printing and dye chemistry in the 18th century (Chapter 11).

  • Indian indigo was the most important natural dye of the 19th century, and the research that led to its synthesis was central to the German dye industry.

  • Indian zinc, steel, saltpetre, borax and other materials were traded internationally and studied by European chemists; Bihar saltpetre in particular was a principal source of nitre for Britain in the period when European chemists made nitre central to their study of combustion (Chapter 13).

Modern chemistry, however, developed in 17th–19th-century Europe from its own sources, including European alchemy and pharmacy. There is no evidence that Sanskrit alchemical texts influenced it. Claims that the rasa texts anticipated the conservation of mass, stoichiometry, catalysis or coordination chemistry rest on reading modern concepts into texts that do not contain them.

docs.title: 15.7 Against Presentism
docs.text:
Several modern ways of describing the Indian tradition deserve particular caution.

“Ancient nanotechnology” Bhasmas and Damascus blades contain very small particles or structures, but their makers did not and could not aim at nanostructures. Calling them nanotechnology misdescribes both the past and the present (Chapters 6 and 9). “Green chemistry” Traditional processes used renewable fuels and plant materials because those were what was available, and some were highly polluting or dangerous to workers (mercury vapour, lead fumes, charcoal-driven deforestation). They are not models of sustainable industry merely because they are old. “Validated by science” When modern analysis confirms that the Delhi pillar resists corrosion, it validates a material, not a theory. When analysis shows that a bhasma contains fine particles, it does not validate the claims made for it as a medicine. “First in the world” Priority claims are often wrong, and always provisional. They also distract attention from what is genuinely interesting: how particular communities solved particular problems with the means available to them.

docs.title: 15.8 Rasaśāstra Today
docs.text:
The present status of rasaśāstra—as a college subject, an industry and a regulated class of medicines—and the toxicological evidence about its products were set out in Chapter 9. Research in Indian institutions has focused on the characterisation and standardisation of these products and on their safety in animals (Kumar et al. 2006; Chaudhari et al. 2016), and some of it has been critical of quality.

Health and Safety Note

Metal-containing traditional medicines remain a recognised cause of lead, mercury and arsenic poisoning in India and abroad (Kales and Saper 2009). Nothing in this book is a recommendation to use them; see the full note in Section 1.1.

The contemporary debate is often framed as a conflict between “tradition” and “Western science”. It need not be. The authors of the rasa texts were themselves concerned with the dangers of metals and devised tests to guard against them; modern toxicology offers better tests. Practitioners and regulators in India have increasingly accepted that metal-containing products must meet modern safety standards, and that claims of efficacy require properly designed clinical trials. Respect for the tradition is compatible with—indeed requires—subjecting it to the best available evidence.

docs.title: 15.9 Caste, Gender and the Ownership of Knowledge
docs.text:
The history of Indian chemistry and metallurgy is also a history of who was allowed to know, to write and to profit. The Sanskrit texts were composed by and for literate men of high status: physicians, ascetics, officials, connoisseurs. The smelters, smiths, miners, dyers, potters and bead-makers who carried out most of the processes described in this volume belonged to hereditary occupational groups whose status in the Brahmanical order ranged from respectable to untouchable. Some iron-smelting and leather-working communities were treated as polluting; forest communities such as the Agaria and Asur were marginal to the agrarian order altogether. As P. C. Ray observed, the separation of learning from manual work was one reason why practical knowledge so rarely entered the learned literature (Ray 1902–1909).

Women’s work is especially poorly recorded. Women took part in many crafts—in mining and ore-dressing (Tavernier saw women and children in the diamond diggings), in bead-making and pottery decoration, in spinning and dyeing, in bangle-making—usually as unpaid family labour or as low-paid workers (Tavernier 1889). In the rasa texts women appear chiefly in ritual roles, and the texts’ theory of sulphur as the Goddess’s generative fluid reflects a male-authored symbolism rather than women’s own knowledge. The modern glass bangle industry of Firozabad, with its home-based women and child workers, shows that these patterns are not only historical.

Recognising this does not diminish the achievements described in this book; it attributes them to the people who made them. A history of Indian chemistry that celebrated the Delhi pillar while ignoring the smelters who made the iron, or the kalamkari while ignoring the dyers, would repeat the very separation of knowledge from labour that Ray regretted.

docs.title: 15.10 Craft Knowledge, Colonial Rule and Decline
docs.text:
Many of the industries discussed in this volume declined in the 19th century: iron smelting, crucible steel, zinc distillation, natural indigo, hand-printed cottons. Colonial rule played a large part—through tariffs and market policies favouring British manufactures, forest laws restricting charcoal, the coercive organisation of indigo cultivation, and the general subordination of the Indian economy. Other causes were global: the industrial production of iron, steel and zinc, the synthesis of dyes, and changes in warfare and fashion affected traditional producers everywhere (Riello 2013; Balfour-Paul 1998; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

Colonial officials and scientists also produced much of our documentation of these industries: Buchanan, Voysey and Heath on steel; the gazetteers and economic surveys; the first chemical analyses. Earlier still, the Mughal administration had recorded the work of its mints and workshops in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Chapter 8), a reminder that the documentation of Indian crafts did not begin with colonial rule. Their records are indispensable, even when written from the perspective of a ruling power interested in Indian resources.

docs.title: 15.11 Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property
docs.text: Since the 1990s, Indian institutions have sought to protect traditional knowledge from inappropriate patenting. Two cases became famous: a United States patent on the use of turmeric for wound healing, revoked in 1997 after the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) showed that the use was documented in old Indian texts; and a European patent on a neem-based fungicide, revoked after opposition proceedings. In response the Government of India created the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), which records formulations from classical Āyurvedic, Unani, Siddha and Yoga texts in a form that patent examiners can consult as prior art. Documenting a formulation as traditional knowledge, it should be noted, does not imply that it is safe or effective.

docs.title: 15.12 Teaching the History of Indian Chemistry
docs.text:
The National Education Policy of 2020 encourages the inclusion of Indian knowledge traditions in education. The history of chemistry and metallurgy is a natural subject for this: it connects the laboratory with the museum and the archaeological site, and it shows students how scientific methods can be used to investigate the past. Good teaching in this field would:

  • use case studies with strong evidence—the Delhi pillar, Zawar, crucible steel, Indo-Pacific beads, indigo and kalamkari;

  • distinguish clearly between what texts claim and what evidence shows;

  • place Indian developments in a comparative frame, alongside Chinese, Islamic and European ones;

  • include the craftspeople, and the social hierarchies that shaped who was allowed to know and to write;

  • treat the medical uses of metals with the safety warnings they require.

docs.title: 15.13 Where to See the Evidence
docs.text:
Much of the material discussed in this volume can be seen in museums and at sites in India and abroad.

Sites The iron pillar stands in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi. The Dhar pillar fragments are at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh. Ancient mine workings and retort heaps survive at Zawar near Udaipur. Harappan sites with museums include Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat; Kodumanal and Keezhadi in Tamil Nadu have been the subject of recent excavations by the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, whose reports have dated the urban levels of Keezhadi to the 6th century BCE and later (Sivanantham and Seran 2019). Indian museums The National Museum, New Delhi, holds Harappan material, including the bronze “dancing girl” from Mohenjo-daro, and a major collection of bronzes and arms. The Government Museum, Chennai, has one of the finest collections of South Indian bronzes. The Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya in Mumbai, the Indian Museum in Kolkata and the Salar Jung Museum in Hyderabad hold metalwork, arms, Bidri, jade and textiles. The Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad has outstanding painted and printed cottons. Museums abroad The British Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum (which holds the jade wine cup of Shāh Jahān and large textile and metalwork collections) and Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery (the Sultanganj Buddha) in Britain, and many museums in Europe, North America and Southeast Asia, hold Indian metalwork, arms and textiles, many of them acquired in the colonial period.

The presence of so many objects abroad raises questions of history and ownership that are now widely discussed. For the historian of technology, wherever they are, the objects themselves—examined with the methods described in this volume—remain the primary evidence.

docs.title: 15.14 Open Questions
docs.text:
1. The beginnings of iron. How early, and where, did regular iron smelting begin in South Asia? The claims of very early dates from Tamil Nadu (Chapter 5) need full publication and independent testing.

  2. Crucible steel. When did crucible steel first appear in South Asia, and how were the South Asian and Central Asian traditions related?

  3. The rasa texts. Few rasa texts have critical editions or reliable translations, and their chronology remains uncertain. Philological work is needed before their history can be written with confidence.

  4. Transmission. Were the Indian, Chinese and Islamic alchemical traditions historically connected, and if so how? Did Indian zinc technology influence China or Europe?

  5. Indo-Persian sources. The Persian literature on alchemy, pharmacy and materials written or copied in India is largely unstudied. Its relationship to the rasa texts, and the history of Unani kushtas, could change our picture of how the two traditions met (Chapter 14).

  6. Salts and acids. When and where were mineral acids first prepared in India, and what were the drāvakas of the late texts? The 19th-century descriptions of saltpetre, alum, sal ammoniac and borax production deserve to be compared with surviving practice and with archaeological evidence (Chapter 13).

  7. Craft documentation. Many traditional metallurgical, ceramic and dyeing practices survive only among elderly practitioners and should be recorded before they disappear.

  8. Safety. The heavy-metal content of traditional medicines and cosmetics, and its health effects, need continued monitoring; any therapeutic claims require properly designed trials.

docs.title: 15.15 Concluding Reflections
docs.text:
The history surveyed in this volume is one of skill, ingenuity and persistence: of smelters who forged a six-tonne pillar that has stood for sixteen centuries, of zinc distillers at Zawar who produced the metal on an industrial scale some centuries before the earliest dated Chinese production and long before European, of dyers whose cottons clothed much of the world, and of alchemists who handled mercury and sulphur with remarkable practical command. It is also a history of hierarchy, in which those who did the work were seldom those who wrote the books, and of danger, in which toxic metals were taken as medicines and continue to be taken today.

To study this history well is to hold both sides in view. The achievements need no exaggeration, and the dangers need no concealment. The materials themselves—the slag heaps of Zawar, the crucibles of the Deccan, the iron of the Delhi pillar, the faded kalamkari in museum stores—remain the most reliable witnesses, and modern science, used carefully, allows them to tell their story.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the practical achievements listed at the start of this chapter, each attested by archaeology and analysis; P. C. Ray’s foundation of the subject; and the specific, mostly indirect routes by which Indian materials entered the history of modern chemistry. Debated: the causes of the 19th-century decline of the crafts, and the weight of colonial policy among them; the safety of metal medicines; and how the knowledge of craftspeople—often of low caste status, and often women—can be recovered from a record written by others.

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text:
The dates below are approximate. Many, especially those of the Sanskrit rasa texts, are disputed; where opinion varies, a broad range is given. Dates for archaeological sites rest on radiocarbon determinations whose calibration and context are often debated.

Date Event, site or text c. 7000–5000 BCE Early farming villages at Mehrgarh (Baluchistan); early pottery; copper beads c. 2600–1900 BCE Mature Harappan (Indus) civilisation: copper and bronze, lost-wax casting, faience, stoneware bangles, etched and long carnelian beads c. 1500–1200 BCE Core of the Ṛgveda; ayas (metal, probably copper/bronze) and hiraṇya (gold) 2nd millennium BCE Early iron in the central Ganga plain and Vindhyas (Malhar, Raja Nal-ka-tila; dates of c. 1800–1500 BCE claimed and debated) and in the Deccan (Hallur) c. 1200–500 BCE Later Vedic texts; “black metal” (kṛṣṇāyas, iron) named c. 1200–600 BCE Painted Grey Ware; early glass in the Ganga plain c. 700–200 BCE Northern Black Polished Ware c. 5th–2nd c. BCE Punch-marked silver coinage 1st millennium BCE Mining of lead–zinc–silver ores at Zawar and Rajpura–Dariba (Rajasthan) c. 3rd c. BCE onwards Crucible steel in south India (Kodumanal and other sites); in Sri Lanka from the 1st millennium CE c. 4th c. BCE–1st c. CE Earliest radiocarbon-dated iron-smelting slag in the Khasi Hills, Meghalaya c. 50 BCE–300 CE Arthaśāstra in its present form (traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya, c. 300 BCE) 1st c. CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea: Indian iron, steel and indigo in Indian Ocean trade; docs.title: Guide to Further Reading
docs.text: This guide points to the works that are most useful as starting points. Full details are given in the Select Bibliography.

docs.title: General surveys
docs.text: The classic survey of Indian chemistry is P. C. Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry (Ray 1902–1909), best used in the revised edition by Priyadaranjan Ray (Ray 1956); its datings and some attributions need correction from later work. A Concise History of Science in India (Bose et al. 1971) contains chapters on chemistry and metallurgy. Arun Kumar Biswas and Sulekha Biswas’s Minerals and Metals in Ancient India (Biswas and Biswas 1996) gathers textual and archaeological evidence. D. P. Agrawal’s Ancient Metal Technology and Archaeology of South Asia (Agrawal 2000) is a convenient archaeological overview, and Paul Craddock’s Early Metal Mining and Production (Craddock 1995) places Indian mining and smelting in world perspective. The chemistry volume of the History of Science, Philosophy and Culture in Indian Civilization, edited by B. V. Subbarayappa (Subbarayappa 1999), is the fullest modern collaborative survey.

docs.title: Rasaśāstra and alchemy
docs.text: David Gordon White’s The Alchemical Body (White 1996) is the essential study of rasaśāstra in its Tantric and Siddha context, with a careful discussion of the chronology of the texts. G. J. Meulenbeld’s History of Indian Medical Literature (Meulenbeld 1999–2002) is the indispensable bibliographical guide to individual texts, authors and dates. Dominik Wujastyk’s article on the “ghost” Rasaratnākara (Wujastyk 1984) is a model of how attributions can be tested, and his Roots of Āyurveda (Wujastyk 2003) offers translated selections from the classical medical texts. Bhagwan Dash’s Alchemy and Metallic Medicines in Ayurveda (Dash 1986) presents the subject from a practitioner’s standpoint. For comparison with European and Arabic alchemy, Lawrence Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (Principe 2013) is an excellent introduction. Barbara Gerke’s study of Tibetan mercury processing (Gerke 2013) and Richard Weiss’s book on Siddha medicine (Weiss 2009) cover two related traditions. For the texts themselves, the Rasārṇava was edited by P. C. Ray and Hariśchandra Kaviratna (Ray and Kaviratna 1908–1910), and the Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdayatantra and the Rasaratnasamuccaya can be read in the GRETIL electronic texts cited in Chapters 2 and 3 (GRETIL 2020a, 2020b). Kamil Zvelebil’s The Siddha Quest for Immortality (Zvelebil 1996) and Richard Weiss’s Recipes for Immortality (Weiss 2009) introduce the Tamil Siddha tradition, and Barbara Gerke’s Taming the Poisonous (Gerke 2021) is the fullest study of mercury in Tibetan medicine.

docs.title: Safety of metal-containing medicines
docs.text: The studies by Saper and colleagues in JAMA (Saper et al. 2004, 2008) are the most widely cited surveys of heavy metals in Ayurvedic products. Ernst’s review (Ernst 2002), the report of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004) and the editorial by Kales and Saper (Kales and Saper 2009) document poisoning cases. On the toxicology of cinnabar, see Liu and colleagues (Liu et al. 2008). For the Indian laboratory and animal studies that defend the products, see for example Kumar and colleagues on the composition of bhasmas (Kumar et al. 2006), Chaudhari and colleagues on the toxicity of copper bhasma in rats (Chaudhari et al. 2016) and the review by Kamath and colleagues (Kamath et al. 2012).

docs.title: Mining and archaeometallurgy
docs.text: Paul Craddock’s Early Metal Mining and Production (Craddock 1995) is a general account of pre-industrial mining with much Indian material, and the survey of the Rajasthan mines by Willies and colleagues (Willies et al. 1984) describes the best-dated ancient workings in South Asia. V. Ball’s Economic Geology (Ball 1881) records the old workings and slag heaps known to 19th-century geologists. For the methods of archaeometallurgy, Killick and Fenn’s review (Killick and Fenn 2012) is a concise introduction, Pollard and Heron’s Archaeological Chemistry (Pollard and Heron 2008) explains the analytical techniques, including lead isotopes, and Bachmann’s handbook (Bachmann 1982) remains the standard guide to the identification of slags; Rehren and Pernicka (Rehren and Pernicka 2008) review the development of the field, including lead isotope provenancing. Srinivasan’s study of South Indian images (Srinivasan 1999) applies these methods to Indian bronzes. On the discoloration of the Taj Mahal see Bergin and colleagues (Bergin et al. 2015).

docs.title: Iron and steel
docs.text: On the beginnings of iron, see Chakrabarti’s Early Use of Iron in India (Chakrabarti 1992) and Tewari’s report of early dates from the Ganga plain (Tewari 2003). R. Balasubramaniam’s Delhi Iron Pillar: New Insights (Balasubramaniam 2002) and his paper in Corrosion Science (Balasubramaniam 2000) are the standard accounts of the pillar; T. R. Anantharaman’s The Rustless Wonder (Anantharaman 1996) is a readable earlier study. Verrier Elwin’s The Agaria (Elwin 1942) remains the classic ethnography of iron-smelters. For Sri Lanka, see Juleff’s work (Juleff 1996, 1998). On the Khasi Hills, see Yule’s early description (Yule 1842) and the radiocarbon study by Prokop and Suliga (Prokop and Suliga 2013); the Tamil Nadu dates of 2025 are published in Rajan and Sivanantham’s report (Rajan and Sivanantham 2025).

docs.title: Crucible steel
docs.text: Sharada Srinivasan and Srinivasa Ranganathan’s India’s Legendary Wootz Steel (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004) is the best general account; Bennet Bronson’s article (Bronson 1986) surveys the historical sources. On the metallurgy of the watered pattern, see Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch (Verhoeven et al. 1998), Wadsworth and Sherby (Wadsworth and Sherby 1980) and Cyril Stanley Smith’s History of Metallography (Smith 1960). Rehren and Papachristou compare South Asian and Central Asian crucibles (Rehren and Papachristou 2003).

docs.title: Zinc, lead and silver
docs.text: The Zawar work is published in Craddock, Gurjar and Hegde’s article (Craddock et al. 1983), in the British Museum volume 2000 Years of Zinc and Brass (Craddock 1998) and, most fully, in Craddock’s Early Indian Metallurgy (Craddock 2017).

docs.title: Bronze, images and the precious metals
docs.text: On Harappan metallurgy see Kenoyer and Miller (Kenoyer and Miller 1999) and Kenoyer’s Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (Kenoyer 1998). Srinivasan and Glover describe the high-tin bronzes of Kerala (Srinivasan and Glover 1995), and Vidya Dehejia’s exhibition catalogue introduces the Chola bronzes (Dehejia 2002). Meera Mukherjee’s Metalcraftsmen of India (Mukherjee 1978) describes the living crafts.

docs.title: Gems
docs.text: Louis Finot’s Les lapidaires indiens (Finot 1896) edits and translates the Sanskrit gem treatises; M. Ramakrishna Bhat’s translation of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (Bhat 1981–1982) includes Varāhamihira’s gem chapters. Tavernier’s Travels (Tavernier 1889) describes the diamond mines, and Dalrymple and Anand’s book on the Koh-i-Noor (Dalrymple and Anand 2017) separates its history from its legends.

docs.title: Glass, beads, dyes and textiles
docs.text: Julian Henderson’s Ancient Glass (Henderson 2013) and the article by Dussubieux and colleagues (Dussubieux et al. 2010) cover glass composition; Peter Francis’s Asia’s Maritime Bead Trade (Francis 2002) and the Arikamedu report (Begley et al. 1996) deal with beads. On indigo, see Jenny Balfour-Paul’s Indigo (Balfour-Paul 1998) and, for the Bengal indigo disturbances, Blair Kling’s The Blue Mutiny (Kling 1966). Giorgio Riello’s Cotton (Riello 2013) sets Indian dyed textiles in the history of global trade.

docs.title: Other chemical crafts
docs.text: For the Harappan vitreous crafts, Kenoyer’s Ancient Cities (Kenoyer 1998) and Massimo Vidale’s Archaeology of Indus Crafts (Vidale 2000) are the best introductions. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (Watt 1889) and his later Commercial Products of India (Watt 1908) remain the fullest sources for the 19th-century production of salts, alkalis, alum, sal ammoniac, borax and saltpetre. On the saltpetre trade see Om Prakash’s study of the Dutch company in Bengal (Prakash 1985) and James Frey’s article (Frey 2009); Irfan Habib’s Technology in Medieval India (Habib 2008) surveys the technologies of the Sultanate and Mughal periods. On distillation see Allchin’s article (Allchin 1979), R. J. Forbes’s Short History of the Art of Distillation (Forbes 1948) and the volume of Science and Civilisation in China on chemical apparatus (Needham et al. 1980); on gunpowder and saltpetre, Iqtidar Alam Khan’s Gunpowder and Firearms (Khan 2004); on sugar, Christian Daniels’s volume in Science and Civilisation in China (Daniels 1996). On perfumery and its literature, see James McHugh’s Sandalwood and Carrion (McHugh 2012). The first book of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873), with its chapters on the mint, the origin and specific gravity of metals, saltpetre, spirits and perfumes, and al-Bīrūnī’s India (Sachau 1888) are rich primary sources for the medieval and early modern periods.

docs.title: Islamic alchemy and Indo-Persian sources
docs.text: Principe’s Secrets of Alchemy (Principe 2013) introduces Arabic alchemy and its transmission to Europe, and Pormann and Savage-Smith’s Medieval Islamic Medicine (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007) the medical and pharmaceutical context, including the translation of Indian works. Ibn al-Nadīm’s Fihrist, in Bayard Dodge’s translation (Ibn al-Nadīm 1970), records the Indian books known in Abbasid Baghdad. Al-Hassan and Hill’s Islamic Technology (al-Hassan and Hill 1986) describes distillation and chemical industry in the Islamic world, and Berthold Laufer’s Sino-Iranica (Laufer 1919) remains useful on the names and trade of sal ammoniac, borax and other substances. Seema Alavi’s Islam and Healing (Alavi 2008) treats the Indo-Muslim medical tradition. Jahāngīr’s memoirs are available in Thackston’s translation (Thackston 1999). Al-Bīrūnī’s books on precious stones and on pharmacy are available in the English translations edited by Hakim Mohammad Said (al-Bīrūnī, Abū Rayḥān 1989, 1973).

docs.title: Modern chemistry in India
docs.text: P. C. Ray’s autobiography (Ray 1932) is the best source for his life and for the beginnings of the chemical industry in Bengal. David Arnold’s Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India (Arnold 2000) and Deepak Kumar’s Science and the Raj (Kumar 1995) place Indian science in its colonial setting, and Gyan Prakash’s Another Reason (Prakash 1999) discusses the nationalist uses of the history of Indian science, including Ray’s.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms are Sanskrit unless marked (Ta. = Tamil, Ka. = Kannada, Te. = Telugu, Pe. = Persian, Ar. = Arabic, Hi. = Hindi). Glosses give the meaning in the texts discussed; identifications of minerals with modern species are often uncertain and are marked “usually identified as”.

Term Meaning abhraka Mica; one of the mahārasas of the rasa texts adhaḥpātana “Downward fall”: distillation in which the vapour is led downwards to a cooler receiver āgama Traditional scripture; in rasa texts, the authority of the teaching lineage ajrakh (Hi.) Block-printed cotton of Sindh and Kutch, resist-printed and mordant-dyed on both sides, usually with indigo and madder ākara A mine; also khani ākarādhyakṣa Superintendent of mines in the Arthaśāstra amlavarga “Sour class”: sour fruits, plant juices and fermented liquids used as reagents in the rasa texts anbīq (Ar.) The head of a still, which condenses the vapour and leads it to a receiver; English “alembic” añjana Collyrium; also a mineral (usually identified as stibnite or galena) used for eye-cosmetics anupāna Vehicle or after-drink with which a medicine is taken apunarbhava “Not becoming again”: the rasa texts’ test that a calcined metal should not revert to metal ʿaraq (Ar.–Pe.) “Sweat”: a distillate; distilled water (Unani ʿaraqiyāt) or spirit (English “arrack”) arka In later texts, a distillate of plant material (after Arabic ʿaraq) aṣṭādaśa saṃskāra The eighteen “processings” of mercury in the rasa texts aṣṭadhātu “Eight metals”: an alloy named in later texts and craft usage for images audbhida “Sprung from the ground”: salt obtained from saline earth ayas In the Ṛgveda, metal (probably copper or bronze); later, iron bandha “Binding”: the fixation of mercury, making it non-volatile or solid bandhani (Hi.) Tie-dyeing: cloth bound tightly with thread at many points so that the bound areas resist the dye bhapkā (Hi.) The receiving vessel of the Kannauj attar still, containing sandalwood oil bhasma “Ash”: a calcined preparation of a metal or mineral bhāvanā Wet grinding of a substance with a plant juice or decoction Bidri (Hi.) Inlaid ware of a blackened zinc alloy, named after Bidar cāraṇa “Feeding”: in the mercury saṃskāras, making mercury absorb other substances centūram (Ta.) A red calcined or sublimed preparation in Siddha medicine cūlikālavaṇa “Hearth salt”: a synonym of navasāra, sal ammoniac dabu (Hi.) A resist paste of mud, gum and lime used in the block printing of Bagru and other Rajasthan centres deg (Hi.) The copper boiling vessel of the Kannauj attar still dehavāda “Doctrine of the body”: the alchemical aim of transforming the body dhātu Metal; in medicine, a bodily tissue dhātuvāda “Doctrine of metals”: alchemy aimed at transmuting metals ḍolāyantra “Swing apparatus”: a bundle suspended in a heated liquid drāvaka “Solvent”: in late texts, distilled liquids said to dissolve shells and metals, possibly mineral acids gandhaka Sulphur garbhadruti “Internal liquefaction”: a mercury saṃskāra haritāla Orpiment (arsenic trisulphide) hiṅgula Cinnabar (mercuric sulphide) iksīr (Ar.) Elixir; the transmuting or life-giving agent of Arabic alchemy jāraṇa “Digestion”: making mercury absorb other substances, especially metals jīvanmukti “Liberation in life”; in the rasa texts, liberation attained in a body made imperishable by mercury kāca Glass kajjalī “Lamp-black”: the black product of grinding mercury with sulphur (black mercuric sulphide) kalamkari (Pe.) “Pen-work” (from Persian qalam, pen): mordant-painted and printed cotton kalmī shorā (Hi.) Refined, recrystallised saltpetre, in long prismatic crystals kāṃsya Bronze; bell-metal kāñjika Sour fermented rice gruel, used as an acid reagent kāṅkṣī Alum (also sphaṭikā; Hindi phiṭkarī) kāsīsa Green vitriol (iron sulphate) khalva Mortar for grinding khani A mine (also ākara) kīmiyā (Ar.–Pe.) Alchemy; in modern Urdu and Arabic, chemistry koṣṭhī Furnace kṣāra Caustic or alkaline substance, especially the alkali made from plant ash kṣāratraya The “three alkalis” of the later rasa texts: yavakṣāra, sarjikākṣāra and borax kushta (Pe.) “Killed”: a calcined metallic or mineral preparation of Indian Unani pharmacy lākṣā Lac, the resinous secretion of the lac insect, source of a red dye lakṣaṇādhyakṣa Superintendent of the mint in the Arthaśāstra lavaṇa Salt, especially common salt loha Metal in general; specifically iron lohādhyakṣa Superintendent of metals in the Arthaśāstra madhūcchiṣṭa Beeswax; madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhāna, the lost-wax method of casting images mahārasa “Great rasa”: a class of minerals in the rasa texts manaḥśilā Realgar (arsenic sulphide) mañjiṣṭhā Indian madder (Rubia cordifolia), a red dye māraṇa “Killing”: calcination of a metal or mineral multānī miṭṭī (Hi.) Fuller’s earth, an absorbent clay used for cleaning, including the cleaning of marble mūrchana “Swooning”: a mercury saṃskāra in which mercury loses its fluidity mūṣā Crucible nāga Lead navaratna The “nine gems” of medieval astrological and ornamental usage navasāra Sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride; also navasādara; Hindi nausādar) nīla Indigo; also blue sapphire (indranīla) pañcaloha “Five metals”: a name for alloys used for images pārada Mercury parpam (Ta.) A calcined powder of Siddha pharmacy pātana Distillation or sublimation (upward, downward or lateral) peori (Hi.) “Indian yellow”, a pigment made, according to an account of 1883, from the urine of cows fed on mango leaves piṇḍadhāraṇa “Preserving the body”: in the Rasārṇava, the aim attained by mercury and breath-control piṣṭi A finely ground (not calcined) preparation, e.g. of pearl or coral puṭa Heating in a closed vessel set in a pit of burning fuel; the size of the pit and fuel defines named grades qalaʿī (Ar.–Pe.) Tinning of copper and brass vessels qarʿ (Ar.) The boiling vessel (cucurbit) of a still rasa Juice, essence, taste; in the rasa texts, mercury rasaka A mineral of the rasa texts, usually identified as calamine (zinc ore) rasakarpūra “Mercury-camphor”: a white mercurial sublimate, usually identified as a mercury chloride rasaśālā Alchemical laboratory rasaśāstra The science of mercury: Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry rasasindūra A red sublimed mercuric sulphide preparation rasāyana Rejuvenation therapy, one of the eight branches of Āyurveda; also, by extension, alchemy ratnaparīkṣā The examination of gems; title of several gem treatises reh (Hi.) White saline efflorescence of north Indian soils, a natural source of soda rīti Brass sajjī (Hi.) Crude soda made from the ash of plants of saline ground saṃskāra Processing, refinement śarāvasampuṭa Two shallow earthen dishes sealed rim to rim, in which a substance is heated in a puṭa sarjikākṣāra Crude soda from plant ash (Hindi sajjī) sattva “Essence”: a metal extracted from a mineral by heating sauvarcala A salt of the medical texts, of uncertain identity, often taken to be a black salt ṣayrafī (Ar.–Pe.) Assayer, especially of the Mughal mint shorā (Hi.) Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) siddha A perfected being; in Tamil, cittar, the authors of Siddha medical and yogic poetry śilājatu A dark exudate from Himalayan rocks (shilajit) śodhana “Purification”: the preliminary processing of a metal, mineral or poison sphaṭikā Alum; to be distinguished from sphaṭika, rock crystal sthapati Architect or master image-maker; the hereditary bronze-casters of Swamimalai sudhā Lime; lime plaster or stucco (the word also means “nectar”) surkhī (Hi.–Pe.) Crushed burnt brick added to lime to make a partly hydraulic mortar sūryakṣāra In late texts, saltpetre (Hindi shorā) sūta Mercury (“that which brings forth”, in the etymology of the rasa texts) suvarṇa Gold svedana “Sweating”: steaming, the first mercury saṃskāra tāmra Copper ṭaṅkaṇa Borax, a flux for metals (English “tincal”) tezāb (Hi.–Pe.) “Sharp water”: acid, especially nitric acid tīkṣṇa loha “Sharp iron”: steel tuttha Blue vitriol (copper sulphate) ukku (Ka., Te.) Steel; source of the English “wootz” uparasa “Secondary rasa”: a class of minerals in the rasa texts ūrdhvapātana Upward sublimation or distillation urukku (Ta.) Steel (literally “melted”), cognate with Kannada and Telugu ukku ūsar (Hi.) Barren saline or alkaline land of the Ganga plain, on which reh forms vaikrānta A mineral of the rasa texts, of uncertain identity vajra Diamond; thunderbolt vajralepa “Adamantine plaster”: a glue of boiled plant materials and resins described in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, used as an adhesive and coating vaṅga Tin vāritara “Floating on water”: a test of fineness for calcined preparations vātam (Ta.) Alchemy in the Tamil Siddha tradition vedha “Piercing”: transmutation of a base metal by processed mercury yantra Apparatus yaśada Zinc (also jasada) yavakṣāra “Barley alkali”: potash from plant ash
